7
Demystifying LLM Theory,
Design, and
Implementation
In this chapter, we delve deep into the intricate world of LLMs and the
underpinning mathematical concepts that fuel their performance. The
advent of these models has revolutionized the field of natural language
processing (NLP), offering unparalleled proficiency in understanding,
generating, and interacting with human language.
As we explore the operations of LLMs, we will introduce the key metric of
perplexity, a measurement of uncertainty that is pivotal in determining the
performance of these models. A lower perplexity indicates the confidence
that a language model (LM) has in predicting the next word in a sequence,
thus showcasing its proficiency. Adding to that, while perplexity remains an
important indicator of a model’s confidence during training, recent modern
LLMs are evaluated using a range of new benchmarks, measuring not only
language modeling ability, but also reasoning, factuality, safety, and
robustness. We will introduce these new evaluation standards later in the
chapter.
This chapter draws on multiple insightful publications that delve into the
mathematical insights of LLMs. These include A Neural Probabilistic
Language Model, Attention is All You Need, and PaLM: Scaling Language
Modeling with Pathways. These sources will guide us in understanding the
robust mechanisms that underpin LLMs and their exceptional capabilities.
With a comprehensive understanding of the mathematical foundations of
LLMs, we will gain a robust knowledge of these advanced AI systems,
paving the way for future innovations and advancements in the field.
Finally, we will discuss the detailed architecture and design of the most
recent models, including the recent GPTs from OpenAI, the Claude 4
family, and Gemini, alongside open source advancements such as Llama,
DeepSeek, and the Mistral family.
Now, let’s look at the topics covered in this chapter:
What are LLMs and how are they different from LMs?
Motivations for developing and using LLMs
Challenges in developing LLMs
Current state-of-the-art LLMs
Evaluation metrics and methods
Technical requirements
For this chapter, you are expected to possess a solid foundation in ML
concepts, particularly in the areas of Transformers and reinforcement
learning. An understanding of Transformer-based models, which underpin
many of today’s LLMs, is vital. This includes familiarity with concepts
such as self-attention mechanisms, positional encoding, and the structure of
encoder-decoder architectures.
Familiarity with concepts such as policy gradients, reward functions, and
Q-learning will greatly enhance your comprehension of this content.
Lastly, coding proficiency, specifically in Python, is crucial. This is because
many of the concepts will be demonstrated and explored through the lens of
programming. Experience with PyTorch or TensorFlow, popular ML
libraries, and Hugging Face’s Transformers library, a key resource for
working with transformer models, will also be beneficial.
However, don’t be discouraged if you feel you’re lacking in some areas.
This chapter aims to walk you through the complexities of these subjects,
bridging any knowledge gaps along the way. So, come prepared with a
mindset for learning, and let’s delve into the fascinating world of LLMs!
What are LLMs and how are
they different from LMs?
A LM is a type of machine learning model that learns a probability
distribution over sequences of tokens, such as words, subwords, or
characters. Depending on the model architecture and training objective, this
may involve predicting the next token in a sequence, reconstructing masked
tokens, or estimating token probabilities given surrounding context. By
learning these statistical patterns from large text corpora, language models
are able to generate fluent text that follows learned linguistic structures and
styles.
Before the advent of Transformer-based models such as generative
pretrained Transformers (GPTs) and Bidirectional Encoder
Representations from Transformers (BERT), there were several other
types of LMs widely used in NLP tasks. Let’s discuss a few of them:
n-gram models: These are some of the simplest LMs. An n-gram
model uses the (n-1) previous words to predict the nth word in a
sentence. For example, in a bigram (2-gram) model, we would use the
previous word to predict the next word. These models are easy to
implement and computationally efficient, but they typically don’t
perform as well as more complex models because they don’t capture
long-range dependencies between words. Their performance also
degrades as n increases, as they suffer from data sparsity issues (not
having enough data to accurately estimate the probabilities for all
possible n-grams).
Hidden Markov models (HMMs): These models consider the
“hidden” states that generate the observed data. In the context of
language modeling, each word would be an observed state, and the
“hidden” state would be some kind of linguistic feature that’s not
directly observable (such as the part of speech of the word). However,
like n-gram models, HMMs struggle to capture long-range
dependencies between words.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs): These are a type of neural
network where connections between nodes form a directed graph along
a temporal sequence. This allows them to use their internal state
(memory) to process sequences of inputs, making them ideal for
language modeling. They can capture long-range dependencies
between words, but they struggle with the so-called vanishing gradient
problem, which makes it difficult to learn these dependencies in
practice.
Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks: An LSTM network is
a special kind of RNN that is designed to learn long-term
dependencies. They do this by using a series of “gates” that control the
flow of information in and out of the memory state of the network.
LSTMs were a big step forward in the state of the art of language
modeling.
Gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks: These are a variation of
LSTMs that use a slightly different set of gates in their architecture.
They’re often simpler and faster to train than LSTMs, but whether they
perform better or worse than LSTMs tends to depend on the specific
task at hand.
Because LLMs are trained via next-token prediction, their performance
during training is traditionally measured using perplexity, a metric we
revisit later in the chapter.
Each of these models has its own strengths and weaknesses, and none of
them are better or worse than the others; it all depends on the specific task
and dataset.
Why LLMs stand out
LLMs are a class of large-scale LMs capable of understanding and
generating human-like language. During pretraining, many LLMs learn by
modeling the probability of token sequences over vast and diverse corpora,
which enables them to capture linguistic structure, factual knowledge, and
contextual relationships.
Through subsequent alignment and instruction tuning, these models go
beyond raw sequence modeling to produce coherent, goal-directed, and
contextually appropriate responses across a wide range of tasks.
LLMs, such as GPT-4.X and Llama, are originally LMs that are trained on a
very large amount of text and have a very large number of parameters. The
larger the model (in terms of parameters and training data), the more
capable it is of understanding and generating complex and varied texts. We
saw this transition from LMs to LLMs in the early 2020’s.
More recently, the definition of LLM has evolved. Beyond sheer scale,
modern LLMs often incorporate advanced architectural innovations, such as
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers for efficiency, or multi-modal
capabilities that allow them to process text, images, and even audio. The
distinction between closed and open source models, as well as the role of
community-driven benchmarks, now also shapes how we assess LLM
progress.
Here are some key differences between LLMs and the smaller LMs:
Data: LLMs are trained on vast amounts of data. This allows them to
learn from a wide range of linguistic patterns, styles, and topics.
Parameters: LLMs have a huge number of parameters. Parameters in
an ML model are the parts of the model that are learned from the
training data. The more parameters a model has, the more complex
patterns it can learn.
Performance: Because they’re trained on more data and have more
parameters, LLMs generally perform better than smaller ones. They’re
capable of generating more coherent and diverse texts, and they’re
better at understanding context, making inferences, and even
answering questions or generating texts on a wide range of topics.
Compute resources: LLMs require a significant amount of
computational resources to train, both in terms of processing power
and memory. They also take longer to train.
Storage and inference time: Large models also require more storage
space, and it takes longer to generate predictions (although this
inference time is still typically quite fast on modern hardware).
Thus, we can say that LLMs are scaled-up versions of smaller LMs.
They’re trained on more data, have more parameters, and are generally
capable of producing higher-quality results, but they also require more
resources to train and use. Besides that, an important advantage of an LLM
is that we can train them unsupervised on a large corpus of data and then
fine-tune them with a limited amount of data for different tasks.
We can now look into one of the core mechanisms of LLMs, the
Transformer.
Transformer models
Transformer models have been at the forefront of the recent wave of LLMs.
They are based on the “Transformer” architecture, which uses self-attention
mechanisms to weigh the relevance of different words in the input when
making predictions. Transformers are a type of neural network architecture
introduced in the paper Attention is All You Need by Vaswani et al. One of
their significant advantages, particularly for training LLMs, is their
suitability for parallel computing.
In traditional RNN models, such as LSTM and GRU, the sequence of
tokens (words, subwords, or characters in the text) must be processed
sequentially. That’s because each token’s representation depends not only
on the token itself but also on the previous tokens in the sequence. The
inherent sequential nature of these models makes it difficult to parallelize
their operations, which can limit the speed and efficiency of the training
process.
Transformers, in contrast, eliminate the necessity for sequential processing
by using a mechanism called self-attention (or scaled dot-product attention).
In the self-attention process, each token’s representation is computed as a
weighted sum of all tokens in the sequence, with the weights determined by
the attention mechanism. Importantly, these computations for each token
are independent of the computations for other tokens, and thus they can be
performed in parallel.
This parallelization capability brings several advantages for training LLMs:
Speed: By parallelizing the computations, Transformers can process
large amounts of data more quickly than RNNs. This speed can
significantly reduce the training time of LLMs, which often need to
process vast amounts of data.
Scalability: Transformers’ parallelization makes it easier to scale up
the model size and the amount of training data. This capability is
crucial for developing LLMs, as these models often benefit from being
trained on larger datasets and having a larger number of parameters.
Long-range dependencies: Transformers can better capture long-
range dependencies between tokens because they consider all tokens in
the sequence simultaneously, rather than processing them one at a
time. This capability is valuable in many language tasks and can
improve the performance of LLMs.
Motivations for developing
and using LLMs
The motivation to develop and use LLMs arises from several factors related
to the capabilities of these models and the potential benefits they can bring
in diverse applications. The following subsections detail a few of these key
motivations.
Improved performance
LLMs, when trained with sufficient data, generally demonstrate far better
performance compared to earlier and smaller models. They are now capable
of understanding context, identifying subtle nuances, and generating
coherent, contextually relevant responses across a wide range of tasks,
spanning text classification, named entity recognition, sentiment analysis,
machine translation, question answering, and text generation.
In the past, model progress was typically measured using the General
Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark, which
evaluates models across a suite of natural language understanding (NLU)
tasks such as sentiment analysis, question answering, and textual
entailment. While GLUE played a pivotal role in advancing NLU research,
recent years have seen a shift toward more challenging and comprehensive
benchmarks that better reflect the capabilities of LLMs.
Today, the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU)
benchmark has emerged as a key standard for comparing state-of-the-art
LLMs. MMLU tests models on a diverse set of academic and professional
subjects, providing a rigorous measure of broad knowledge, reasoning, and
world knowledge. The results in Table 7.1 demonstrate the substantial leap
in performance achieved by leading closed and open source LLMs on this
benchmark.

In addition to MMLU, other modern benchmarks, such as the Graduate-
Level Professional Question Answering (GPQA) benchmark, have been
introduced to evaluate LLMs on advanced reasoning and specialized
knowledge, pushing the boundaries of what these models can achieve.
As the field rapidly evolves, these benchmarks play a central role in
highlighting the remarkable improvements of the latest LLMs over their
predecessors.
Broad generalization
LLMs trained on diverse and expansive datasets can generalize better
across a wide spectrum of tasks, domains, and linguistic styles. Their ability
to absorb patterns from varied data makes them effective not only for
classic NLP tasks, but also for entirely new frontiers. Modern LLMs can
adapt seamlessly to applications ranging from chatbots and information
retrieval to creative writing, document summarization, and technical
question answering.
Crucially, today’s LLMs exhibit generalization capabilities that extend
beyond basic language understanding. The newest models, such as GPT-4.5,
Claude 3.5, Gemini, Llama 3.1, Mistral Large 2, and DeepSeek-V3, have
shown strong proficiency in the following:
Reasoning and logic, including solving complex problems and
performing multi-step deductions
Code generation and software understanding, enabling high-quality
code completion, explanation, and debugging across multiple
programming languages
Multi-modal understanding, where models process not only text, but
also images, tables, and in some cases audio or video
Long-context management, with support for context windows of up
to 1 million tokens, allowing the models to synthesize, summarize, and
reason over large documents or extended conversations
The increased parameter counts and more sophisticated training strategies
of these models enable them to capture and represent more complex
relationships, yielding much greater versatility across both familiar and
novel tasks. As illustrated in Figure 7.1, larger and more capable LLMs
continue to demonstrate superior performance on a variety of benchmarks.
Figure 7.1 – LLMs’ performance based on their size and training

Another major development is the emergence of multi-agent LLM systems,
where multiple specialized LLMs or agents can collaborate, each leveraging
unique strengths or domain knowledge, to tackle complex workflows and
provide more robust, accurate results. This “collaborative AI” paradigm is
opening new doors for real-world applications, from research assistants to
autonomous business processes.
As the field continues to progress, broad generalization is not just about
understanding language, but also about reasoning, integrating multiple
modalities, and orchestrating intelligent systems composed of many
cooperating models.
However, it’s important to note that while larger models tend to be more
generalizable, they also pose challenges such as increased computational
requirements and the risk of overfitting. It is also essential to ensure that the
training data is representative of the tasks and domains the model is
expected to perform in, as models might carry over any biases present in the
training data.
Few-shot learning
The ability of LLMs to learn from just a handful of examples, known as
few-shot learning, was first popularized by models such as GPT-3. Since
then, this capability has advanced dramatically with new generations of
models such as GPT-4, GPT-4.5, Claude 3.5, and Gemini. These state-of-
the-art LLMs now demonstrate not only robust few-shot learning, but also
zero-shot reasoning: solving new problems without any task-specific
examples!
Today’s top models excel at in-context learning across a wide variety of
domains:
Complex reasoning tasks (multi-step logic, symbolic manipulation)
Code generation and debugging
Tool use (API calls, function invocation, integrating with external
systems)
Dialogue safety and alignment (responding appropriately to
adversarial or ambiguous prompts)
This is made possible by massive context windows and improved model
architectures, allowing the LLM to process more information and follow
longer or more nuanced chains of reasoning.
Modern benchmarks specifically evaluate these abilities:
MT-Bench (developed by LMSYS) focuses on multi-turn dialogue
and reasoning, providing an automated and human-rated comparison
of LLMs’ conversational and task-solving skills
Chatbot Arena is a crowd-sourced leaderboard that pits models head-
to-head in blind comparisons, measuring real-world user preferences
and dialogue robustness
Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) and other
leaderboards further assess generalization, robustness, and fairness in
in-context and zero-shot scenarios
A practical advantage of in-context learning is that developers can rapidly
adapt LLMs to new domains or tasks simply by providing a small set of
relevant examples or instructions, without the need for model retraining.
For instance, when using an LLM as a research or coding assistant, you can
“teach” it your preferred style or requirements simply by including those
examples in your prompt.
With these advances, modern LLMs not only perceive the intention from a
few examples, but they can often compete with or surpass domain-specific
models on many reasoning and generation tasks, simply through in-context
adaptation.
Understanding complex
contexts
LLMs excel at understanding complex contexts thanks to their deep neural
architectures, extensive training on diverse data, and ever-increasing
parameter counts. This enables them to comprehend subtle nuances in
topics, styles, and intent, even when reasoning over ambiguous or technical
language.
Recent state-of-the-art models have further advanced these capabilities by
dramatically expanding their context window: the amount of information
they can process in a single interaction. Where earlier models were limited
to just a few thousand tokens, today’s leading LLMs, such as Gemini 1.5,
Claude 3 Sonnet, GPT-4.5, and others, support context windows ranging
from 200,000 to over 1 million tokens. This leap allows these models to
read, synthesize, and summarize entire books, lengthy reports, or multi-
document conversations. It also enables the models to support advanced use
cases such as RAGs, where the LLM can reference and reason over large
external knowledge bases or document collections. Moreover, having such
large context windows lets LLMs maintain continuity across extended
dialogues or complex workflows.
In addition, the newest LLMs are increasingly multi-modal, making them
capable of understanding and generating not just text, but also images,
tables, and even audio. For instance, Gemini 1.5, GPT-4.5, and Claude 3
Sonnet can analyze images and charts, answer questions about them, and
seamlessly blend visual and textual reasoning. This unlocks new
applications in fields such as document analysis, medical imaging, scientific
research, and multimedia content creation.
For example, a modern LLM can now summarize a complicated scientific
article with embedded figures, extract key trends from a financial report, or
assist a user in analyzing both the written and visual content of a technical
manual, all within a single, unified workflow.
By combining long-context understanding and multi-modal processing, the
latest LLMs set a new bar for contextual comprehension, making them
powerful tools for complex real-world tasks.
Multilingual capabilities
Modern LLMs have pushed the boundaries of multilingual understanding,
making it possible to support high-quality language tasks for users around
the globe. Unlike earlier models that focused on translation or single-task
multilinguality, today’s leading LLMs demonstrate robust, near-human-
level performance across dozens or even hundreds of languages, enabling
global applications in research, business, education, and beyond.
State-of-the-art multilingual LLMs include the following:
Gemini 1.5: Excels in cross-lingual tasks, supports over 100
languages, and achieves top scores on multilingual reasoning and
translation benchmarks
GPT-4o: Delivers strong multilingual capabilities, offering high-
quality text generation, understanding, and translation for more than 50
languages, with especially notable improvements in low-resource
languages
Claude 3 models: Demonstrates competitive performance in
multilingual dialogue and comprehension, with strengths in both high-
resource and underrepresented languages
DeepSeek-V3: An open source model showing impressive results in
language generation and translation tasks across many languages
Llama 3 and 4: Open-weight models with advanced multilingual
coverage, achieving parity or near-parity with top closed models on
major benchmarks
Recent models are evaluated on rigorous benchmarks such as FLORES-
200, which measures translation quality across 200 languages, and
XTREME, which assesses cross-lingual understanding and information
retrieval, covering 40 typologically diverse languages. For the first time,
open source models such as Llama 3 and DeepSeek-V3 are rivaling or
exceeding the performance of proprietary models in many languages,
especially for widely spoken or well-resourced languages.
Here are the key leaderboard results:
On FLORES-200, Gemini 1.5, GPT-4o, and Llama 3/4 all achieve
BLEU and COMET scores approaching or matching human-level
performance in translation for many language pairs
On XTREME, Claude 3 and Llama 3/4 demonstrate robust
performance in cross-lingual retrieval, NER, and QA, further closing
the gap between open and closed models
This new era of multilingual LLMs means organizations can deploy global,
language-inclusive applications with confidence, whether leveraging closed
platforms or fully open models. Multilingual LLMs now enable use cases
such as multilingual chatbots, document search, automated translation, and
inclusive digital assistants, supporting a truly global user base.
Human-like text generation
Today’s leading LLMs set a new bar for human-like text generation,
producing responses that are increasingly indistinguishable from those
written by people. They can conduct nuanced conversations, write essays
and technical articles, compose poetry and stories, and even adapt their
style to match a specific user’s preferences or a particular domain.
Recent advances have been validated by large-scale human evaluations:
Benchmarks such as MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena crowdsource and
aggregate direct human ratings for qualities such as coherence, helpfulness,
harmlessness, and creativity. On these leaderboards, models such as GPT-
4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Mistral Large have scored at or near
human-level performance, sometimes even exceeding the ratings given to
expert human annotators in structured tests.
MT-Bench evaluates models across multi-turn conversations, requiring
them to maintain consistency, remember context, and follow nuanced
instructions. Chatbot Arena uses head-to-head “blind” conversations to
collect user preferences, revealing which models users prefer in real-world
dialogue.
Modern LLMs excel not only in single-turn tasks, but also in multi-turn
dialogue, demonstrating memory, reasoning, and contextual awareness over
extended conversations. They can leverage tool use (such as calling APIs or
integrating with databases), generate code, and create structured data (such
as JSON or tables). We will touch on all of those in later chapters, and we
will apply those in code. Also, thanks to multi-modal models such as
Gemini 1.5, GPT-4o, and Claude 3 Sonnet, modern LLMs produce or
interpret images, charts, and even audio.
Risks and considerations
While the progress is remarkable, deploying human-like LLMs comes with
new challenges. These include ensuring the models do not produce
misleading or biased outputs, managing resource and energy demands, and
addressing privacy and safety risks. Research continues into responsible
deployment, model interpretability, and robust evaluation, helping
organizations take full advantage of these generative models while
minimizing potential harm. In the next section, we will expand on risk
causes.

Challenges in developing
LLMs
Developing LLMs poses a unique set of challenges, including but not
limited to handling massive amounts of data, requiring vast computational
resources, and the risk of introducing or perpetuating bias. The following
subsections outline the detailed explanations of these challenges.
Amounts of data
LLMs require enormous amounts of data for training. As the model size
grows, so does the need for diverse, high-quality training data. However,
collecting and curating such large datasets is a challenging task. It can be
time-consuming and expensive. There’s also the risk of inadvertently
including sensitive or inappropriate data in the training set. To have more of
an idea, BERT has been trained using 3.3 billion words from Wikipedia and
BookCorpus. GPT-2 has been trained on 40 GB of text data, and GPT-3 has
been trained on 570 GB of text data. Table 7.3 shows the number of
parameters and the size of training data of a few early LMs.

Recent LLMs such as GPT-4o, Claude 4, and Gemini 2.5 are trained on
corpora estimated at trillions of tokens, collected from multilingual, multi-
modal, and high-quality domain-specific sources. The details are often
proprietary, but the data scale is at least an order of magnitude larger than
earlier LLMs.
Computational resources
Training LLMs requires substantial computational resources. These models
often have billions or even trillions of parameters and need to process vast
amounts of data during training, which requires high-performance hardware
(such as GPUs or TPUs) and a significant amount of time. This can be
costly and could limit the accessibility of developing such models to only
those who have these resources. For example, training GPT-3 took 1 million
GPU hours, which cost around 4.6 million dollars (in 2020). Table 7.4
shows the computational resources and training time of a few early models.
Model Hardware Training time
LLaMA 2048 80G A100 21 days
Bloom 384 80G A100 105 days
GPT-3 1024x A100 34 days
GPT-4 25000 A100 90–100 days
Table 7.4 – The hardware and training time of a few early LMs
Training the latest models, which are more demanding than GPT-4, may
involve tens of thousands of high-end GPUs or TPUs over months, with
compute budgets measured in tens of millions of dollars.
Risk of bias
LLMs can learn and perpetuate biases present in their training data. This
could be explicit bias, such as racial or gender bias in the way language is
used, or more subtle forms of bias, such as the underrepresentation of
certain topics or perspectives. This issue can be challenging to address
because bias in language is a deeply rooted societal issue, and it’s often not
easy to even identify what might be considered bias in a given context.
The scale and diversity of today’s LLMs do help mitigate some forms of
bias, but new risks emerge, especially for languages, dialects, or modalities
that are underrepresented in the training data. Prompt injection, social
engineering, and adversarial prompts can trigger biases or undesirable
behavior.
Model robustness
It’s challenging to ensure that LLMs will perform well in all possible
scenarios, particularly on inputs that differ from their training data. This
includes dealing with ambiguous queries, handling out-of-distribution data,
and ensuring a level of consistency in the responses. Making sure that the
model is not overtrained can help to have a more robust model, but much
more is needed to have a robust model.
Robustness is also challenged by the rise of multi-modal and multi-agent
systems. Ensuring consistent, safe, and reliable outputs when LLMs are
exposed to novel visual or audio inputs, or when collaborating as part of
larger agentic systems, remains an open research area.
Interpretability and debugging
LLMs, like most deep learning models, are often described as “black
boxes.” Understanding why a model makes a particular prediction or how it
arrives at a conclusion remains a significant challenge. This lack of
transparency complicates debugging, especially when the model produces
incorrect, unexpected, or inappropriate outputs. Improving interpretability
is an active and critical area of research.
Classic interpretability methods include feature importance analysis and
input perturbation, where parts of the input (such as individual words) are
removed or altered and the resulting change in output is observed. Gradient-
based methods can help identify which input components have the greatest
influence on the model’s prediction. Libraries such as LIME and SHAP
provide practical tools for these analyses, making model interpretation more
accessible.
In today’s LLM landscape, interpretability efforts have expanded in scope
and complexity. Here are some aspects of the modern interpretability of
language models:
For multi-modal models, researchers are now developing attribution
techniques that highlight which parts of an image, table, or audio file
most influenced the model’s response, in addition to textual
explanations.
With multi-turn and agentic workflows, using tools such as
LangGraph and AutoGen, which we’ll touch on later in the book,
interpretability includes tracking the internal state and decision paths
of the LLM across an extended dialogue or task sequence. This is
especially important for debugging when the model is used as part of a
larger, tool-using, or agentic system.
As LLMs increasingly integrate with external tools such as APIs,
databases, and code executions, it becomes necessary to trace not just
the model’s textual reasoning, but also the sequence of actions and tool
calls, and to understand how external data shapes the final output.
Safety and security
considerations
As LLMs boom, especially open source models, new safety and supply-
chain risks have emerged:
Open source models are easier for adversaries to modify or “jailbreak,”
making it possible to bypass safety filters, introduce malicious
behaviors, or repurpose models for harmful tasks.
The risk of malicious model modifications—for example, inserting
backdoors, trojans, or data poisoning during pretraining—is an
increasing concern, both for proprietary and open models. This threat
extends across the supply chain: from training data curation to model
distribution.
Prompt injection and adversarial inputs remain active attack vectors,
especially for LLMs that are integrated into software tools, browsers,
or cloud services.
Best practices for interpretability and safety now include the following:
Regular auditing and red teaming of models to identify vulnerabilities
Transparency in model architecture, training processes, and data
sources
Provenance tracking and cryptographic signing of open model weights
to help guard against supply-chain attacks
Ongoing research into explainable AI for multi-modal and multi-agent
systems
With multi-modal and open source models, data leakage and privacy risks
are growing. Attackers may use prompt injection to extract confidential data
or exploit model outputs for social engineering. As LLMs continue to
expand their reach, the intertwined challenges of interpretability,
debugging, and safety are more important than ever for both researchers
and practitioners.
Environmental impact
The high computational resources needed for training LLMs can have
significant environmental implications. The energy required for training
these models can contribute to carbon emissions, which is a concern from a
sustainability perspective.
The community has begun to address environmental concerns via shared
compute facilities, more energy-efficient architectures (e.g., sparsity,
quantization), and carbon impact tracking/reporting.
Example designs of state-of-
the-art LLMs
In this section, we examine the design and architectural choices behind
several state-of-the-art LLMs. The goal is not to catalog models
exhaustively, nor to rank them. We will instead illustrate how the concepts
introduced earlier in this chapter materialize in real systems. You will see
how foundational ideas such as Transformer architectures, scaling laws,
training objectives, alignment techniques, and evaluation considerations are
applied in practice. These examples highlight both shared design patterns
across modern LLMs and the trade-offs different organizations make
depending on their priorities.
This discussion also serves a broader purpose within the book.
Understanding how leading LLMs are built provides context for later
chapters that focus on fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, agentic
systems, evaluation, and real-world deployment. Rather than treating LLMs
as black boxes, we encourage you to reason about model behavior in terms
of architectural and training decisions.
It’s important to note that while specific models may change over time, the
design principles explored here are durable and transferable. You’ll have the
conceptual tools needed to evaluate new LLMs as they emerge, rather than
relying solely on benchmark scores or marketing claims.
GPT models and their use in
ChatGPT
LLMs in the GPT series have evolved rapidly. Early versions of ChatGPT
were powered by GPT-3.5, an autoregressive model trained on large
corpora of text to predict the next token in a sequence. As OpenAI has
developed more advanced models, ChatGPT has been updated: it now uses
GPT-5.X models with enhanced intelligence, faster performance, and
broader multimodal capabilities.
It is important to distinguish between GPT models and ChatGPT itself.
GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and GPT-5.X are LLMs (i.e., statistical engines that
generate text by modeling token sequences). ChatGPT, on the other hand, is
a user interface product built on top of these models. It wraps a GPT engine
in a conversational interface and adds layers for memory, safety filtering,
user preferences, and tool integration. In other words, GPT provides the
core language-generation engine, while ChatGPT provides a polished, user-
friendly experience with additional controls and plugins.
What GPT models are
GPT models are Transformer-based, autoregressive LLMs. They process
text from left to right and are trained to predict the next token given the
preceding tokens. This unidirectional design makes them well-suited for
generating coherent sequences of text. GPT-3, one of the early models
underpinning ChatGPT, contains around 175 billion parameters. Later
models such as GPT-4 and GPT-5 scale to much larger sizes, widely
estimated to exceed one trillion parameters, although OpenAI has not
officially disclosed the exact parameter counts or architectural details. Each
new generation typically expands the context window, improves factuality
and reasoning, and adds multimodal capabilities. Starting from GPT-4 and
GPT-4o, LLMs have been accepting both text and images in prompts. GPT-
4o also introduces faster token processing and improved memory handling
for interactive use.
Training pipeline: pretraining and
alignment
The development of GPT models follows a two-phase training pipeline. In
the pretraining phase, the model learns general language patterns using
causal (next-token) language modeling. It is trained on a diverse mixture of
publicly available and licensed text data to maximize the likelihood of each
token given its previous context.
Formally, the training dataset consists of
tokenized text sequences, where each sequence . The
model is trained to maximize the log-likelihood of each token ,
conditioned on its preceding tokens, across the entire dataset:
where θ denotes the model parameters and is the autoregressive
probability distribution implemented using Transformer-based architecture,
typically a decoder-style variant such as GPT. This training paradigm is
known as causal language modeling (CLM).
Importantly, the dataset is composed of publicly accessible text,
but the model does not memorize or store specific documents. Rather, it
learns to model general statistical patterns and syntactic-semantic
relationships in language.
After pretraining, the model undergoes a fine-tuning phase designed to
align its outputs more closely with human intent and safety standards. This
phase includes both supervised learning and reinforcement learning with
human feedback (RLHF). Initially, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is
performed using a dataset , where each is a human-
written prompt and is the ideal response. Supervised fine-tuning and
RLHF will be explained in detail in the next chapter.
Efficiency and rumors of mixture-of-
experts
OpenAI’s GPT-4 technical report notes that GPT-4 is still a Transformer-
based model, but it does not disclose the model size or detailed architecture.
Industry analysts and independent researchers have speculated that GPT-4
might use MoE techniques to scale efficiently, where only a subset of
specialized experts is activated for each token. However, these details
remain unverified; the key takeaway for practitioners is that GPT-4 and
GPT-4o achieve higher performance without a proportional increase in
inference cost. When comparing models, it is better to focus on measurable
improvements such as reasoning ability, factual accuracy, and speed rather
than speculative internal designs.
GPT-5 series
Since late 2025, OpenAI has released GPT-5 and incremental updates such
as GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2. These models are marketed as a unified system
with multi-stage routing and improved reasoning. Public announcements
highlight features such as enhanced conversational warmth, better tool use,
and expanded multimodal capabilities, but there are no official technical
specifications regarding parameter counts, architecture, or training data.
Analysts therefore treat the GPT-5 series as an evolutionary step focused on
product experience rather than a disclosed architectural breakthrough. For
now, the important point is that ChatGPT continues to evolve alongside its
underlying GPT engine, and newer versions of the model offer practical
improvements even if their internal details remain proprietary.
Understanding how GPT models are constructed and trained lays the
groundwork for subsequent chapters. The next chapter delves deeper into
alignment, explaining supervised fine-tuning, RLHF and direct preference
optimization. These methods convert a powerful but generic language
model into a helpful, safe, and task-adaptable assistant.
LLaMA
Large Language Model Meta AI (LLaMA) is a family of autoregressive,
decoder-only Transformer models designed to achieve strong performance
with fewer parameters compared to models such as GPT-3. Architecturally,
it follows the standard Transformer design with stacked self-attention and
feed-forward layers connected via residual paths, but it introduces several
innovations to improve efficiency, stability, and long-context performance.
One of the first changes is the replacement of LayerNorm with Root Mean
Square Normalization (RMSNorm), which normalizes activations using
only their root mean square instead of subtracting the mean. Given a hidden
vector , RMSNorm is defined as:
where is a learned weight vector. This design reduces computation and
improves stability for deep networks by avoiding mean subtraction.
The feed-forward networks in LLaMA use SwiGLU, a gated activation
variant that improves expressiveness. Given an input x and learned weight

where σ is the SiLU (Swish) activation function and ⊙ denotes elementwise
multiplication. The gating mechanism allows the network to control
information flow more effectively than ReLU or GELU.
Another key novelty is Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), which
injects relative positional information directly into the query and key
vectors of the self-attention mechanism. For a token at position with
embedding vector , RoPE applies a rotation in 2D subspaces of the
embedding dimension:
where is a block-diagonal rotation matrix with angles proportional to
the position . This allows the attention mechanism to natively handle
relative positions and extrapolate better to longer sequences.
Together, these innovations—RMSNorm for stable normalization, SwiGLU
for more expressive feed-forward layers, and RoPE for efficient positional
encoding—allow LLaMA to deliver high performance with optimized
training efficiency and strong generalization to long-context scenarios.
Later versions further extend context length using Grouped Query
Attention (GQA), enabling the models to scale to 8K tokens or more
without a proportional increase in computational cost.

Claude
Claude, developed by Anthropic, is a family of LLMs that follows the
standard decoder-only Transformer architecture, similar to models such as
GPT, but with several unique optimizations aimed at efficiency, safety, and
alignment. At its core, Claude is built on stacked Transformer blocks that
consist of causal self-attention layers and feed-forward networks connected
via residual connections and pre-normalization layers. These blocks process
token embeddings augmented with positional information, possibly through
rotary or relative positional embeddings, which enable the model to handle
long sequences efficiently. Claude’s feed-forward layers possibly use
modern activations such as SwiGLU, which improve expressiveness while
maintaining computational efficiency, and pre-normalization (e.g.,
RMSNorm) is used to stabilize very deep models.
The architectural novelties of Claude focus heavily on long-context
handling and safety-oriented training. Claude models, especially Claude 2
and 3, can process sequences exceeding 100K tokens, which is achieved
through memory-efficient attention mechanisms such as Grouped Query
Attention (GQA) or similar optimizations. This allows Claude to retain
performance on long documents without a proportional increase in
computation or memory usage. Another notable aspect is its integration of
constitutional AI during training and fine-tuning. Instead of relying solely
on traditional RLHF, Claude uses a “constitution” of predefined ethical and
behavioral principles to guide self-critique and self-revision. This approach
allows the model to evaluate its own outputs, reduce harmful or biased
responses, and align with safety principles without requiring extensive
human ranking for every response.
Overall, Claude’s novelty lies in its combination of efficient, scalable
Transformer design and a unique alignment methodology. Its architecture is
optimized for handling extremely long contexts, and its fine-tuning pipeline
leverages constitutional AI to produce outputs that are helpful, honest, and
harmless (HHH). By pairing modern Transformer efficiency techniques
with principled self-alignment, Claude achieves a balance between raw
language modeling performance and trustworthy, safe interactions.
Gemini
Gemini, the multimodal LLM developed by Google DeepMind, represents a
significant evolution in artificial intelligence, extending beyond the
capabilities of traditional LLMs and even advanced systems such as GPT-4.
Unlike prior models that are primarily text-centric with added visual
capabilities, Gemini is conceived as natively multimodal, integrating text,
images, audio, and potentially video into a unified architecture. This design
enables seamless cross-modal reasoning and allows the model to perform
tasks that require a holistic understanding of both linguistic and visual
information.
At its core, Gemini is built upon the Transformer architecture but
incorporates substantial innovations inspired by Google’s Pathways
framework. The model leverages a combination of an autoregressive
Transformer decoder for language modeling and a multimodal encoder-
projection system that aligns various input modalities into a shared latent
space. Images, audio, and other non-text inputs are first converted into
embeddings and projected into the same representational space as text
tokens. This alignment allows the attention mechanism of the Transformer
to operate across modalities in a unified manner, enabling the model to
reason about relationships between language and perception.
Another notable innovation in Gemini is its possible use of MoE and
conditional computation. Rather than activating all parameters for every
input, the model dynamically routes tokens to a subset of specialized expert
networks, selected via a gating function.
This approach allows Gemini to scale to trillions of parameters without
incurring the full computational cost of a dense model while enabling
specialization among experts for different modalities or task domains. In
practice, this results in improved efficiency and enhanced performance on
complex reasoning tasks, long-context analysis, and multimodal
comprehension.
Gemini also distinguishes itself in its handling of long-context reasoning.
Experimental reports suggest that the model supports input lengths
extending to hundreds of thousands, and in some cases up to one million
tokens. Achieving this capability requires efficient attention mechanisms,
such as those inspired by Flash Attention, and positional encoding methods
with strong extrapolation properties, likely rotary position embeddings
(RoPE). This extended context window allows the model to process long
documents, multi-step instructions, or even extended video and audio
sequences while maintaining coherence and contextual understanding
across large spans of input.
Safety and alignment are central to Gemini’s design, reflecting DeepMind’s
emphasis on responsible AI. The model employs RLHF and reinforcement
learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), integrating both text and multimodal
reward signals. The reward function is defined over entire output
trajectories, accounting for correctness, safety, and human preference:
where is a multimodal reward model, and the KL term stabilizes
alignment with a reference policy. This approach allows the model not only
to generate accurate outputs but also to remain sensitive to safety
constraints in both textual and visual contexts.
Through this combination of native multimodality, expert-based conditional
computation, long-context reasoning, and robust alignment, Gemini
achieves a level of performance and versatility that surpasses previous
models in real-world applicability. It can synthesize information across text
and visual inputs, navigate large code bases, analyze complex documents,
and interpret diagrams or multimedia content with a unified reasoning
approach. More than a scaled-up language model, Gemini embodies a new
generation of AI systems designed to operate as general-purpose,
multimodal reasoning agents, moving closer to practical artificial general
intelligence.
DeepSeek
DeepSeek represents a major advancement in the field of LLMs, originating
from the Hangzhou-based firm under the High-Flyer hedge fund.
Established in 2023, the initiative has rapidly gained international attention
for producing models that rival the capabilities of state-of-the-art systems
such as GPT-4 and Claude 3, while operating at a fraction of their
computational and financial cost. This achievement is enabled through an
innovative sparsely activated MoE architecture, combined with highly
efficient optimization techniques that reduce both resource requirements
and training overhead.
The flagship model, DeepSeek-V3, is a 671-billion-parameter Transformer
with MoE specialization, of which approximately 37 billion parameters are
activated per token. This sparse-activation mechanism is managed by
DeepSeekMoE, which incorporates an auxiliary-loss-free load-balancing
strategy, ensuring that expert networks are effectively utilized without
introducing instability during training. In addition, the model introduces
Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), designed to improve long-context
reasoning efficiency, and adopts multi-token prediction objectives to
accelerate convergence. Leveraging these design principles, DeepSeek-V3
was trained on 14.8 trillion tokens, consuming fewer than 3 million GPU-
hours on NVIDIA H800 clusters, at a total cost of reportedly under 6
million USD—demonstrating a drastic improvement in training efficiency
relative to comparable large-scale LLM projects.
Expanding upon this foundation, DeepSeek-R1 was developed as a
reasoning-centric model, capable of advanced multi-step problem-solving
and chain-of-thought generation. Its initial variant, R1-Zero, was trained
exclusively via reinforcement learning (RL) without any prior supervised
fine-tuning, resulting in emergent reasoning behaviors such as self-
reflection and verification. However, the outputs of R1-Zero were often
poorly structured and exhibited language mixing. The refined DeepSeek-R1
overcomes these limitations by integrating cold-start supervised data and
adopting Group Policy Optimization (GPO), a novel RL-based training
paradigm that enhances the model’s reasoning stability and alignment.
GPO generalizes standard policy-gradient reinforcement learning by
optimizing model policies over groups of related trajectories rather than
individual samples, thereby improving sample efficiency and consistency
across semantically linked inputs. Let denote the model’s policy, and
Rϕ a multimodal or text-based reward function. For a group of related
prompts G⊂g, the objective function can be expressed as:
where is a reference policy, and β controls the trade-off between
reward maximization and divergence from the reference distribution. This
approach allows DeepSeek-R1 to generate coherent reasoning chains across
similar queries while maintaining stability and alignment throughout the
optimization process.
Through the combination of MoE sparsity, multi-token prediction, and
GPO, DeepSeek models have achieved exceptional results on reasoning and
knowledge benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, and
USMLE, often approaching or surpassing the performance of leading
proprietary systems. The reasoning-enhanced architecture also enables
efficient long-context inference and chain-of-thought generation, making
DeepSeek models particularly effective in mathematics, coding, and
scientific domains.
Despite these advancements, DeepSeek models still present notable safety
challenges, including hallucinations, cultural and linguistic biases, and
susceptibility to adversarial prompts. Evaluations such as
CHiSafetyBench
emphasize the necessity for continued research in alignment and robustness.
Nevertheless, the open source release of R1’s distilled models (ranging
from 1.5 billion to 70 billion parameters) under permissive licenses has
made DeepSeek a disruptive force in global AI research. By demonstrating
that competitive frontier-level LLMs can be trained at low cost while
maintaining high reasoning capability, DeepSeek fundamentally challenges
existing paradigms in large-scale AI development and deployment.
PaLM
PaLM is a 540-billion-parameter, densely activated Transformer LM that
was trained on 6,144 TPU v4 chips using Pathways, a new ML system that
enables highly efficient training across multiple TPU pods.
PaLM has been shown to achieve breakthrough performance on a variety of
natural language tasks, including the following:
Multi-step reasoning tasks
The recently released Beyond the Imitation Game Benchmark
(BIG-bench)
Multilingual tasks
Source code generation
The BIG-bench benchmark is worth expanding on as it serves as a
recognized collection of benchmarks to measure against. BIG-bench is an
extensive assessment mechanism specifically designed for large-scale LMs.
It is a broad-based, community-focused benchmark that presents a diversity
of tasks to evaluate a model’s performance in different disciplines and its
competence in natural language comprehension, problem-solving, and
reasoning. With a total of 204 tasks from 450 contributors across 132
institutions, BIG-bench covers an eclectic mix of subjects, including
linguistics, childhood development, mathematics, common-sense reasoning,
biology, physics, software development, and even social bias. It
concentrates on challenges believed to be currently beyond the reach of
existing LMs. The primary goal of BIG-bench extends beyond mere
imitation or Turing test-style evaluations, aiming instead for a deeper, more
nuanced appraisal of the abilities and constraints of these large models. This
initiative is founded on the conviction that an open, collaborative approach
to evaluation paves the way for a more comprehensive understanding of
these LMs and their potential societal ramifications.
PaLM 540B excels beyond the fine-tuned state-of-the-art across various
multi-step reasoning tasks and surpasses average human performance on the
BIG-bench benchmark. Many BIG-bench tasks exhibit significant leaps in
performance as PaLM scales to its largest size, demonstrating discontinuous
improvements from the model scale. PaLM also has strong capabilities in
multilingual tasks and source code generation. For example, PaLM can
translate between 50 languages, and it can generate code in a variety of
programming languages.
The authors of the PaLM paper also discuss the ethical considerations
related to LLMs, and they discuss potential mitigation strategies. For
example, they suggest that it is important to be aware of the potential for
bias in LLMs and that it is important to develop techniques for detecting
and mitigating bias.
PaLM employs the conventional Transformer model architecture in a
decoder-exclusive setup, which allows each timestep to attend only to itself
and preceding timesteps. Several modifications were applied to this setup,
including the following:
SwiGLU activation: Instead of standard ReLU, GeLU, or Swish
activations, PaLM utilizes SwiGLU activations (Swish(xW) · xV) for
multilayer perceptron (MLP) intermediate activations due to their
superior performance in enhancing quality. This approach, however,
requires three matrix multiplications in the MLP as opposed to the
conventional two.
Parallel layers: Rather than the typical “serialized” approach, PaLM
uses a “parallel” formulation for each Transformer block.
The standard structure is given by the following:
The parallel structure is instead the following:
This leads to roughly 15% quicker training speed at larger scales due
to the fusion of MLP and attention input matrix multiplications.
Multi-query attention: In the conventional Transformer formulation,
k attention heads are employed. For each timestep, the input vector is
linearly projected into query, key, and value tensors, which have a
shape of [k, h], where h denotes the size of the attention head. In the
new approach, the projections for “key” and “value” are shared across
all heads, meaning “key” and “value” are projected to [1, h], while
“query” maintains the shape [k, h]. The authors claimed that this
approach doesn’t notably affect model quality or training speed, while
it does result in significant cost reductions during autoregressive
decoding. The reason for this lies in the inefficiency of standard multi-
headed attention on accelerator hardware during autoregressive
decoding, as the key/value tensors are not shared across examples and
only one token is decoded at each moment.
Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) embeddings: RoPE
embeddings, shown to perform better on longer sequence lengths, are
preferred over absolute or relative position embeddings.
Shared input-output embeddings: The input and output embedding
matrices are shared, a practice that is common, though not universal, in
previous work.
No biases: The model abstains from using biases in any dense kernels
or layer norms, which enhances training stability for larger models.
Vocabulary: PaLM uses a 256k-token vocabulary
SentencePiece
designed for diverse languages in the training corpus, ensuring
efficient training without excessive tokenization. This preserves all
whitespaces and out-of-vocabulary Unicode characters while splitting
numbers into individual digit tokens for clarity.
Overall, PaLM is a powerful LM that has the potential to be used for a wide
variety of applications. It is still under development, but it has already
demonstrated the ability to achieve breakthrough performance on a number
of tasks.
It is interesting to note that each of these models has its own strengths and
weaknesses, and the best choice of model can depend on the specific task,
the amount and type of available training data, and the computational
resources available.
Evaluation
Evaluation in generative AI is fundamentally different from evaluation in
traditional supervised learning. In classification tasks, performance can
often be summarized with a single metric such as accuracy or F1 score
against a fixed ground truth. Generative models, however, produce open-
ended outputs where multiple answers may be acceptable, partially correct,
stylistically different, or subtly flawed. As a result, evaluation is no longer
just about matching labels but instead about assessing behavior across
reasoning, factual grounding, safety, robustness, and overall linguistic
quality.
This distinction matters because a model can achieve low perplexity or
strong benchmark accuracy while still hallucinating facts, failing under
adversarial prompts, or producing unsafe outputs in edge cases. Project-
level deployment exposes these failure modes quickly, especially in
domains such as healthcare, legal analysis, or financial decision-making.
For this reason, evaluation frameworks have expanded beyond traditional
training metrics to include multiple dimensions that reflect how LLMs are
actually used.
In the following sections, we examine these dimensions in detail, beginning
with perplexity as a foundational language modeling metric and then
moving toward broader assessments of reasoning, factuality, safety,
robustness, fluency, coherence, and diversity.
Perplexity and language
modeling performance
A foundational metric in language modeling is perplexity, which measures
how well a language model predicts a sequence of tokens. Perplexity is
derived directly from the probabilistic objective used during model training
and is closely tied to next-token prediction.
Intuitively, perplexity reflects a model’s uncertainty when generating text. A
lower perplexity indicates that the model assigns higher probability to the
observed tokens and is therefore more confident in its predictions.
Formally, perplexity is defined as the exponential of the average negative
log-likelihood of the tokens in a dataset. For a token sequence ,
perplexity can be expressed as:
Because autoregressive LLMs such as GPT models are trained to maximize
this likelihood, perplexity has historically served as a primary metric for
evaluating language models during training and benchmarking.
Improvements in perplexity generally correlate with better fluency and
grammatical correctness in generated text.
However, perplexity has important limitations. It evaluates a model’s ability
to predict the next token, not its ability to reason, follow instructions,
remain factual, or behave safely. Two models with similar perplexity scores
can exhibit markedly different behavior when performing tasks such as
multi-step reasoning, code generation, or conversational interaction.
As LLMs have evolved from pure language models into general-purpose
reasoning and interaction systems, evaluation has expanded beyond
perplexity. Modern assessment frameworks incorporate task-specific
benchmarks for reasoning, factuality, robustness, safety, and human
preference alignment. In practice, perplexity remains a useful diagnostic
metric during training and ablation studies, but it is no longer sufficient as a
standalone measure of overall LLM quality.
The following subsections introduce evaluation methods that better capture
these broader capabilities.
Reasoning evaluation
Reasoning measures whether a model can solve tasks using logical, step-by-
step thinking rather than memorization or pattern-matching. It is crucial for
tasks such as multi-hop question answering, mathematics, coding, and
structured problem-solving. A model’s reasoning ability can be evaluated
using datasets such as GSM8K (arithmetic reasoning), MMLU (multi-task
reasoning), and ARC-Challenge (commonsense reasoning).
To measure reasoning, accuracy is commonly computed as
However, modern reasoning evaluation also considers chain-of-thought
(CoT) consistency, where each intermediate step is assessed for logical
validity. In some evaluations, step-level accuracy is calculated:
Reasoning evaluation often combines automatic scoring with human
assessment, especially when intermediate steps are complex or require
domain expertise.
Factuality evaluation
Factuality measures whether model outputs are truthful and grounded in
real-world knowledge, avoiding hallucinations. This is critical in
knowledge-intensive applications such as medical, legal, or scientific
question answering.
In closed-domain tasks with reference answers, factuality is often evaluated
using BLEU and ROUGE metrics:
BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) measures n-gram
precision, evaluating how much of the generated output overlaps with
the reference text:

= weight for each n-gram (usually uniform)
BP = brevity penalty to penalize overly short outputs
ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation)
primarily measures n-gram recall, checking how much of the reference
appears in the generated output:
Factuality in open-domain settings often uses , , or
TruthfulQA FactScore
automated LLM-based verifiers that compare outputs against retrieved
documents. Retrieval-augmented pipelines are commonly used to validate
outputs against authoritative knowledge bases.
Safety evaluation
Safety ensures the model is harmless, unbiased, and aligned with ethical
principles. Unsafe outputs include toxicity, hate speech, illegal instructions,
or content that violates privacy or fairness.
Safety evaluation often measures the probability of generating unsafe
content:
Toxicity scoring can use classifiers such as Perspective API or Detoxify,
producing a probability . Models are also evaluated using
bias metrics, such as or , which measure the
StereoSet BiasBench
preference of a model toward stereotypical completions. Human red-
teaming complements automatic evaluations, testing the model against
adversarial prompts to ensure it avoids producing harmful outputs.
Robustness evaluation
Robustness measures whether a model is resilient to noise, adversarial
prompts, and distribution shifts. A robust model should respond consistently
even if inputs are paraphrased, contain typos, or include adversarial
triggers.
A simple robustness score can be defined as:
Robustness is often tested with adversarial datasets such as or
AdvGLUE
, and against prompt-injection attacks. Stability can also be
Dynabench
quantified using output variance—models that generate widely different
outputs for similar inputs are considered less robust.
Fluency, coherence, and
diversity
Beyond the core evaluation dimensions, fluency and coherence measure
how natural and readable the outputs are, while diversity ensures the model
avoids repetitive or generic responses.
Fluency is often judged with BLEU, ROUGE, or BERTScore, and via
human ratings
Coherence measures whether the generated text is logically consistent
across sentences
Diversity is measured using Distinct-n:
High indicates the model avoids repetitive or dull outputs,
improving user experience.
Some of the evaluation metrics for generative AI models, particularly in
open-ended NLP tasks, are inherently difficult to assess using only human
evaluators. While humans can reliably judge attributes such as fluency or
coherence, evaluating reasoning correctness, factuality, and robustness can
be challenging, time-consuming, and prone to inconsistency.
For example, reasoning evaluation often requires validating each step of a
CoT to ensure the logic is sound. Humans may miss subtle reasoning errors,
especially in long or technical outputs such as mathematical proofs, legal
arguments, or programming tasks. Factuality is even more challenging
because humans need to fact-check outputs against large knowledge bases
or domain-specific sources. In tasks such as scientific QA or medical
diagnosis, this requires subject-matter expertise, which is costly and
limited. Similarly, robustness testing involves generating and reviewing
hundreds of adversarial or paraphrased inputs, something that is tedious and
error-prone for humans alone.
LLM-as-a-judge
Modern evaluation frameworks in generative AI increasingly rely on LLM-
as-a-judge, a paradigm in which LLMs themselves serve as evaluators. In
this approach, an LLM is either fine-tuned or carefully prompted to score,
rank, or critique the outputs of other models according to predefined criteria
such as reasoning validity, factual accuracy, safety, or stylistic quality. This
method offers several notable advantages over purely human evaluation.
First, it provides scalability, as an LLM can assess thousands of samples far
more quickly than human annotators. Second, it offers consistency, because
an LLM judge delivers reproducible scores and avoids the variability and
fatigue that can affect human evaluators. Additionally, LLMs enable multi-
dimensional evaluation, since they can assess reasoning, factuality, and
stylistic alignment in a single pass. Through techniques such as self-
consistency or cross-model voting, LLM judges can also enhance self-
improvement by reducing biases when combining multiple judgments.
Formally, if we define an evaluation prompt , where x is the input
and y is the model output, the LLM judge produces a score or a
ranking among candidate responses:
In some cases, these judges act as chain-of-thought evaluators, generating
intermediate reasoning steps that justify their scoring decisions. This
methodology has been widely adopted in evaluation frameworks such as
OpenAI’s Eval, Anthropic’s Constitutional AI, and DeepMind’s Gemini
pipelines, forming the backbone of scalable model assessment.
Despite these advantages, human oversight remains critical to ensure
reliability. LLM judges may inherit biases or produce hallucinated
judgments, so hybrid evaluation strategies are considered best practice. In
such an approach, LLMs conduct the first-pass scoring for reasoning,
factuality, safety, and robustness across large datasets, while humans audit a
subset of the results to validate and calibrate the scores. Any discrepancies
are analyzed to refine prompts, evaluation protocols, or the LLM judge
itself. This hybrid pipeline combines the efficiency of automated evaluation
with the reliability and ethical oversight of human review.
Summary
In this chapter, we examined the dynamic world of state-of-the-art LLMs,
focusing on their architectures, capabilities, and evaluation methods.
Modern models such as GPT-4, LLaMA, DeepSeek, and Gemini illustrate
remarkable generalization across a wide variety of tasks, excelling at
understanding nuanced contexts, performing complex reasoning, and
generating coherent and contextually appropriate outputs.
We explored how these models achieve their performance through
architectural innovations. LLaMA introduced efficiency-oriented features
such as RMSNorm, SwiGLU activations, and RoPE positional encodings,
enabling strong results with smaller models. GPT-4 pushed the frontier of
language understanding and reasoning through advanced scaling and
alignment methods. DeepSeek leveraged MoE to balance high capacity
with cost-effective inference, while Gemini expanded into multi-modal
reasoning and integrated stronger safety and reliability measures.
The chapter also discussed the evaluation of LLMs, emphasizing reasoning,
factuality, safety, and robustness as critical dimensions of assessment.
While traditional metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE remain useful for
measuring n-gram similarity and summarization quality, modern evaluation
increasingly employs LLM-as-a-judge approaches, where large models
assess the outputs of other models at scale. These automated evaluations are
combined with human auditing to ensure reliability and to detect subtle
biases or errors.
Overall, this chapter provided a concise yet comprehensive overview of
today’s LLM landscape, covering the key models, their architectural
innovations, and the evolving methodologies used to evaluate their
reasoning, factual correctness, and safety.

8
Parameter-Efficient Fine-
Tuning and Reasoning in
LLMs
While LLMs are impressive generalists, their true value in production often
comes from their ability to function as domain-specific experts. This chapter
is about how to transform a foundation model into such a specialist without
updating billions of parameters. It is also about alignment: how to ensure the
adapted model not only produces fluent text but also behaves in ways users
find helpful, safe, and grounded in sound reasoning.
We begin with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), the family of
methods that unlock efficient adaptation of very large models. You will learn
how LoRA inserts low-rank adapters into key linear projections, and how
QLoRA extends this idea by storing the frozen backbone in 4-bit precision
while training adapters in fp16 or bf16. But adapting parameters is only part
of the story. Models must also be aligned with what people actually want.
We therefore connect LoRA and QLoRA to the three major preference-based
alignment families. First, RLHF with PPO: training a reward model from
human preferences and optimizing the policy while keeping it close to a
fluent reference. Second, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which
skips reinforcement learning entirely and instead fits policy logits directly to
pairwise comparisons. Third, Group-Relative Policy Optimization
(GRPO), a more recent variant that normalizes trajectories against one
another within a prompt to stabilize optimization. Each of these objectives
can be implemented efficiently with adapters alone, making them practical at
scale.
Finally, we address reasoning itself. We will formalize reasoning as a
probabilistic process over latent steps. By the end of this chapter, you will
understand not only how to adapt large models, but also how to align and
evaluate them so they can reason as specialists in your domain. We will
bridge the gap between theoretical mechanics and practical engineering,
preparing you to make the critical choices that define a production-ready
system: which layers to adapt, what rank and scaling factors to choose,
whether to merge or serve adapters separately, and how to set up A/B tests or
versioning pipelines in the field.
In a nutshell, here are the main topics we’ll cover:
Fine-tuning LLMs with LoRA and QLoRA
Reinforcement learning with human feedback
Advanced RLHF techniques for LLMs
Reasoning in LLMs
Technical requirements
To follow along with the implementations and theory in this chapter, you
should be comfortable with the following:
Core architectures and math: A solid understanding of Transformers
(specifically self-attention and MLP blocks), automatic differentiation,
and basic PyTorch.
The Hugging Face ecosystem: Familiarity with the Transformers and
PEFT libraries, as well as bitsandbytes for quantized training, will be
essential for reproducing our examples.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) foundations: A basic grasp of concepts
such as policy, reward, and PPO is useful. However, we will build the
necessary intuition for these concepts carefully to ensure the chapter
remains accessible.
Fine-tuning LLMs with LoRA
and QLoRA
Building on our understanding of how large models process information, this
section provides a guide to fine-tuning LLMs with LoRA and QLoRA. We
focus on these specific techniques because they solve the primary bottleneck
in modern AI development: the massive hardware requirement for full-
parameter updates. You will learn how to steer a general-purpose model
toward specialized tasks, such as drafting clinical notes or adopting a
specific brand voice, without the need for industrial-scale compute clusters.
By the end of this section, you will be able to configure adapter matrices and
utilize 4-bit quantization to train specialized models on a single consumer-
grade GPU, providing a practical blueprint for building efficient, high-
performance domain experts.

Gradients in LoRA
Before we examine the specific mechanics of a LoRA-augmented layer, it is
essential to revisit the role of gradients. In the context of neural networks, a
gradient represents the direction and magnitude of the steepest increase in a
loss function; by moving in the opposite direction, we “tune” the model’s
weights to minimize error.
In traditional full fine-tuning, calculating and storing these gradients for
billions of parameters is what creates the massive memory and compute
overhead that makes LLM training so costly. LoRA changes this dynamic by
freezing the original weights and only calculating gradients for the tiny,
newly inserted adapter matrices. This allows the model to learn complex
task-specific corrections with orders-of-magnitude fewer trainable
parameters, effectively approximating the impact of a full update at a
fraction of the cost.

flow through a LoRA-augmented linear submodule. Consider a LoRA-
augmented linear submodule with a minibatch of inputs

Dropout on the adapter path
While the core mechanics of LoRA focus on efficiency, the choice to include
dropout is a strategic decision rather than a structural necessity. This
technique is often categorized as optional because its value depends heavily
on the size of your training data and the complexity of the task at hand. By
introducing a dropout layer, you can steer the model toward better
generalization, ensuring that the adapter matrices learn robust features
instead of overfitting to the specific noise of a small dataset.
Some implementations apply dropout to the bottleneck activations :

Takeaway
Constraining to the low-rank form concentrates
learning into a small subspace. This yields the same simple
gradient structure as a dense layer but with far fewer
trainable parameters, lower memory, and modest extra
compute—while retaining enough flexibility to adapt large
models effectively.
Where to apply LoRA
When deciding where to apply LoRA, the common practice is to insert the
low-rank adapters into the projection matrices of the Transformer’s attention
and, optionally, its feedforward layers. In a standard multi-head self-
attention block, we have four key projection matrices: , each
of shape , where is the model’s hidden size. Applying LoRA to these
matrices means that we learn small low-rank updates for each of
them, while leaving the original weights frozen. This approach is effective
because the attention projections control how information is distributed and
mixed across tokens, so adapting them gives the model a strong ability to
specialize to new tasks with very few additional parameters.
If the hidden size is , then each of these four projections contributes

tasks, LoRA is also applied to the MLP (feedforward) projections inside the
Transformer block, particularly when more expressive fine-tuning is needed,
but the dominant practice remains focusing on the attention weights because
they have the largest effect on model behavior for many tasks.
This placement strategy is what makes LoRA both parameter-efficient and
task-effective: by targeting the weights most responsible for token
interaction (attention projections), we get maximal representational
flexibility with minimal overhead. This design choice also helps keep
memory usage and compute cost low, enabling fine-tuning even LLMs on
relatively modest hardware. Figure 8.2 shows the places that LoRA can be

Merging for inference
After training, LoRA adapters can be merged into the base model weights to
produce a single, self-contained set of parameters suitable for inference.
Recall that LoRA introduces a low-rank update
where and are the learned adapter matrices and is
the scaling factor. At inference time, we can fold this update directly into the
frozen base weight matrix :
This operation produces a single weight matrix that combines the original
pre-trained weights and the learned low-rank correction. Once this merge is
done, the model behaves exactly as if LoRA adapters were still present, but
there is no additional runtime overhead—we have effectively transformed
the model back into a standard dense Transformer with updated weights.
Merging is particularly straightforward when the base model is stored in
standard floating-point precision (e.g., FP16 or FP32): we simply add to
and save the result. For quantized models such as those fine-tuned with
QLoRA, merging requires a dequantization step: the base quantized weights
must first be temporarily converted back to a higher-precision format
(typically FP16 or FP32) so that the sum can be computed
accurately. After the merge, the resulting weights can be re-quantized if
desired, producing a single quantized checkpoint ready for efficient
inference.
This merging procedure is highly useful in production environments because
it removes the need to carry around separate adapter weights and apply them
dynamically at runtime, leading to faster loading, lower memory usage, and
simpler deployment pipelines.
Quantized LoRA (QLoRA)
QLoRA extends the idea of LoRA to enable fine-tuning of LLMs on a single
GPU. The core idea is to keep the base model frozen and stored in 4-bit
quantized precision, while training the LoRA adapters in higher precision
(such as bfloat16 or float16). This achieves two goals simultaneously:
Drastically reducing memory requirements
Allowing the adapters to both compensate for quantization error and
adapt the model to downstream tasks
In this section, we will analyze how QLoRA compares to standard LoRA in
practice, focusing on the trade-offs between memory reduction and model
fidelity. We will specifically demonstrate how techniques such as NF4 (4-bit
NormalFloat) and paged optimizers allow us to recover the quality of full
fine-tuning while significantly lowering the barrier to entry for model
adaptation.
