Practical training flow for LoRA
and QLoRA
Fine-tuning LLMs with LoRA and QLoRA follows a structured pipeline.
The aim is to adapt massive pretrained models efficiently, both in terms of
memory usage and compute cost, while maintaining high stability during
training. In this section, we will describe the process step by step—from data
preparation to optimization—and illustrate both the mathematical details and
the practical engineering choices. Beyond the high-level workflow, these
choices require balancing model capacity against hardware constraints—
specifically selecting which layers to target and determining the optimal
rank. You will also navigate trade-offs in efficiency and stability by
configuring 4-bit NF4 quantization, paged optimizers, and adapter dropout
for regularization. Ultimately, these engineering decisions culminate in how
you deploy, choosing between the low-latency benefits of merging adapters
or the modular flexibility of maintaining independent versioning pipelines.
Data and objective
The choice of training data depends on the downstream task. For instruction-
tuning, we prepare input-output pairs (prompt → response), whereas for
general language modeling, we simply use next-token prediction data.
The objective function is typically the causal language modeling loss:
where the model predicts each token given its context.
However, when the dataset is small or domain-specific, there is a risk that
the adapters overfit and drift too far from the base model’s general
distribution. To counter this, a regularization term is often added in the
form of a KL divergence between the adapted model’s predictions and
the base model’s frozen predictions :
where controls how strongly the fine-tuned model is encouraged to stay
close to the base model. This stabilizes training, especially in low-resource
regimes.
Targeted modules
One of LoRA’s key strengths is that it does not need to be applied
everywhere. Instead, it targets a small set of weight matrices where
adaptation has the greatest impact. In transformer architectures, these are
typically:
Attention projections ( )
Feed-forward (MLP) projections ( )
For decoder-only LLMs in particular:
Applying LoRA to Q, V, O is often sufficient, giving excellent trade-
offs
Adding LoRA to MLPs provides extra expressivity but increases
adapter size
This selective targeting explains why LoRA is so parameter-efficient—we
adapt only the “bottleneck” weights that control token interactions.

Optimization strategy
Once the adapters are in place and initialized, training proceeds much like
standard fine-tuning, but with a lighter optimization footprint. Because only
a small number of parameters are updated, LoRA and QLoRA can use more
aggressive settings while remaining stable.
Selecting the right configuration is a balancing act between model capacity
and computational efficiency. While the default values provide a strong
baseline, fine-tuning these hyperparameters allows you to tailor the adapter’s
influence to the complexity of your specific dataset. By carefully adjusting
the following settings, you can optimize the learning signal while
maintaining the stability required for large-scale model adaptation.
Optimizer: AdamW
Precision: mixed precision (bfloat16 is common)
Learning rates: higher than full fine-tuning (since adapter capacity is
small), typically
Schedules: linear warmup (1–3% of steps) followed by cosine decay
Gradient clipping: , especially important in QLoRA due to
quantization noise
Memory management and long
contexts
As context lengths grow, training quickly becomes memory-bound. In
practice, most VRAM is consumed by activations rather than model
parameters. To reduce memory load, do the following:
Use gradient checkpointing to trade compute for memory
Employ FlashAttention kernels to reduce attention memory usage
In QLoRA, use paged optimizers (such as 8-bit Adam or Lion) to
avoid CPU/GPU memory spikes
These techniques make it possible to fine-tune models with billions of
parameters on a single GPU.
Hyperparameter choices
LoRA introduces a small but important set of additional hyperparameters.
While optimal values are task-dependent, the following rules of thumb work
well in practice:
Rank : 4–32. Small is sufficient for small tasks; larger for domain
shifts
Scaling : usually 8–64, giving an effective scale
LoRA dropout: 0–0.1 for small datasets (adds robustness)
Target modules: start with , add and MLP for higher
accuracy
Batch size: as large as VRAM allows
LoRA vs QLoRA
The choice between LoRA and QLoRA is largely driven by memory
constraints and deployment requirements:
LoRA: Use when the base model can fit in fp16/bf16. Simple, efficient,
supports merging adapters back into weights.
QLoRA: Use when VRAM is limited. Stores the base model in 4-bit
precision, dequantizes on-the-fly, and trains adapters in higher
precision. Adapters recover performance close to full fine-tuning.
At inference time, you can do one of the following:
Keep the base quantized and add adapters
Dequantize the base and merge adapters into final weights

So far, we have explored parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as
LoRA and QLoRA, which allow LLMs to be adapted efficiently to new
tasks while keeping memory and compute costs manageable. These methods
emphasize structural efficiency: instead of modifying all of a model’s
billions of parameters, we introduce lightweight adapters or quantization
strategies that retain most of the pretrained knowledge while enabling
targeted adaptation. However, while these techniques are powerful for
supervised fine-tuning and domain adaptation, they are fundamentally
limited by the quality of the training data. Instruction-tuned models, even
when efficiently adapted, can only reproduce patterns and preferences
directly encoded in their datasets. To align models more closely with human
values, preferences, and nuanced goals, we need approaches that go beyond
standard supervised objectives.
This is where Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)
provides a way to train models not only on static labeled data but also on
interactive, preference-driven signals that reflect what humans actually want
from the system. The next part of this chapter will explore advanced RLHF
techniques for LLMs, including reward modeling, preference optimization,
and newer methods that extend or refine the standard RLHF pipeline. These
approaches represent the natural next step: moving from efficient adaptation
of parameters (LoRA/QLoRA) to efficient adaptation of behavior through
human feedback and reinforcement learning.
Reinforcement learning with
human feedback
RLHF is a training framework that helps align LLMs more closely with
human expectations. Instead of relying only on supervised datasets, RLHF
introduces a feedback loop in which human judgments guide the
optimization of model behavior. This makes the model’s responses not only
plausible in terms of language, but also more useful and safe in terms of
what people actually want.
The process begins with supervised fine-tuning, where the model is trained
on carefully curated prompt–response examples. These examples, often
written or verified by humans, provide the model with an initial sense of
how to respond in a helpful and coherent way. But supervised fine-tuning
alone has limitations, because it cannot cover the vast diversity of prompts a
user might ask, and it tends to make the model mimic the style of the
examples without deeper alignment to preferences. To address this, RLHF
introduces a reward model. Human annotators are asked to compare and
rank outputs from the language model for the same prompt. By indicating
which response is better—perhaps more accurate, more polite, or less
harmful—they create training data that allows a reward model to learn to
predict human preferences. This reward model then becomes the scoring
mechanism that tells the system whether a new output is “good” or “bad.”
The final stage applies reinforcement learning, usually with an algorithm
such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Here, the original model is
treated as a policy that generates text given a prompt. Instead of optimizing
for next-token prediction as in pretraining, the policy is now optimized to
maximize the score from the reward model. In practice, this means the
language model gradually learns to produce responses that humans are more
likely to prefer, while avoiding those that people tend to reject.
This approach is especially important for LLMs because raw pretrained
models, although powerful, often produce outputs that are unhelpful,
irrelevant, or even unsafe. They may generate biased language, confidently
state incorrect information, or fail to follow instructions. RLHF helps correct
these issues by shifting the training signal from purely statistical likelihoods
to values informed by human judgment. The benefits are that models
become more aligned with user intent, safer to deploy, and more engaging to
interact with. They are better able to strike the right balance between
accuracy and politeness, which leads to improved reliability in real-world
applications. In a broader sense, RLHF transforms an LLM from a system
that simply imitates the patterns of its training data into one that adapts to
human values and goals. It is the reason modern conversational models such
as ChatGPT feel more cooperative and aligned with the way people expect
an assistant to behave.
While the standard RLHF pipeline has proven remarkably effective, it is not
without its challenges. Training a separate reward model, collecting high-
quality human preference data, and running reinforcement learning at scale
are all resource-intensive steps. Moreover, RLHF can sometimes introduce
instability, reward hacking, or overly cautious model behavior. These
limitations have motivated researchers to explore advanced extensions and
alternatives to the classic pipeline.
It’s time now to examine more advanced RLHF techniques. Topics such as
reward shaping, direct preference optimization, and hybrid approaches that
combine supervised signals with reinforcement learning have emerged as
promising ways to improve both efficiency and stability. Together, these
methods represent the ongoing evolution of alignment strategies, moving
beyond the basic RLHF recipe toward more refined techniques that bring
LLMs even closer to human intent.
Advanced RLHF techniques
for LLMs
The standard RLHF pipeline, consisting of supervised fine-tuning, reward
modeling, and reinforcement learning with PPO, has proven to be one of the
most effective frameworks for aligning LLMs with human intent. In its
simplest form, the model learns a policy that generates outputs
for prompts , while a reward model provides a scalar signal
estimating human preference. The objective of reinforcement learning is
then to maximize the expected reward:
often with an added KL penalty to keep the fine-tuned model close to the
original pretrained distribution :
This baseline approach is powerful but comes with well-known challenges.
Reward models are imperfect proxies for human judgment, reinforcement
learning introduces instability, and the need for large volumes of human
preference data can be prohibitively expensive. These limitations have
motivated the development of more advanced techniques that either refine
the reward signal, simplify the optimization procedure, or combine multiple
alignment signals into a more robust training objective.
Among these refinements, we focus on three complementary directions.
First, we examine Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which removes
the explicit reinforcement learning loop and instead aligns models directly
from preference data using a contrastive objective. Second, we introduce
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a scalable reinforcement
learning variant that stabilizes policy updates by normalizing rewards across
groups of candidate responses. Then, in the next and final section of this
chapter, we broaden the discussion beyond alignment objectives to consider
reasoning in LLMs, introducing a formal framework for modeling and
training intermediate reasoning steps under supervised, latent, and
preference-based regimes.
Direct Preference Optimization
(DPO)
While traditional RLHF relies on reinforcement learning with a learned
reward model and a policy optimization algorithm such as PPO, Direct
Preference Optimization (DPO) simplifies the pipeline by eliminating the
explicit reinforcement learning step. Instead, it directly optimizes the
model’s likelihood to match human preferences using a contrastive objective
derived from preference data. This makes DPO both simpler to implement
and more stable in practice.
To see how this works, it helps to start from the kind of data we actually
collect in alignment settings. Suppose we have a dataset of preference pairs:
for each prompt , humans rank two candidate responses , where
is preferred over . In the standard RLHF pipeline, this data would be used
to train a reward model . DPO, by contrast, avoids training a
separate reward model and instead directly adjusts the policy .
The key assumption is that there exists a latent reward function such that
the probability of preferring over follows a logistic model:

The crucial insight is that this reward does not need to be modeled explicitly.
Instead of learning explicitly, DPO shows that we can express this
preference probability in terms of the ratio between the fine-tuned policy
and the reference (pretrained) policy :
This connection allows us to directly optimize the model toward preferred
responses without an intermediate reward model.

becomes straightforward. Given a preference pair , the DPO

where is a temperature-like parameter that controls how strongly the policy
is updated relative to the reference. Figure 8.6 shows how DPO works:
Figure 8.6: The training process of DPO
At an intuitive level, this objective behaves in a very familiar way:
The reference model anchors the fine-tuned model, ensuring it does
not drift too far from the pretrained distribution (similar to the KL
penalty in RLHF)
The policy is optimized so that preferred responses get a higher
likelihood relative to the baseline than the dispreferred ones
Unlike PPO-based RLHF, there is no explicit reinforcement learning
loop, no learned reward model, and no need for rollouts; optimization
reduces to standard gradient descent on a classification-like loss
What makes DPO particularly appealing is the set of components it
deliberately omits. DPO eliminates the need for an explicit reinforcement
learning loop, a separately trained reward model, and the generation of
rollouts. Instead, optimization reduces to standard gradient descent on a
classification-style objective defined over preference pairs. Conceptually,
DPO is substantially closer to supervised fine-tuning than to policy-
gradient–based reinforcement learning.
This simplification confers several practical advantages. By removing the
reward model, DPO avoids the additional training overhead and the
instability commonly associated with PPO-style updates. Because the
objective operates directly on log-likelihood ratios, training is typically more
stable and easier to diagnose. From a computational perspective, the training
loop closely resembles supervised fine-tuning, with preference pairs
replacing single target outputs. Despite its simplicity, DPO demonstrates
strong alignment with human preferences and, across many benchmarks,
matches or exceeds the performance of traditional RLHF methods.
Group Relative Policy
Optimization (GRPO)
If DPO represents a simplification of RLHF by removing the explicit
reinforcement learning loop, GRPO tackles a different pain point: the cost
and instability of policy-gradient methods at a large scale. GRPO is a
reinforcement learning method proposed in DeepSeek-V3 as a scalable
alternative to Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). It was designed to
improve sample efficiency, training stability, and computational cost
when fine-tuning LLMs with reinforcement signals.
Instead of computing rewards for single samples independently (as in PPO),
GRPO introduces group-based normalization: responses are sampled in
groups, and their rewards are normalized relative to each other. This
reduces variance in gradient estimates and avoids the need for a separate
learned value function (critic), which is typically required in PPO.
In standard PPO, the objective is to maximize the expected reward with a
KL penalty to keep the new policy close to the old policy . The
clipped objective is:
where
is the likelihood ratio, and is the advantage function, usually
estimated by a separate critic network.
While effective, this setup is expensive and operationally complex. PPO
requires training and maintaining both a policy model and a value model,
along with careful tuning of clipping thresholds, advantage estimation,
normalization, and rollout collection. As model sizes grow, these costs
quickly dominate training.
GRPO simplifies this picture by changing how advantages are computed. It
eliminates the need for a critic by normalizing rewards within a group of
responses to the same prompt.
1. For each prompt , sample a group of responses from the
current policy .
2. Compute their scalar rewards (from human feedback,
automated metrics, or preference models).
3. Normalize these rewards within the group:
where and are the mean and standard deviation of rewards
across the group.
4. The GRPO objective is then deceptively simple:
with
This resembles policy-gradient optimization, but with group-relative
advantages instead of critic-based ones.
This small shift has several important consequences:
No value function needed: Unlike PPO, GRPO doesn’t train a critic
model. Advantages are computed by normalizing rewards across
sampled responses.
Lower variance: Group normalization stabilizes updates, since the
relative quality of responses is more consistent than absolute reward
values.
Scalable to LLMs: Sampling multiple responses per prompt is natural
in large-batch distributed training.
Better sample efficiency: Each prompt provides multiple useful
gradient signals, not just one.
The intuition behind GRPO is simple. Instead of asking: “Is this single
response good in absolute terms?”
GRPO asks: “Within this group of responses to the same prompt, which ones
are better and by how much?”
This makes optimization more robust, since models often care about relative
preference (choosing the best answer among candidates) rather than
absolute reward magnitudes.
At this point, we have seen several complementary ways of aligning model
behavior. Across PPO-based RLHF, DPO, and GRPO, the common goal is
the same: when faced with many plausible continuations, the model should
consistently favor the ones humans prefer. These methods differ mainly in
how they trade off stability, complexity, and scalability.
Alignment alone, however, is not the full story. A model that prefers the right
answers does not automatically know how to arrive at them. Many tasks,
including mathematics, coding, planning, and data analysis, benefit when the
model reasons through intermediate steps before producing a final response.
The next section turns to this problem directly. It formalizes the notion of
reasoning and shows how to train it, both when step-by-step solutions are
available and when only final answers are labeled. These objectives pair
naturally with the LoRA or QLoRA adapters trained earlier, or with the
aligned policies produced by the methods discussed here.
Reasoning in LLMs
To study reasoning in LLM, we need a formal framework that makes explicit
what the model observes, what it constructs internally as intermediate
reasoning, and how this reasoning leads to a final answer. By grounding
reasoning in equations and notation, we can analyze training objectives that
directly supervise reasoning, indirectly encourage it, or align it through
preferences.
Inputs, reasoning, and outputs
Let the input prompt or problem be denoted by
This input could be a natural language question, a conversational history, or
a structured query. The role of the model is to transform this input into a
reasoning process and, ultimately, an answer.
Rather than producing an answer in a single step, reasoning unfolds as a
sequence of intermediate states or “tokens of thought.” We denote these by
Here, is the length of the reasoning process, and each can represent a
natural language token, a symbolic operation, or an action in a latent
reasoning space.
If the model is performing chain-of-thought reasoning, each corresponds
to one token in the reasoning chain. If the model is executing program-like
reasoning, may instead represent function calls or logical steps.
After completing the reasoning process, the model produces a final answer:
This is the explicit response to the user’s query (e.g., “Paris” as the capital
of France). While task success is usually judged by the correctness or
usefulness of , the intermediate sequence provides insight into how the
model arrived at that answer.
In practice, what an LLM actually emits is a single trajectory string

Probabilistic modeling
An LLM is fundamentally a probabilistic generative model. Its behavior is
determined by a high-dimensional set of parameters, which we denote by
These parameters encompass all of the model’s neural weights (e.g., the
matrices within attention layers, feed-forward layers, and embedding layers).
Collectively, they encode the statistical knowledge acquired during
pretraining.
Formally, given an input prompt , the model defines a conditional
distribution over possible output trajectories:
Here:
is a trajectory consisting of reasoning tokens and a final
answer.
Each token is drawn sequentially, conditioned on the prompt and
all preceding tokens.
The autoregressive factorization makes this explicit:
where . This factorization underlies the model’s ability
to generate coherent sequences one token at a time while still defining a
valid probability distribution over complete trajectories.
In practice, especially in alignment settings, we do not optimize the model
distribution in isolation. Instead, we compare it to a reference policy .
The reference policy is typically a pretrained model before alignment or
fine-tuning, such as the base LLaMA, GPT, or Falcon checkpoint. Its
purpose is to serve as an anchor.
The reference policy plays several distinct roles:
Language fluency anchor: The reference policy ensures that the model
retains general language competence and does not diverge toward
unnatural or incoherent outputs during alignment.
Regularization role: Alignment objectives often involve explicit or
implicit KL-divergence penalties that keep the aligned policy close to
:
This acts as a safeguard against mode collapse, distribution drift, or
over-optimization toward narrow objectives.
Baseline for preference models: In preference-based alignment (e.g.,
RLHF or DPO), the reference policy provides the baseline logits that
are adjusted based on human or synthetic feedback.
Latent-step factorization
While the autoregressive formulation describes how trajectories are
generated, it does not explicitly distinguish between intermediate reasoning
steps and the final answer. To model reasoning more explicitly, we introduce
a latent-variable perspective.
Let represent the sequence of intermediate reasoning
tokens, and let be the final answer. Then the joint distribution can be
written as:
This decomposition reflects the idea that reasoning trajectories are causal
mediators between the input and the final prediction . The model first
samples a rationale conditioned on the problem, and then produces an
answer conditioned on both the rationale and the input.
Training regimes
Given this probabilistic formulation, reasoning can be trained under several
distinct regimes, depending on what supervision signals are available. In
some settings, intermediate reasoning steps are explicitly labeled, allowing
the model to learn directly from human-provided rationales. In others, only
final answers are observed, requiring the model to infer and marginalize over
latent reasoning processes. Finally, when neither steps nor answers are fully
specified, preference-based signals can be used to shape entire reasoning-
and-answer trajectories. The following sections examine these regimes in
turn.
Regime 1: Supervised reasoning with
ground-truth steps
In many reasoning datasets, the intermediate steps are explicitly annotated.
This is often referred to as chain-of-thought supervision, where annotators
provide not only the correct final answer but also a detailed sequence of
reasoning steps. Such data gives us direct access to the latent reasoning
variables introduced in the previous section, turning them from hidden to
observed quantities.
Formally, for each training example, we are given the following:
A problem or prompt:
A sequence of ground-truth reasoning steps:
A ground-truth final answer:
The combined trajectory is then
Because the reasoning steps are observed, marginalization over is no
longer required. The training objective reduces to maximizing the likelihood
of the observed trajectory. Recall the latent-step factorization:
When reasoning steps are unobserved, the model must marginalize over all
possible rationales. This is intractable in practice. However, when reasoning
steps are annotated ( ), the marginal collapses to a single joint term:
The supervised objective then becomes the negative log-likelihood of the
observed trajectory:
Since the LLM is autoregressive, the joint likelihood in equation (A) can be
factorized token by token. Writing the trajectory string , we have:
where denotes all tokens before step .
Plugging this into equation (B) yields the familiar teacher-forced likelihood:
This is the standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) loss applied to
trajectories that include explicit reasoning.
Training on annotated reasoning has several important effects:
Lower-entropy predictions: Each reasoning token conditions the
next, making the conditional distributions narrower than predicting
directly
Better generalization: The model learns reusable inference patterns,
not just direct input–output mappings
Interpretability: Because the model is trained to emit reasoning steps,
its predictions provide natural explanations
In short, the model learns not only what to answer but also how to arrive at
the answer.
Practical implementation
Supervised reasoning with explicit rationales is powerful but
computationally intensive, since trajectories are longer than single-shot
answers. In practice, the following techniques make training feasible:
LoRA / QLoRA adapters: Instead of tuning all weights, insert low-
rank adapters into key matrices (e.g., ). Update only the adapter
parameters . With QLoRA, the base is quantized to 4-bit for
further memory savings.
Gradient checkpointing: Recompute intermediate activations during
backpropagation to reduce memory consumption for long rationales.
Mixed-precision training: Training with fp16 or bf16 precision
improves efficiency without compromising stability.
Micro-batching: Split long sequences into smaller sub-batches,
accumulate gradients, and update jointly.
This supervised setting illustrates the most straightforward use of the latent-
step framework. When reasoning steps are latent, we must marginalize over
them (Equation 1). When they are observed, we can directly condition on
them, yielding the preceding simple negative log-likelihood objective.
Supervised chain-of-thought training can therefore be viewed as the
observed-variable special case of the general probabilistic reasoning model,
anchoring the model’s internal reasoning distribution to human-provided
rationales and making optimization both easier and more interpretable.
Regime 2: Supervised reasoning with
answers only (latent steps)
Fully annotated reasoning data is rare. In most practical settings, datasets
provide only final answers, while the reasoning process remains latent. This
is the setting of supervised reasoning with latent steps: the reasoning
variables are not observed, but we still want the model to learn a
distribution over them that supports accurate prediction.
Given a prompt and a labeled final answer , the ideal training objective
would be to maximize the log-likelihood of the answer:
Here, the sum runs over all possible reasoning trajectories . Intuitively, the
model is asked to assign high probability to the correct answer regardless of
which reasoning path supports it.
However, in practice, this marginalization is intractable: the space of
possible rationales is exponentially large, and summing over them directly
is computationally infeasible. To address this challenge, we introduce an
auxiliary inference model (sometimes called a teacher or guide), denoted by
This model proposes candidate reasoning trajectories conditioned on both
the input and the correct answer. For example:
could be a stronger teacher LLM that generates rationales
It could be a self-trained sampler, producing candidate chains filtered
by a verifier
Or, it could be a program generator if the reasoning steps are executable
instructions
Using the inference model, we apply variational inference. Starting from the
ideal objective:
Jensen’s inequality gives us a tractable lower bound, known as the Evidence
Lower Bound (ELBO):
Expanding the joint likelihood inside the expectation yields the ELBO
objective:
This formulation has a clear interpretation:
The answer likelihood term encourages the model to make use of
reasoning steps to predict the correct answer
The reasoning prior term encourages the model to favor plausible
reasoning paths that are consistent with the input distribution
The inference regularizer prevents the inference model from
collapsing to degenerate solutions by regularizing its posterior
distribution
Several practical designs exist for . One option is rationale distillation,
where a stronger teacher LLM generates reasoning traces that are transferred
to the student model. Another approach is self-sampled rationales, in which
the model proposes candidate reasoning paths that are filtered using a
verifier for correctness or consistency. When reasoning steps are naturally
executable, such as in mathematical derivations or code, a program generator
can be used to provide structured reasoning trajectories.
When neither explicit reasoning steps nor gold answers are available, this
supervised framework gives way to preference-based objectives, where
training proceeds using preferences over complete reasoning-and-answer
trajectories. This setting is explored in the next regime.
Practical implementation
Although the ELBO formulation makes explicit the probabilistic structure
underlying reasoning, its practical realization requires a concrete data
representation that can be consumed by a training pipeline. In particular,
variational reasoning assumes access to triplets , where denotes the
input prompt, denotes a candidate reasoning trajectory, and denotes the
target answer. In practice, these quantities are serialized and stored in a
structured format, most commonly as JSON Lines (JSONL), with one
record per training instance.
Each record encodes the input as a text prompt, the reasoning process
as an ordered sequence of intermediate steps, and the final
answer as a text completion. A representative example is shown here.
{
“input”: “If Alice has 3 apples and buys 2 more, how many appl
“reasoning”: [
“Alice starts with 3 apples.”,
“Buying 2 more increases the total by 2.”
],
“answer”: “5 apples”
}
This representation aligns directly with the ELBO objective. The answer
likelihood term is optimized by conditioning the
generative model on the concatenation of the input and the reasoning
sequence and maximizing the likelihood of the final answer. The reasoning
prior term is implemented by training the model to
assign high probability to plausible reasoning trajectories given the input
alone. The inference regularization term is
computed by an inference model that scores the same reasoning sequence
when conditioned jointly on the input and the target answer.
Under this formulation, each serialized training example provides all
components necessary to evaluate and optimize the ELBO. As a result,
variational reasoning can be implemented using standard sequence-to-
sequence training infrastructure, with the distinction between the generative
model and the inference model realized through different conditioning
contexts rather than specialized data structures. This grounding of abstract
probabilistic objectives in an explicit data format closes the gap between
theoretical analysis and practical implementation.
Regime 3: Preference-based
reasoning objectives
In the previous sections, we studied supervised reasoning in two regimes:
when reasoning steps are explicitly annotated, and when only final answers
are available. However, in many practical alignment scenarios, neither
explicit rationales nor even large numbers of gold answers are available.
Instead, we may only have preferences between candidate trajectories.
That is, for a given prompt , we may observe that a trajectory
is judged preferable to another trajectory
These preferences could be collected from human annotators or derived from
automated heuristics (e.g., safety filters, correctness checks, or user
engagement signals). Preference data tells us which reasoning-and-answer
combination is better, without requiring explicit labels for the reasoning
steps.
The standard framework for learning from preferences is RLHF. In this
approach, a reward model is first trained from pairwise preference
data using a probabilistic ranking model, commonly the Bradley–Terry
formulation:
This allows us to estimate a scalar reward for each trajectory.
The language model policy is then optimized using Proximal Policy
Optimization (PPO), with KL regularization against a reference policy :
Here:
is the importance ratio.
is the advantage estimate.
The KL penalty ensures that the aligned model remains close to the
pretrained reference, preventing reward hacking or degeneration of fluency.
Overall, PPO pushes the model toward trajectories that receive higher
learned reward while maintaining stability through KL control.
While PPO requires explicit reinforcement learning, DPO bypasses RL
entirely. Instead, it directly optimizes the policy to respect preferences. The
DPO objective takes the form:
Here, the difference between log-probabilities of preferred and rejected
trajectories forms the central signal, and the reference model provides
implicit KL regularization. DPO aligns the policy directly with preferences
without requiring a separate reward model or explicit policy-gradient
updates. Since trajectories include both reasoning and answers , DPO
implicitly aligns reasoning styles (e.g., clarity, truthfulness, safety) in
addition to correctness.
Another approach is GRPO, which compares multiple candidate trajectories
for the same prompt.
For a given prompt , sample trajectories
Each trajectory’s reward is normalized relative to the group mean:
Policy updates are then performed using these group-relative advantages. By
focusing on relative quality within a set of candidates for the same prompt,
GRPO reduces variance and improves stability. This is particularly important
for reasoning tasks, where absolute reward magnitudes may vary
substantially with problem difficulty or rationale length.
Practical implementation
All preference-based objectives (PPO, DPO, and GRPO) can be
implemented efficiently using LoRA/QLoRA adapters. In these setups, only
the low-rank adapter matrices are updated, while the base model
remains frozen and is often quantized to 4-bit precision in the QLoRA case.
This allows preference-based alignment to scale to very large language
models without prohibitive memory or compute costs.
Summary
This chapter showed how to turn a broad, pretrained language model into a
reliable specialist without touching most of its billions of weights. We began
with parameter-efficient fine-tuning, introducing LoRA as a low-rank update
inserted into selected linear modules so the base model
stays frozen while a tiny set of adapter parameters learns the task. With the
paper-standard initialization , the update is zero at step
zero, preserving the pretrained function and stabilizing optimization. QLoRA
then pushed efficiency further by storing the frozen base in 4-bit
quantization (e.g., NF4 with double-quantized scales) and training the same
adapters in bf16/fp16; dequantization happens just-in-time for compute, so
very large models can be adapted on a single modern GPU. We closed the
loop operationally: where to place adapters (typically , and
optionally and MLP), how to choose ranks and scales, and when to
merge adapters into the base for lowest-latency inference versus serving
them as a separate branch for flexibility.
On top of adaptation, we treated alignment as the art of shaping model
behavior toward human preferences while remaining anchored to a fluent
reference policy. RLHF framed alignment as reward-guided policy
optimization with PPO under a KL constraint to the reference; DPO replaced
explicit RL with a direct, reference-anchored preference objective; and
GRPO stabilized learning by comparing candidates within the same prompt
using group-relative advantages. Because each of these methods updates
only adapter parameters, they pair naturally with LoRA/QLoRA, giving you
practical knobs to trade data, stability, and compute.
Finally, we formalized reasoning itself. A trajectory
comprises latent steps and an answer , generated autoregressively
Viewing as a mediator yields
. When steps are annotated, supervised
fine-tuning reduces to teacher-forced likelihood over , typically
lowering entropy and improving generalization. When only answers are
labeled, a variational treatment introduces an inference model
and optimizes an ELBO that balances using steps to predict answers,
preferring plausible steps, and regularizing the posterior. When neither steps
nor gold answers are plentiful, preference learning over whole trajectories
aligns both the answer and the style of reasoning.
The next chapter turns from shaping parameters and behavior to shaping
context. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) equips your aligned,
adapter-tuned model with fresh, verifiable evidence at inference time. We
will also introduce the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard way for
models to discover and call tools and data sources.

Advanced Setup and
Integration with RAG and

The era of LLMs marks a profound shift in software engineering. What
began as a research curiosity has rapidly matured into the core intelligence
layer for countless enterprise applications, fundamentally changing how
organizations process information, automate workflows, and interact with
data. Building a modern LLM application is far more complex than a simple
API call; it requires orchestrating a multi-layered cognitive stack that
integrates GPU hardware, data retrieval systems, persistent memory, and
dynamic decision-making agents. This engineering challenge spans model
efficiency, factual grounding, regulatory compliance, and system-level
observability, demanding expertise that bridges data science and distributed
systems architecture.
This chapter serves as a deep technical blueprint for constructing such
production-ready systems. We move beyond the basics of prompt
engineering to dissect the foundational elements that ensure LLM
applications are scalable, trustworthy, and cost-effective. We will trace the
architectural journey from bare-metal compute requirements, through the
choice between closed API and local open source models, to the design of
highly advanced, self-optimizing agent networks. The core focus is on
transforming a static LLM into dynamic, grounded, and composable
intelligence, using industry-leading frameworks such as LangChain,
LlamaIndex, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to solve real-world
problems in regulated sectors such as finance and healthcare.
In a nutshell, this chapter will cover the following main topics:
Core requirements for building LLM systems
Settng up an LLM application – API-based closed sourced models
Settng up an LLM application – local open sourced models
Advanced system design – retrieval-augmented generation
LangChain as an orchestration layer
LlamaIndex (GPT Index)
Advanced RAG optimizations
MCP: Seamless integration between LLM applications and external
tools

graphs
Core requirements for
building LLM systems
Developing, training, and deploying LLM applications requires a
sophisticated understanding of both hardware and software foundations.
Modern LLM systems are computationally intensive and sensitive to
variations in hardware performance, memory layout, and runtime
configuration. Furthermore, the infrastructure must adhere to strict standards
for security, privacy, and reproducibility, particularly in regulated
environments such as healthcare, finance, and government sectors.
This section provides a comprehensive overview of the core technical
requirements for building efficient, scalable, and secure LLM systems.
Hardware and compute
foundations
At the core of modern LLM systems is the choice of compute hardware, with
Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) serving as the primary enabler of large-
scale model training and inference. Their architecture, optimized for
massively parallel computation, allows for the high-throughput tensor
operations required by transformer models. While CPUs remain valuable for
preprocessing, orchestration, and lightweight inference (such as sentence
embeddings or reranking models), GPUs dominate both fine-tuning and
large-scale inference.
For most practitioners, the choice of GPU dictates model capacity and speed.
A single consumer-grade GPU with 24 GB VRAM (e.g., NVIDIA RTX
4090) can efficiently serve models up to 13 billion parameters in 4-bit
quantization. Professional-class GPUs such as NVIDIA A100 and H100,
equipped with 80–96 GB VRAM, enable inference of 70B+ parameter
models and support mixed precision (FP16, BF16) and tensor parallelism at
scale.
As an example, running Llama-3-70B in full FP16 precision requires
approximately 140–160 GB VRAM, typically distributed across two or more
A100s with model sharding enabled. In contrast, a quantized 4-bit version
can operate comfortably within 40 GB VRAM, making it deployable on a
single high-end GPU node.
Beyond raw hardware selection, practitioners must reason about the
computational cost of training and fine-tuning workloads in more formal
terms. These workloads are commonly estimated using Floating-Point
Operations (FLOPs). Each forward pass in a transformer block roughly
scales with , where is hidden dimension and is the number of
layers. For instance, a 7B parameter model requires approximately 1.4 × 10¹³
FLOPs per forward pass for a batch of 2,048 tokens.
Efficient pipeline design—such as activation checkpointing, tensor
parallelism, and gradient accumulation—is essential for distributing this
computational burden across devices. When fine-tuning, balancing memory
footprint against throughput determines whether a setup should emphasize
data parallelism (multiple replicas of the model on different data shards) or
tensor/model parallelism (splitting model parameters across GPUs).
To further reduce computation cost, many production systems rely on
quantization as a first-class optimization technique. Quantization techniques
significantly reduce both the VRAM footprint and the computational
overhead of LLMs. Transitioning from FP16 to INT8 or INT4 precision can
lead to 2–4× throughput gains with minimal accuracy loss when using
libraries such as bitsandbytes or GPTQ. Additionally, runtime systems such
as vLLM and Text Generation Inference (TGI) optimize memory paging
and kernel fusion, allowing sustained high-throughput inference under real-
world latency constraints.
As model sizes and workloads grow, single-device deployments quickly
reach their limits, making multi-GPU scaling unavoidable. Tensor
parallelism and pipeline parallelism allow horizontal scaling across GPU
clusters. Frameworks such as DeepSpeed and Accelerate automate
distributed computation setup, managing device placement, communication
backends (e.g., NCCL), and optimizer sharding.
When deploying production workloads, system architects must carefully
benchmark tokens per second (throughput) versus GPU utilization to ensure
cost-efficient scaling. Underutilized GPUs often indicate suboptimal batch
sizing or I/O bottlenecks—both of which can be alleviated using streaming
datasets and asynchronous prefetching.
Software ecosystem
A robust software ecosystem underpins every LLM application, translating
raw compute into usable, maintainable systems. Most modern LLM stacks
center around a small set of foundational libraries that abstract model access,
training workflows, and inference pipelines. Chief among these is Hugging
Face Transformers, which provides pretrained model checkpoints and
unified APIs for inference, fine-tuning, and tokenization across PyTorch,
TensorFlow, and JAX backends.
Complementary tools include the following:
Hugging Face Accelerate: Simplifies distributed training, gradient
accumulation, and mixed precision setup
bitsandbytes: Enables low-bit quantization and memory-efficient
inference
vLLM: Designed for ultra-fast inference with continuous batching and
memory-efficient KV caching
TGI: A production-ready server optimized for Hugging Face model
deployment with gRPC/REST endpoints
Ensuring reproducibility across this software stack is a critical operational
concern, particularly when multiple developers or teams collaborate.
Environment managers such as conda and Poetry lock dependencies,
maintain Python version consistency, and prevent conflicts between CUDA
and PyTorch releases.
A sample environment YAML might look as follows:
name: llm_env
dependencies:
- python=3.10
- pytorch=2.3
- cudatoolkit=12.1
- pip:
- transformers
- accelerate
- bitsandbytes
- vllm
For long-term maintainability, developers often containerize these
environments using Docker. A minimal Dockerfile includes the base CUDA
image, necessary drivers, and mounted model weights. This ensures parity
between local testing and production deployments.
Always tag Docker images with versioned model identifiers (e.g., llama3:7b-
instruct-v0.1) to maintain traceability in MLOps pipelines.
Beyond local reproducibility, production LLM systems benefit from
automation that integrates model workflows into standard CI/CD processes.
To streamline repetitive tasks, automated workflows using Makefiles or
GitHub Actions help validate model integrity, test latency benchmarks, and
trigger model reloads. For enterprise teams, integrating LLM applications
into CI/CD systems ensures that model updates propagate safely and
reproducibly.
Security, privacy, and
compliance
Security and compliance considerations are inseparable from production
LLM deployments, particularly in domains such as healthcare, finance, and
government. LLM applications frequently interact with multiple APIs—
embedding providers, vector databases, or model inference endpoints.
Storing credentials in plaintext within configuration files is a critical
vulnerability. Recommended best practices include the following:
Storing tokens in encrypted secret managers (e.g., AWS Secrets
Manager, HashiCorp Vault)
Using environment variables ( ) that are excluded from version
.env
control
Rotating keys regularly and restricting scopes to the minimum required
permissions
In parallel, sensitive data, especially in domains such as healthcare and
finance, must be encrypted both at rest and in transit. Adopt AES-256
encryption for stored datasets and enforce TLS 1.2+ for all network
communication. For datasets with Personally Identifiable Information
(PII), anonymization pipelines can substitute names, IDs, or addresses with
synthetic placeholders before entering the model’s context window.
Techniques such as federated learning or differential privacy can be
employed to train models collaboratively without centralizing raw data,
which is critical for institutions adhering to privacy regulations.
Regulatory compliance introduces additional, domain-specific constraints
that must be addressed. In healthcare applications, compliance with the
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) mandates
that all systems maintain the confidentiality, integrity, and auditability of
Protected Health Information (PHI).
For European deployments, General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
compliance requires mechanisms for data erasure (“right to be forgotten”)
and explicit consent tracking. Developers should ensure that all LLM logs,
caches, and vector stores allow selective deletion of user data upon request.

A strong technical foundation defines the ceiling of performance and
reliability for any LLM-driven system. Choosing the right compute,
maintaining reproducible environments, and implementing airtight security
practices form the triad of sustainable success. As models and frameworks
evolve, these principles remain the constant backbone upon which scalable
and trustworthy AI solutions are built.
Setting up an LLM
application – API-based
closed source models
API-accessed, closed source LLMs have become foundational infrastructure
for enterprises that require high availability, scalability, and access to frontier
model performance without the burden of model maintenance. Platforms
such as OpenAI (GPT-4/4o), Anthropic (Claude 3), Google Gemini, and
Cohere Command R expose fine-tuned instruction models via standardized
REST and streaming APIs.
From an engineering standpoint, these systems transform the traditional
model-centric workflow into a service-oriented paradigm where inference is
obtained as an on-demand transaction.
This section details the technical aspects of using hosted LLM APIs at
production scale: authentication, concurrency design, caching, prompt
optimization, and reliability engineering. It concludes with a fully specified
summarization agent example demonstrating asynchronous orchestration,
semantic caching, and deployment architecture.
Architecture of the API
paradigm
At a systems level, API-based LLMs can be understood as remote execution
environments, where each inference request corresponds to a forward pass
performed entirely within the provider’s infrastructure. A serialized JSON
request encapsulates the following:
Prompt context: Messages, role annotations, or input tokens
Decoding parameters: Temperature, top-p, maximum tokens
Control metadata: User/session identifiers, request IDs, trace tags
The provider performs tokenization, model inference, and detokenization
internally, returning structured completions and telemetry (token counts,
latency, and finish reason).
This architecture abstracts the physical model topology and accelerators
away from the client.
Figure 9.1: API-based workflow
Because inference is fully externalized, API-based systems behave closer to
RPC calls than local model invocations. Network latency, bandwidth, and
provider throttling thus become critical system-level considerations.
Advantages and trade-offs
From an engineering perspective, this architectural shift introduces a distinct
set of benefits and limitations. On the upside, API-based LLMs provide
immediate access to frontier models trained on trillion-token corpora, elastic
scaling without GPU life cycle management, and relatively stable latency
and version control managed by the provider. These properties make hosted
APIs particularly attractive for rapid prototyping and early-stage production
deployments.
At the same time, this convenience comes with trade-offs that must be
explicitly acknowledged. API consumers typically lack access to model
weights and internal representations, limiting interpretability and
customization. Applications also inherit dependencies on provider
availability, pricing structures, and update cadence. From a data governance
standpoint, transmitting prompts to external services introduces potential
privacy exposure, and continual model updates can result in non-
deterministic outputs over time. Taken together, these characteristics favor
architectures optimized for API-layer efficiency and resilience rather than
deep model-level control.
API integration and resilience
design
Designing reliable integrations with hosted LLM APIs requires treating them
as non-deterministic, network-bound dependencies rather than deterministic
local functions. Authentication is typically handled via bearer tokens or
service-specific credentials. Tokens must be stored in isolated secret
managers (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or GCP Secret Manager) and
injected at runtime via environment variables:
import os
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.environ[“OPENAI_API_KEY”])
Secrets should never be persisted in container layers, logs, or version
control, and access scopes should follow the principle of least privilege,
ideally bound to a single service account.
Once authenticated, applications interact with LLM APIs using a
standardized request schema. Most providers follow a message-array format
that supports multi-turn conversational context, allowing system, user, and
assistant messages to be composed dynamically. A canonical OpenAI-style
request might look as follows:
msgs = [
{‘role’: ‘system’, ‘content’: ‘You are an expert tec
{‘role’: ‘user’, ‘content’: ‘Explain rotary embeddin
]
response = client.chat.completions.create(
model=’gpt-4o’,
messages=msgs,
temperature=0.4,
max_tokens=400
)
text_output = response.choices[0].message.content
Underneath, tokenization and decoding are deterministic given identical
seeds and model snapshots, though many APIs intentionally disable fixed
seeds in multi-tenant environments to preserve fairness. Even with identical
inputs, outputs can vary due to sampling and provider-side changes, so treat
responses as non-deterministic.
From a reliability standpoint, LLM APIs must be treated as non-
deterministic network resources. Transient failures such as timeouts, HTTP
429 rate-limit responses, or 5xx server errors should trigger retry logic with
exponential backoff. A common pattern is to wrap API calls in resilient
async functions, as in this example (make sure to install the
pip backoff
package):
import httpx, asyncio, backoff
@backoff.on_exception(
backoff.expo, (httpx.RequestError, httpx.HTTPStatusError)
)
async def invoke_llm(prompt):
async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=45) as s:
r = await s.post(
“https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions”,
headers={
“Authorization”: f”Bearer {os.getenv(‘OPENAI_API
},
json={
“model”: “gpt-4o”,
“messages”: [{“role”: “user”, “content”: prompt}
}
)
r.raise_for_status()
return r.json()[“choices”][0][“message”][“content”]
Such wrappers are often combined with task pools and semaphores to
maintain bounded concurrency and ensure compliance with provider-
imposed rate limits.
Because API calls are primarily I/O-bound, throughput scales with
concurrency rather than raw compute. Event-driven designs built on
frameworks such as Python’s asyncio or Node.js streams can sustain
thousands of concurrent in-flight requests per process. Architecturally, this
pattern decouples request ingestion from execution:
Figure 9.2: Asynchronous, rate-limited request pipeline
This decoupling allows the overlapping of computation (pre/postprocessing)
with I/O (network calls). Empirically, concurrency improves tokens-per-
second throughput up to the limit of provider quotas and network bandwidth.
Many providers also expose streaming interfaces that further improve
responsiveness and user experience. Using Server-Sent Events (SSE) or
WebSockets, tokens can be streamed incrementally as they are generated
rather than returned as a single payload. This reduces perceived latency,
often delivering the first token within tens of milliseconds, and enables
interactive user experiences such as live “typing” effects in chat interfaces.
Streaming implementations typically resemble the following simplified loop:
with client.chat.completions.stream(
model=’gpt-4o’,
messages=msgs
) as stream:
for event in stream:
if event.type == ‘token’:
print(event.token, end=’’, flush=True)
To support structured outputs in streaming mode, applications should
integrate incremental parsers capable of handling partial JSON fragments
without waiting for full completion.
System-level optimization
patterns
API efficiency becomes a cost and latency concern, making system-level
optimizations essential. Repetitive prompts are common in enterprise
applications. Implement a semantic cache layer keyed by vectorized by
vectorized prompt embeddings (code is conceptual):
if cache.exists(embedding(prompt)):
return cache.get(embedding(prompt))
else:
result = call_api(prompt)
cache.store(embedding(prompt), result)
This approach avoids redundant API invocations for semantically equivalent
queries, significantly reducing both latency and billing. Caches can be
implemented via FAISS or Redis vector similarity search, integrated through
middleware such as LangChain’s semantic cache.
Token efficiency is another critical optimization lever. Since token budgets
are hard upper bounds in API calls, prompt compression and context pruning
techniques are commonly employed. These include the following:
Context distillation: Retain only the last n conversational turns
relevant to the query
Symbolic compression: Replace repeated instruction blocks with
identifiers ( )
<POLICY_1>, <STYLE_GUIDE>
Summarized memory: Maintain rolling summaries of earlier
conversation history rather than raw text
These optimizations reduce token payloads and improve latency
predictability.
For downstream automation, enforcing structured outputs improves
determinism. Many APIs support JSON mode or function-calling interfaces
that constrain model outputs to predefined schemas:
functions=[{
“name”: “extract_entities”,
“parameters”: {
“type”: “object”,
“properties”: {“disease”: {“type”: “string”}, “drug”: {“
}
}]
This paradigm replaces brittle regex parsing with strongly typed
deserialization, increasing determinism in LLM pipelines.
A production-grade deployment must expose metrics that help teams
understand how the system behaves in practice, not just whether it is
running. Instrumentation should track request and response latency, input
and output token usage, model versions and decoding parameters, cache
effectiveness, and error patterns over time. By integrating OpenTelemetry
tracing and propagating correlation IDs across service boundaries, teams
gain end-to-end visibility into how requests move through the system. With
this foundation in place, centralized monitoring can surface subtle
regressions (whether triggered by prompt changes, traffic shifts, or provider-
side model updates) before they become user-facing issues.
Reliability, rate-limiting, and
governance
Providers typically impose per-minute and per-day quotas, requiring clients
to implement deterministic rate limiters backed by distributed counters in
stores such as Redis or DynamoDB. Without such controls, localized spikes
can cascade into global throttling events across microservices.
From a privacy standpoint, data transmitted to external APIs may traverse
multiple jurisdictions. Mitigation strategies include client-side encryption of
sensitive payloads, pseudonymization of PII, and, where available, the use of
provider options that guarantee zero-retention inference. For regulatory
frameworks such as HIPAA and GDPR, applications should enforce
ephemeral storage policies and implement explicit data deletion hooks
aligned with organizational compliance requirements.
API evolution introduces an additional governance challenge. Providers may
silently upgrade underlying models or decoding behavior, potentially
altering output style or factual grounding. To detect and manage such drift,
teams often deploy shadow inference pipelines that compare responses
across model versions. Prompt templates should be version-controlled
alongside application code to preserve reproducibility and auditability.
Example use case –
asynchronous document
summarization agent
To illustrate these concepts in practice, consider a document summarization
microservice that converts long research papers into concise abstracts using
an API-hosted model such as GPT-4o or Claude 3 Sonnet. At a high level,
the service can be understood as a sequence of loosely coupled stages, each
responsible for a distinct part of the summarization workflow:
1. Document ingestion layer: Receives uploads via REST endpoint and
extracts text with parsers such as or .
pdfminer.six python-docx
2. Preprocessing layer: Normalizes encoding, removes boilerplate, and
divides content into semantically coherent segments (~2,000 – 3,000
tokens) using cosine-based sentence similarity clustering.
3. Async inference layer: Each chunk is dispatched to the API
asynchronously using the resilient wrapper from the API integration
and resilience design section. Results stream back as partial summaries.
4. Aggregation layer: Combines partial summaries via another API call
that performs hierarchical synthesis, producing an executive abstract.
5. Semantic cache: Maintains a vector index of previously summarized
chunks for deduplication.
6. Postprocessing: Optionally performs factuality checks using retrieval-
augmented verification before returning the final output.
A minimal implementation skeleton might resemble the following:
async def summarize_chunk(text):
msgs = [
{“role”: “system”, “content”: “Summarize this text in 3
{“role”: “user”, “content”: text}
]
return await invoke_llm(msgs)
async def summarize_document(chunks):
results = await asyncio.gather(*[summarize_chunk(c) for c in
merged = “\n”.join(results)
synthesis_prompt = [
{“role”: “system”, “content”: “Merge the following summa
{“role”: “user”, “content”: merged}
]
return await invoke_llm(synthesis_prompt)
The asynchronous aggregation yields near-linear throughput improvement
with respect to available network bandwidth and API concurrency
allowance.
In practice, production deployments must also address the following:
Concurrency control: Employ semaphores or distributed queues to cap
concurrent API calls
Backpressure: If the provider slows, queue upstream documents in a
message broker (RabbitMQ or Kafka)
Persistence: Store intermediate summaries temporarily for auditability,
then purge them post-completion
Monitoring: Export metrics—average latency, token count per chunk,
and cache hit ratio—to Prometheus
Security: Encrypt all uploaded files at rest; remove plaintext after
summarization
This architecture demonstrates how a fully asynchronous, stateless service
can achieve high throughput using only external LLM inference endpoints,
with no on-premises GPU resources.
Setting up an LLM
application – local open
source models
While API-accessed LLMs simplify access to frontier intelligence, many
organizations demand on-premises or private cloud deployments to regain
control over data, latency, and model customization.
Running open source foundation models locally, such as Meta’s Llama 3,
Mistral, Falcon, or DeepSeek, enables complete autonomy across the model
life cycle: from fine-tuning and evaluation to secure deployment under
corporate governance.
This section provides a technical walk-through of how to architect, fine-tune,
and deploy local LLMs efficiently using modern open source infrastructure.
Selecting the right open source
model
The starting point for any local deployment is choosing the model. In
practice, model selection usually comes down to balancing three competing
considerations:
Parameter scale (capacity): Correlates with reasoning ability but
scales quadratically in compute and memory cost
Architecture design: Influences inference throughput and efficiency
(e.g., grouped query attention versus multi-head attention)
Tokenizer vocabulary: Affects token density and downstream fine-
tuning data compatibility
A 7B–13B parameter model represents the optimal “sweet spot” for most
enterprise applications—capable of robust reasoning while remaining
deployable on a single high-memory GPU.

Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), for example, reduces memory and
compute overhead by allowing multiple query heads to share key-value
projections, often delivering noticeable inference speedups without
materially degrading attention quality.
Once a candidate model has been identified, the next constraint is almost
always memory. Model storage and runtime footprint scale with both
parameter count and numerical precision, making quantization an essential
tool rather than an optional optimization. As shown in Table 9.3, moving
from FP32 to BF16, INT8, or INT4 dramatically reduces memory
requirements:

Environment and inference
setup
With a model selected, the next challenge is far more practical: getting it to
run reliably on real hardware. Local LLM deployments are particularly
sensitive to environment mismatches, so reproducibility and CUDA
compatibility need to be established before anything else. In practice, this
means pinning the Python runtime, deep learning framework, CUDA toolkit,
and supporting libraries from the outset:
conda create -n llm python=3.10 pytorch=2.3 cudatoolkit=12.1
pip install transformers accelerate bitsandbytes peft vllm
Before loading any models, it is worth validating that the runtime
environment is internally consistent. The following command provides a
concise snapshot of the active PyTorch, CUDA, and driver configuration:
python -m torch.utils.collect_env
In multi-GPU setups, teams should also verify that NCCL communication is
functioning correctly across devices, as misconfigured transports are a
common source of deadlocks during distributed training or inference.

Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
(PEFT)
Full-parameter fine-tuning is rarely practical for modern open source LLMs,
which is why parameter-efficient techniques have become the default. PEFT
methods dramatically reduce resource requirements by updating only small
subsets of weights while keeping the base model frozen.
One of the most widely adopted approaches is Low-Rank Adaptation
(LoRA), which injects trainable rank-decomposed matrices into existing
weight tensors:
where , and .
During training, only and are optimized, leaving the frozen base model
intact. Here’s an example implementation using the PEFT library:
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
config = LoraConfig(
r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=[“q_proj”,”v_proj”],
lora_dropout=0.05)
lora_model = get_peft_model(model, config)
This approach yields fine-tuned performance comparable to full-parameter
updates while reducing GPU memory footprint by >90%.
QLoRA extends this idea by pairing LoRA with aggressive quantization. By
keeping the frozen base model in 4-bit precision and training adapters in 16-
bit precision, QLoRA achieves near-fully fine-tuned quality on a single high-
memory GPU, such as an A100 80 GB.
The key parameters are the following:
bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.float16
bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True
for memory trade-offs
gradient_checkpointing=True
This hybrid quantized-fine-tuned design supports datasets of up to hundreds
of thousands of samples using 1–2 GPUs.
Data preparation plays an equally important role in fine-tuning outcomes.
Instruction-response datasets are commonly stored in JSONL or Parquet
format, with preprocessing steps that enforce consistent prompt templates,
respect context-length limits, and apply dynamic padding for efficient
batching. Validation sets should mirror production prompt styles to avoid
overfitting to academic or synthetic distributions.
Lastly, training stability depends on disciplined optimization and
checkpointing practices. Training should employ fused optimizers (e.g.,
AdamW8bit or Lion) combined with cosine learning rate schedules and
mixed-precision training ( ) to accelerate throughput while
bf16=True
maintaining gradient stability.
For reliability, do the following:
Save LoRA adapters every few epochs ( )
peft.save_pretrained
Enable gradient checkpointing to fit longer sequences
Evaluate using task-specific metrics (BLEU, ROUGE-L, or factual
consistency)
Model serving and deployment
Once fine-tuning is complete, inference servers expose the model via REST,
gRPC, or WebSocket endpoints. Modern inference stacks such as vLLM and
TGI dominate due to their optimized attention kernels and memory-efficient
KV caching.
vLLM introduces PagedAttention, an optimized GPU memory manager
enabling continuous batching and dynamic KV cache reuse. A local vLLM
instance can be launched as an API server with a configuration such as the
following:
python -m vllm.entrypoints.api_server \
--model mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 \
--quantization bitsandbytes \
--tensor-parallel-size 2 \
--max-num-batched-tokens 8192
In production settings, this design translates into several operational benefits:
Token throughput up to 10× Hugging Face baseline
Automatic batching across concurrent requests
Token streaming and OpenAI-compatible REST schema
TGI, built by Hugging Face, is a production-grade Rust–Python hybrid
serving layer optimized for low latency. A minimal deployment might look
like this:
text-generation-launcher --model-id meta-llama/Llama-3-8b-instruc
Out of the box, TGI is designed to support the following:
Multi-GPU sharding via tensor parallelism
Advanced sampling (temperature, top-k, nucleus)
CORS-enabled HTTP endpoints and metrics export
Both vLLM and TGI expose OpenAI-compatible APIs, enabling direct
integration with frameworks such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, or custom
frontends without modification.
In real deployments, inference engines are rarely exposed directly to end
users. Instead, lightweight application layers, often built with FastAPI, act
as proxies in front of vLLM or TGI instances. A typical service exposes an
endpoint such as or backed by a FastAPI microservice
/generate /chat

under load. Prometheus and Grafana are commonly used to monitor average

Because clinical summarization systems are frequently used in interactive or
near-real-time settings, inference performance also matters. Persistent key-

during incremental decoding, while pinned memory transfers and

Pre-batching tokenization reduces Python-side overhead, and mixed-

Advanced system design –
retrieval-augmented
generation
LLMs are powerful generative priors but remain knowledge-stale—they can
only reason over information encoded in their training data. This limitation
becomes immediately visible in enterprise settings, where answers must
reflect current policies or proprietary knowledge. To enable up-to-date
factual grounding, enterprise systems integrate external retrieval components
that feed domain-specific context into the model’s prompt. This hybrid
architecture, known as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), bridges
the gap between static pretraining and dynamic real-world data access.
Formally, RAG decomposes response generation into two coupled stages:
where is the user query and returns top-k relevant
documents from a corpus, using a semantic embedding similarity function.
This section presents a full stack design of a production-grade RAG system
—from data ingestion and chunking to embedding, retrieval, prompt
assembly, and evaluation—with engineering-level depth.
RAG pipeline
From an engineering perspective, a production RAG system is best
understood as a pipeline rather than a single component. At its core, even a
minimal RAG system is composed of several loosely coupled layers that
transform raw data into grounded model inputs. These include the following:
1. Data ingestion layer: Collects unstructured or semi-structured content
(PDFs, knowledge bases, SQL, API feeds)
2. Chunking layer: Segments raw text into manageable, semantically
coherent units
3. Embedding layer: Maps chunks into dense vector space for efficient
similarity computation
4. Retrieval layer: Performs Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN)
search to identify context-relevant documents
5. Generation layer: Injects retrieved content into the model’s prompt
and generates the response
Each layer has tunable design parameters that directly affect latency, recall,
grounding, and hallucination rates.
Chunking: The forgotten critical
stage
Chunking—the process of splitting documents into semantically coherent
units—is the single most underestimated variable in RAG performance.
Chunk granularity determines both retrieval recall (how often relevant
information is retrieved) and prompt efficiency (how many tokens the LLM
consumes).
The simplest approach relies on fixed-length, overlapping windows. Text is
divided into overlapping windows of tokens with stride, .
If and , each chunk overlaps by 384 tokens:
def sliding_window_chunk(tokens, window=512, stride=128):
for i in range(0, len(tokens), stride):
yield tokens[i:i+window]
This strategy preserves continuity but introduces redundancy, inflating
storage requirements and index size while often including irrelevant context
within each chunk.
To reduce this redundancy, more sophisticated approaches rely on sentence
boundaries and semantic coherence. Instead of slicing text mechanically,
documents are first segmented into sentences using tools such as spaCy or
NLTK. Embeddings are then computed for adjacent sentences and merged
into chunks until semantic similarity drops below a defined threshold. The
result is variable-length chunks (often 150–400 words) that are denser in
meaning and less prone to cross-topic contamination.
More recent systems extend this idea further by adopting hierarchical
chunking strategies. In these designs, documents are represented at multiple
resolutions:
Micro-chunks of roughly 128–256 tokens for fine-grained retrieval
Macro-chunks of 512–1024 tokens for context summarization or cross-
document linking
Retrieval operates across both levels, selecting whichever representation best
matches the query:
This yields robust recall across heterogeneous corpora.
Building upon this standardized data flow, the optimization of text
segmentation within RAG systems necessitates a strategic choice between
structural and semantic partitioning methodologies to ensure high-fidelity
information retrieval. RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter offers a
computationally efficient, rule-based approach that hierarchically applies
separators—such as double newlines, single newlines, and spaces—to
preserve the structural integrity of paragraphs and sentences while adhering
to specific character limits. Conversely, semantic chunking prioritizes
thematic coherence by utilizing embedding models to compute the cosine
similarity between adjacent sentences, triggering a segment split only when
the semantic relationship falls below a predetermined threshold. While the
structural approach provides a lightweight solution for general document
processing, the semantic method effectively mitigates cross-topic
contamination by producing variable-length chunks that are denser in
meaning and more precisely aligned with the logical progression of the
source material.
Best practice would be to persist both levels in the vector index with
metadata referencing parent documents for traceability.
Chunking considerations extend beyond plain text. For tabular or structured
data, chunking involves schema flattening or record serialization:
{“table”: “patient_labs”, “columns”: [“date”,”test”,”value”], “r
For example, serializing rows from a clinical database into compact JSON
structures allows embeddings to support hybrid retrieval across text and
structured records—a requirement in many biomedical and financial
applications.

representations
Once documents are chunked, the next step is to map those chunks into a
vector space where semantic similarity can be computed efficiently.
Embeddings convert text into numerical vectors, , and the choice of
the embedding model defines the semantic topology of the search space.

structure and behavior of the retrieval space:

This two-stage approach balances recall (fast vector search) with precision
