We will now get into advanced methods and techniques when building
solutions with LLMs.
Enhancing LLM performance:
choosing between local, free
and remote, paid LLMs
Let’s consider the LLM itself to be a swappable inference backend behind
that retrieval layer. In software engineering terms, this follows the
dependency inversion principle: higher-level application logic depends on
an abstraction, not on a specific model provider or deployment choice.
Sometimes we want a free, local model, favorable for privacy and cost
control. Other times, a remote, paid model may be optimal, which may
enhance quality, latency, and tooling. We’ll also introduce LLMPop, a
Python library that assists us by providing a unified command for invoking
LLMs, local or remote, while the rest of the pipeline remains unchanged.
The next two subsections give us a practical decision flow. First, at the
application level, what we choose to deploy for a given product or
environment. Then, per request, how to route calls dynamically at runtime.
In this chapter, we start with explicit, rule-based routing for clarity and
transparency. More advanced approaches, such as semantic routing, where a
lightweight model classifies intent or task complexity before selecting the
target LLM, naturally build on the same abstraction and are discussed later
as an evolutionary next step.
Application-level model
selection
When we are choosing the default LLM stack for a product, we start with
the constraints of the application rather than abstract model scores:
Security and data residency: If our RAG corpus contains regulated or
high-sensitivity material such as PII, PHI, or trading IP, we may prefer
a local model path (e.g., Ollama on an air-gapped server or developer
laptop), so retrieved chunks never leave our boundary. Remote APIs
may still be viable, assuming that the compliance professionals
approve the relevant provider terms, data retention policies, and
regional hosting.
User experience expectations: Enterprise copilots and public-facing
assistants often warrant a remote, paid model because frontier models
deliver more consistent reasoning, better tool use, and longer contexts,
which are key for multi-hop answers and complex prompts. Internal
back-office tools, batch jobs, or prototyping flows can often run well
on local models, currently ranging from 7B to 13B parameters, with
acceptable quality.
Cost and scale: If we expect spiky or high traffic and strict SLOs,
remote providers give us elasticity and detailed per-token spend. If
usage is steady and we control the hardware, local models provide
near-zero marginal cost after setup, which is attractive for heavy
retrieval workloads.
Platform and licensing: Verify open-model licenses for commercial
use and redistribution. Verify API terms for caching, data use, and
safety requirements. Deployment targets, such as desktop versus server
versus edge, may further nudge us toward a particular option.
Technical maturity: If you already operate hardware that can support
local LLMs, those could be a fast win. If you want to move quickly
with minimal infrastructure setups, start remote and add local later for
specific tenants or workflows.
It is interesting to keep in mind that there is another option. Many
applications benefit from hybrid routing: run most traffic on a local “good-
enough” model for optimal cost/privacy, and escalate specific requests to a
stronger paid model when the task is hard, such as a weak retrieval signal,
multi-step reasoning, long context, or user-marked “high stakes.” This free
web app lets you experiment simultaneously with free LLMs and paid
LLMs and evaluate them against each other:
https://github.com/LiorGazit/llmpop/blob/main/note
books/multi_llm_webapp.ipynb.
Request-level model routing
Once we have made an application-level decision about our default
deployment, we still face a second, finer-grained problem: not every request
has the same requirements. Even within a single product, some questions
are trivial and well-supported by retrieved context, while others are
ambiguous, high-stakes, or require deeper reasoning. Request-level model
routing addresses this by deciding, at runtime, which model should handle a
specific task or user message. For each task, and sometimes each user
message, we route based on a small set of practical signals:
Capability and reliability: Frontier remote models tend to be best at
multi-hop reasoning, long context, tool use, and following instructions.
Local models have improved rapidly (quantized 7B–13B, some 70B
on strong hardware), but may lag on nuanced reasoning. In practice,
routers often treat context length as a first-class signal, estimating
prompt “pressure” by tracking the combined token count of
instructions, retrieved documents, conversation history, and the user
query, and escalating when this total length approaches the effective
context window of the local model.
Privacy and data gravity: If our retrieved snippets contain sensitive
IP or PHI, local inference avoids sending prompts off-box. With
remote APIs, we must validate provider data policies and opt-outs.
Latency and throughput: Local models are predictable once warmed
up, but depend on our hardware; remote models offer great latency
under typical load, with occasional rate limits.
Cost and predictability: Local models are $0 per token at runtime
(you pay in setup + hardware) but may incur electrical cost; remote is
usage-based with transparent per-token costs and good observability.
Licensing and deployment: Open-model licenses must be reviewed
for commercial redistribution, while API terms govern data usage,
caching, and safety obligations.
A pragmatic production stance is policy-driven routing. Here, we default
to a cost-efficient capable model, and escalate to a stronger paid model
when either of the following applies:
Retrieval returns low-confidence evidence
The user asks for high-stakes outputs
The task requires a long context or complex tool orchestration

any(re.search(p, text, re.IGNORECASE)
for p in math_markers + reasoning_terms)
def detect_specialization(text: str) -> Optional[str]:

These heuristics are intentionally basic but effective enough to steer routing
decisions in the absence of a trained classifier.
Capturing a resource snapshot
for local awareness
Since local models share hardware resources, we capture the current CPU
and available RAM. High CPU usage or low memory may cause the router
to prefer a remote model, even if the prompt would normally run locally:
def snapshot_resources() -> Dict[str, Any]:
try:
cpu = psutil.cpu_percent(interval=0.2)
mem = psutil.virtual_memory()
avail_gb = round(mem.available / (1024**3), 2)
return {“cpu_percent”: cpu, “available_gb”: avail_gb}
except Exception:
return {“cpu_percent”: None, “available_gb”: None}
This resource snapshot helps avoid running heavy local models when the
machine is already under load.
Scoring candidate models
according to routing goals
We combine the optimization target ( , , or ), prompt
speed cost depth
complexity, specialization, and resource snapshot to compute a numeric
score for each model. Lower scores are better:
def score_candidate(

“reasoning” in spec.tags or “complex” in spec.tags)

The cost-based weighting used here implicitly reflects a prior cost-benefit
study, translating per token pricing and model size into a simple cost proxy.
This allows the router to approximate relative cost efficiency without
computing an explicit dollar total per request.
Initializing and calling models
via a unified interface
We wrap the model initialization:
def init_model(spec: ModelSpec):
if spec.provider == “ollama”:
return init_llm(
model=spec.name,
provider=”ollama”,
provider_kwargs={“auto_install”: True,
“auto_serve”: True, “pull”: True},
temperature=0.0,
)
elif spec.provider == “openai”:
return init_llm(
model=spec.name,
provider=”openai”,
temperature=0.0,
)
else:
raise ValueError(f”Unknown provider: {spec.provider}”)
def call_model(
chat_model, user_prompt: str,
system_msg: str = “You are a helpful assistant.”
):
from langchain_core.messages import SystemMessage, HumanMes
result = chat_model.invoke(
[
SystemMessage(content=system_msg),
HumanMessage(content=user_prompt)
])
return getattr(result, “content”, str(result))
This unified interface makes it easy to switch between local and remote
models, while the rest of the pipeline stays unchanged.
Routing and dispatching the
request
The core router puts everything together. It builds the catalog, analyzes the
prompt, samples resources, scores candidates, and initializes the top-ranked
model. If initialization fails, it falls back to the next candidate:
def route_and_dispatch(
prompt: str,
*,
conversation_ctx: Optional[List[Dict[str, Any]]] = None,
optimization: str = “speed”,
runtime_info: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
allow_paid_models: bool = True
) -> Dict[str, Any]:
catalog = build_catalog(allow_paid_models)
complex_prompt = is_complex_prompt(prompt)
specialization = detect_specialization(prompt)
resources = snapshot_resources()
# Apply penalties if API quotas are low (for illustration)
quotas = (runtime_info or {}).get(“api_quotas”, {})
openai_quota_low = quotas.get(“openai_remaining”, 1000) < 5
ollama_quota_low = quotas.get(“ollama_remaining”, 1000) < 1
scored = []
for spec in catalog:
s = score_candidate(spec,
optimization=optimization,
complex_prompt=complex_prompt,
specialization=specialization,
resources=resources)
if spec.provider == “openai” and openai_quota_low:
s += 1.0
if spec.provider == “ollama” and ollama_quota_low:
s += 0.5
scored.append((s, spec))
scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
chosen = scored[0][1]
# Initialize and call; if fails, fallback to next candidate
error = None
response = None
try:
chat_model = init_model(chosen)
response = call_model(chat_model, prompt)
except Exception as e:
error = f”{type(e).__name__}: {e}”
if len(scored) > 1:
alt = scored[1][1]
chat_model = init_model(alt)
response = call_model(chat_model, prompt)
chosen = alt
return {
“chosen_model”: chosen.name,
“provider”: chosen.provider,
“notes”: chosen.notes,
“complex_prompt”: complex_prompt,
“specialization”: specialization,
“optimization”: optimization,
“resources”: resources,
“error”: error,
“response”: response,
}
This function encapsulates the routing logic, returning both the answer and
metadata about why the model was selected.

Understanding the trade-offs
we make and their
consequences
Given an identical retrieved context, differences in outcomes typically
surface with coverage, precision, and exposition:
Local: Concise, grounded, sometimes misses a subtle link or hedges
more, often perfectly usable for triage, especially when the context is
clear and short
Remote: Richer justification, better cross-referencing between
snippets, higher compliance with output format constraints
In business settings, discuss these trade-offs explicitly with the
stakeholders:
Quality vs. cost: Remote models’ answers cost money and export
data; local models’ answers are free and private, but may need more
follow-up
Latency vs. control: Local latencies are hardware-bound but
predictable; remote is fast on average with external rate limits and
quotas
Privacy vs. capability: If context includes sensitive material, err on
local unless you have strong contractual/legal support
Hardcoding a single backend wastes money (over-paying for easy
questions) or hurts quality (under-serving hard questions). We apply a
policy-driven routing:
Defaults to a capable local model
Escalates to a stronger remote model when any of the following hold:
Low retrieval confidence (e.g., cosine or inner-product
similarity below some threshold , thin context, or high
disagreement between top-k)
High-stakes intent (detected via rules or a small classifier, e.g.,
“surgery scheduling,” “legal exposure,” or “dosage changes”)
Task complexity (long questions, multi-step reasoning cues,
required tool use, or long context windows)
De-escalates back to local when the question becomes routine
With the mechanics of the router in place, we now step back and look at its
behavior. Rather than walking through code again, let’s focus on how the
same routing logic responds under different optimization goals and
constraints, and what trade-offs those choices imply in practice.
In our notebook, we have a lightweight router that
Ch10_LLM_routing.ipynb
chooses the inference backend per request rather than hardcoding a single
model for the entire application. The goal is pragmatic: keep the RAG
pipeline identical (same retriever, same prompt template, same formatting),
and vary only the LLM backend (local for privacy/cost and remote for
frontier reasoning) when the request characteristics suggest it.
Let’s observe how the code performs in different scenarios based on its
routing policy. We run the notebook, ideally in Google Colab, and observe
the following scenarios that are driven by different trade-offs.
Demo entrypoint and a first run: We run the router on a concrete
prompt – a code task asking for a Fibonacci function plus complexity
analysis – and print the decision summary. We see whether the router
chose a local or remote model, why it leaned that way (complexity,
specialization), and observe the model’s output.
Scenario – Optimize for depth on a coding task: We set the
optimization target to , which biases scoring toward reasoning-
depth
capable models. With paid models allowed, the router tends to prefer a
remote reasoning model. If paid models are disallowed, it picks the
strongest available local alternative. This demonstrates how a single
flag flips between enterprise-grade and offline modes without altering
the calling code.
Scenario – Optimize for cost on a math puzzle: We switch to ,
cost
pushing the router toward cheap or free paths. The same prompt flows
through the pipeline, but the candidate ranking changes, often selecting
a small local model unless the heuristic signals make a compelling
case for remote. The scoring weights used here implicitly reflect a
prior cost-benefit analysis, where factors such as per-token pricing and
model size were translated into a simple cost proxy, allowing the
router to approximate relative cost efficiency without computing an
explicit dollar total per request.
Scenario – Optimize for speed on a math puzzle: We set the target to
, favoring faster models according to their estimated base latency
speed
and size rank. On capable hardware, a small local model may win; if
local resources are busy, the router can tilt toward a fast remote option.
Variants without paid models: For each scenario, we also run with
paid providers disabled. The router still applies the same logic,
complexity, specialization, and resources, but the choice is constrained
to local candidates. This validates graceful degradation and ensures
that teams can operate fully offline when required.
What we learn from this notebook is that the router turns model choice into
a data-driven, per-request decision while the rest of the stack (retriever,
prompts, and evaluation) stays unchanged. We can articulate why a model
was selected, reproduce decisions, and iterate on policy parameters over
time. Most importantly, this approach scales from a developer laptop to
production clusters and supports both local privacy-first and remote frontier
deployments with a single, unified interface.
Case study 1: LangChain in
healthcare
In Chapter 9, we covered advanced RAG methods so the model can
reason over current, domain-specific facts rather than hallucinating or
demanding expensive fine-tuning. Now, we can dive into hands-on
examples in code.
Here, we’ll apply our skills to a concrete scenario and walk through the
architecture, the design choices, and the trade-offs between local (free) and
remote (paid) LLMs, without locking ourselves to any one vendor. The
code behind this example uses a compact stack (SentenceTransformers +
FAISS + a LangChain-compatible chat model) and an abstraction layer, so
we can swap the LLM backend in a few lines.
We must stress that these aren’t real medical notes and that
the people described in the notes aren’t real.
The scenario is that a hospital’s care team wants a faster way to surface
patient records based on random queries that they have:
“Who was that patient I saw last year who was pregnant with triplets?”
“Did I have a patient with a family history of cancer on both sides who
asked about a clinical trial?”
These are fuzzy, recall-driven queries. Traditional keyword search often
misses these because the note phrasing rarely matches the clinician’s
memory. A RAG pipeline is a better fit: we embed notes, retrieve
semantically similar passages, and then ask an LLM to synthesize an
answer only from the retrieved evidence.
Here are the requirements we’ll satisfy:
Relevance: Return the right charts/notes from semantic retrieval, not
string matches
Grounded answers: LLM replies must point to retrieved snippets
(reduced hallucinations).
Privacy options: Run locally when notes are sensitive, and switch to
remote when you need frontier reasoning
Swappable LLM: Keep retrieval the same while changing the
inference backend (local vs. remote)
At a high level, the flow is the following:
Figure 10.1: The pipeline we will apply for our healthcare use case
We’ll implement the following key components:
Embeddings: Use a SentenceTransformers model (for example, all-
MiniLM-L6-v2) to generate dense vectors for each note. This family
provides good quality-to-latency ratios and is widely deployed in
production RAG. The choice is pragmatic: fast, small, multilingual
variants exist, and they’re easy to run on a CPU.
Vector store (indexing): Store embeddings in FAISS. FAISS is
lightweight, fast, and free. For small to medium corpora and offline
demos, a flat index works well.
Retriever: At query time, embed the clinician’s question and search
top-k neighbors. In production, we’ll likely adopt the following:
Maximal marginal relevance (MMR) to encourage diversity in
the retrieved set
A hybrid retriever (sparse + dense), so obvious keyword hits
aren’t lost
Optional re-ranking (e.g., cross-encoder) when precision at
small k matters
Prompt composer: Assemble a prompt that instructs the LLM to
answer only from the provided context. Include the following:
A system instruction (domain role, tone, and a grounding rule)
The retrieved snippets (with short citations or note IDs)
The user’s question
Optional constraints (format JSON, list note IDs referenced,
include confidence)
LLM backend (swappable): We use a unification layer so the same
chain can call either of the following:
A local model (e.g., Llama 3.x/Mistral via Ollama) for private,
$0/token runs
A remote model (e.g., OpenAI GPT-5 class) for higher reasoning
quality and longer context
To make these routing ideas concrete, we now walk through a practical
implementation of an in-house healthcare chatbot. Using a simple rule-
based approach, this example shows how model selection can be performed
dynamically at runtime while keeping the rest of the RAG stack unchanged.
Follow the next steps to understand each part of the notebook and see how
you can build and extend this solution on your own.
You can follow along with the full implementation by
referring to the accompanying GitHub repository,
specifically, the
Ch10_in_house_chatbot_healthcare.ipynb
notebook, which mirrors the steps discussed here. To access
the repository link, follow the steps in the “Download the
example code files” section in the Preface.

Implement a simple LLM router
To avoid hardcoding our model choice, we can route each query
dynamically. The function bases its decision on the
choose_llm()
maximum similarity score of retrieved chunks, whether the query is
“highstakes,” and whether an OpenAI API key is present. The router
defaults to local unless the context is weak or highstakes. The
route_llm()
helper both reports and instantiates the chosen model:
def choose_llm(query, docs, api_key_present,
good_similarity=0.6, weak_similarity=0.3
):
max_similarity = docs[0][1]
high_stakes = any(kw in query.lower() for kw in [
“diagnos”, “treatment”, “prescrib”,
“legal”, “contract”, “compliance”,
“deadline”, “critical”, “must”, “policy”
])
if not api_key_present:
return “local”
elif max_similarity >= good_similarity:
return “local”
elif max_similarity <= weak_similarity or high_stakes:
return “openai”
else:
return “local”
def route_llm(query, docs, verbose=True):
api_key_present = bool(
os.environ.get(“OPENAI_API_KEY”, “”).startswith(“sk-”))
choice = choose_llm(query, docs, api_key_present)
if verbose:
print(f”The chosen model is {choice}.”)
if choice == “local”:
return init_llm(model=”llama3.2”, provider=”ollama”)
else:
return init_llm(model=”gpt-5.2-2025-12-11”, provider=”o
The function evaluates three simple signals:
choose_llm()
1. API availability: If there is no OpenAI key configured, we must run
locally. This covers laptops, air-gapped environments, or demos where
cloud access is intentionally disabled.
2. Retrieval tightness – maximum similarity:
Compute the maximum similarity among the retrieved items.
If , retrieval is confident:
max_similarity ≥ good_similarity
answers are likely “close to the surface.” We prefer local; it’s
cheaper, private, and good enough when the context is crisp.
If , retrieval is thin; the
max_similarity ≤ weak_similarity
model will need more reasoning and careful interpolation of
sparse cues. We escalate to remote to maximize quality.
3. High-stakes heuristics:
A minimal keyword check flags sensitive/critical intents (e.g.,
diagnosis, treatment, legal, compliance, and deadline).
If the request sounds high-stakes, we escalate to remote, even
when similarity is middling, prioritizing accuracy, instruction
following, and format compliance.
Retrieval confidence is a strong predictor of how much reasoning the LLM
must supply. The term confidence is meant to reflect the relevance of the
retrieved chunks with regard to the query. The
max_similarity = docs[0]
variable holds the maximal inner-product value for the retrieved
[1]
chunks, reflecting the relevance of the top retrieved chunk.
High-confidence retrieval means the answer is basically in the text; low-
confidence retrieval means the LLM must bridge gaps, where frontier
models pay off. The router uses this confidence signal, along with the
escalation rules described earlier, to determine how each request is handled:
Default behavior: When none of the escalation conditions hold, we
route to local. This lowers spend and keeps data in-house while still
producing grounded answers thanks to RAG.
Return value: The router returns a choice: local or OpenAI’s. The
wrapper that follows instantiates the proper chat.
Now, let’s review some particular examples and how the router dealt with
them.
Example 1: Simple
Let’s start with a simple query:
What patient complained about migraine
or headaches?
From a retrieval perspective, this is a straightforward case. Symptom
keywords ( / ) appear explicitly or via close paraphrase
migraine headaches
in many notes; the top-k results include a passage mentioning headaches
with high similarity ( ). In other words, the answer is
≥ good_similarity
retrieval-obvious.
Given this context, the router evaluates a few basic conditions. An API key
is available, and the maximum similarity score from retrieval is high. Based
on these signals, the router routes the request to a local model.
A local model is appropriate here for several reasons:
The task is mostly extractive. Identify which retrieved snippet
mentions headaches and synthesize a short answer citing that patient
ID.
Local small models handle shallow reasoning and short context
grounding well, especially when the prompt enforces “answer only
from provided context, cite IDs.”
We save costs and keep protected content on-box.
When reviewing the output, there are a few things to look for. The response
should be concise and should clearly reference the retrieved patient ID or
IDs. The risk of hallucination is minimal in this case, since the context
contains an explicit mention of headaches. If the local model’s answer is
minimal, that is acceptable here: the requirement is correctness and proper
citation, not stylistic richness.
Example 2: Difficult
Now, let’s look at a more difficult query:
Which patient could possibly
have relatives in Europe?
From a retrieval standpoint, this question is indirect and intentionally
ambiguous. The notes may not contain an explicit statement about relatives
in Europe, but instead offer weaker signals such as a recent trip to Spain,
immigration from Poland, or mentions that family members live abroad. As
a result, the top-k retrieved passages tend to be only loosely related to the
query, and the maximum similarity score often falls into a grey area,
somewhere between the and thresholds.
weak_similarity good_similarity
Given these signals, the router evaluates the situation more carefully. An
API key is available, but the maximum similarity score is not high enough
to indicate a retrieval-obvious answer. The query is also not high-stakes,
since it does not trigger a clinical decision or action. Under the default
policy, the router still routes the request to a local model, unless the
similarity score drops below the threshold, in which case
weak_similarity
the request would be escalated to a stronger model.
This makes the query a useful “borderline” test case for the routing policy:
If the local model is able to produce a correct, grounded inference
based on the retrieved context, it reinforces the default-to-local
strategy
On the other hand, if the model hedges appropriately or fails to make
the inference, the logs will typically show low similarity or low
confidence signals
When reviewing the output, there are a few key behaviors to watch for:
Does the model explicitly tie the claim to a retrieved snippet?
If the context doesn’t support a firm conclusion, does it suggest it lacks
sufficient evidence per the instructions? That behavior is more
valuable than an overconfident guess.
Example 3: Very difficult
Finally, let’s consider a very difficult query:
I might not have captured it
in my notes, but one of my patients seemed angry. Who might that
have been?
From a retrieval perspective, this is the hardest case so far. The query is
ambiguous and effective, asking about emotional state rather than an
explicit fact. Clinical notes rarely label emotions directly, so the retrieval
step often surfaces only weak or indirect matches. Similarity scores
frequently fall at or below the threshold. Any potential
weak_similarity
signal tends to come from subtle phrasing, such as repeated complaints,
mentions of raised voices, or tense interactions, if such cues exist at all.
Given these conditions, the router’s decision becomes clearer. An API key
is available, and the maximum similarity score is at or below the weak
threshold, which triggers escalation to a remote model. Even without that
explicit trigger, the nature of the task itself points toward escalation.
Inferring sentiment from sparse, implicit cues is something frontier models
handle more reliably than smaller local models.
So why escalate?
This is precisely the long tail where remote models justify cost: they
can parse nuance, follow stricter output formats, and avoid brittle
keyword dependence
If the evidence is truly insufficient, remote models are also better at
stating limits clearly while preserving citations
When evaluating the output, there are two acceptable outcomes. Either a
well-justified candidate with explicit reference or a one-sentence
“insufficient evidence” reply with a brief rationale.
Taken together, these examples highlight why simple routing rules are
effective. They are transparent and easy for stakeholders to audit, which is
especially important in regulated domains. They are also inexpensive to
maintain, since no additional training is required, and behavior can be
adjusted through threshold tuning. Most importantly, they align routing
decisions with business risk, escalating only when retrieval is thin or when
the task demands deeper reasoning.
With routing behavior established, we can now move on to the final feature
in this solution: conversation memory.
Applying conversation memory
At this point, our clinical staff is able to fetch patients’ records and details
based on ad-hoc questions. However, in real-world settings, the staff
member isn’t always able to articulate what they are looking for in a single
comprehensive question. It may be a discovery process. They may start by
asking one question, and then, based on the response, they may form a
follow-up question, and so on. In such a case, a memory mechanism must
be implemented. Without memory, the conversation could look like this:
Question: “Are there any patients who are above 65 years of age
Answer: “Yes, patient X is 67 years old, and patient Y is 93 ye
Question: “Is any of them living alone?”
Answer: “Your question asks about ‘them’ but you have not provi
As we can see from this conversation, the LLM has no context for the term
them in the second question, as the history of the conversation isn’t
available for the LLM with our current setting. So, let’s fix that.
To do that, we will simply enhance the full prompt that we send to the LLM
to include a clause for the conversation’s history. That means that after
every response, we will log the question that the user sent and the response
that the LLM gave, and we will add that to the next prompt. As a design
note, consider that the context (meaning the retrieved chunks that are
relevant for the conversation) may need to accumulate as well, so as to
always allow the LLM to have all the context necessary:
task_template_with_memory = “””{instructions}
Context:
{context}
Conversation history, later appears last:
{history}
Question: {question}
---
Response:
“””
That’s it, as simple as that.
We then put together the loop that iterates over the live conversation,
allowing the user to take turns with the LLM:
expended_top_k = 4
history = “”
retrieved_docs_memory = OrderedDict()
while True:
print(“\nYour input:”)
query_live = input()
if query_live.lower() == ‘stop’: break
print(“\nResponse:”)
docs_live = vector_db.similarity_search_with_score(
query_live, k=expended_top_k)
# Accumulate retrieved documents across turns
for doc, score in docs_live:
retrieved_docs_memory[doc.id] = doc
accumulated_context = format_documents(
[(doc, None) for doc in retrieved_docs_memory.values()
chosen_llm_live = route_llm(
query_live, docs_live, verbose=False)
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template(
task_template_with_memory)
response = (prompt | chosen_llm_live).invoke(
{
“instructions”: instructions,
“context”: accumulated_context,
“history”: history,
“question”: query_live
}
).content
print(response)
history += f”User Query: {query_live}\nResponse: {response}
Feel free to converse with the LLM about the patients’ information and try
different scenarios.
There is a point to be stressed with accumulating conversation history. Keep
in mind that as the conversation progresses, more and more history is
appended. That makes the prompt longer and longer and may go beyond the
maximum token count that the LLM can process. For that purpose, it is best
practice to implement a mechanism to keep the history below a certain
length. There are many ways to do so. The simplest one is to remove the
oldest part of the conversation history from memory (i.e., first in, first out).
More advanced techniques may be to identify the least relevant parts of the
conversation history, to summarize the conversation history, or even to
embed the conversation history and to apply a RAG mechanism to retrieve
the part of the conversation’s history on demand based on the current user
query.
To conclude this example of a full prototype of a practical solution to a real-
world problem, we can reflect on its practical implementation in response to
a need that healthcare professionals have, and how it can enhance their
practice while translating to a better care experience for patients. Both of
us, as the authors of this book and its previous edition, have experienced
firsthand how effective it is to join hands with medical staff and apply our
methods for supporting both research and clinical care. Some of those
projects have been written about and will give you a good view of applied
ML and AI in the healthcare setting, in particular (Daly et al., 2022; Do et
al., 2021; Agrawal et al., 2022).
Now that we have laid out the entire pipeline incrementally and derived a
full solution, let us see how it can be applied to a new use case from a new
industry, legal.
Case study 2: LangChain
design for legal document
analysis
We now have the “recipe” for a complete, end-to-end prototype of an in-
house chatbot. This is a full proof of concept that can be applied to any real-
world use case where the data is available in the form of free text, and the
wish is to automate the process of searching through the various text data,
and to converse with a model about the data that it finds.
Let’s see how, for example, we apply it to a case from the legal space,
where the data is the content of legal contracts.
Legal teams are drowning in contracts, vendor MSAs (Master Services
Agreements), NDAs (Non-Disclosure Agreements), DPAs (Data Processing
Agreements), SOWs (Statement of Work), each with subtly different
clauses that matter for risk, timelines, and revenue. Attorneys and ops
partners need fast, reliable answers to questions such as “Do we allow
automated data collection?” or “Which agreements mandate a 30-day
termination notice?” without manually skimming hundreds of pages. An in-
house, contract-aware chatbot turns unstructured agreements into a
searchable, conversational interface: it retrieves the exact clauses, cites
where they came from, and adapts to follow-up questions. The business
impact is shorter deal cycles, fewer missed obligations, and a stronger
compliance posture, while keeping sensitive documents inside our
boundary. With the same RAG skeleton we already built, we simply swap
the corpus and add light domain instructions to deliver immediate value to
legal and commercial teams.
To see how easily we can pivot our RAG plus routing pipeline from
healthcare to legal, let’s walk through a hands-on example using a dataset of
plain-English contracts. This notebook uses the same underlying stack:
SentenceTransformers for embeddings, FAISS for retrieval, and a simple
rule-based router to decide between a local and a remote model, while
tuning a few choices for the legal domain. Follow these steps to understand
the code and its rationale.
You can follow along with the full implementation by
referring to the accompanying GitHub repository,
specifically, the
Ch10_in_house_chatbot_legal.ipynb
notebook, which mirrors the steps discussed here. To access
the repository link, follow the steps in the “Download the
example code files” section in the Preface.

Format retrieval results for
grounding and citation
To feed retrieved clauses into a language model and ask it to reason over
them, we convert the (document, score) pairs into a human-readable string
that includes both the contract text and the identifying metadata. This helper
function will be reused for prompting and citation:
def format_documents(doc_list):
formatted_entries = []
for doc, _ in doc_list:
entry = (
f”Row index: ‘{doc.metadata.get(‘Table index’, ‘’)}
f”source: ‘{doc.metadata.get(‘source’, ‘’)}’\n”
f”page_content=’{doc.page_content}’\n”
“\nEnd of case.\n---\n”
)
formatted_entries.append(entry)
return “\n”.join(formatted_entries)

Implement a legal-aware LLM
router
The same simple routing logic used for healthcare can work here, but we
refine the “high stakes” keyword list to reflect legal concepts: terms such as
, , , or . If the query
governing law jurisdiction indemnify termination

def choose_llm(query, docs, api_key_present,
good_similarity=0.6, weak_similarity=0.3
):
# List of legal keywords that indicate high-stakes clauses
legal_high_stakes_terms = [
# Dispute resolution
“arbitration”, “aaa”, “class action”, “jury trial”, “in
# Liability and warranty
“indemnify”, “limitation of liability”, “damages”, “war
# Governing law and venue
“governing law”, “jurisdiction”, “venue”, “choice of la
# IP and licensing
“intellectual property”, “license”, “reverse engineer”,
# Termination and breach
“terminate”, “breach”, “notice”, “material breach”,
# Privacy and data
“privacy policy”, “personal data”, “gdpr”,
# Other catchalls
“refund”, “fees”, “export”, “assignment”, “third party”
“terms of service”, “acceptable use”
]
high_stakes = any(
term in query.lower() for term in legal_high_stakes_ter
max_similarity = docs[0][1] # highest similarity score amo
if not api_key_present:
return “local”
elif max_similarity >= good_similarity:
return “local”
elif max_similarity <= weak_similarity or high_stakes:
return “openai”
else:
return “local”
def route_llm(query, docs, verbose=True):
# Check if an OpenAI key is available
api_key_present = bool(
os.environ.get(“OPENAI_API_KEY”, “”).startswith(“sk-”))
choice = choose_llm(query, docs, api_key_present)
if verbose:
print(f”The chosen model is {choice}.”)
if choice == “local”:
return init_llm(model=”llama3.2”, provider=”ollama”)
else:
return init_llm(model=”gpt-5.2-2025-12-11”, provider=”o
This router ensures that straightforward contract queries run locally for
privacy and zero cost, while more complex or legally sensitive questions
can tap remote models when available.

Summary
In this chapter, we turned RAG from a concept into a production-minded
pattern we can reuse across domains. The core stack (SentenceTransformers
for embeddings, FAISS for vector search, and a LangChain-compatible chat
interface) stayed constant, while the model choice became a policy decision
rather than a hardcoded dependency. We learned how to navigate the trade-
offs between local (free) and remote (paid) models. Local models excel
when privacy, cost control, and offline operation matter; remote models
shine on multi-hop reasoning, long context, and strict format compliance.
We then operationalized those ideas with a per-request router. Lightweight
signals, retrieval confidence, prompt complexity, domain hints, resource
snapshots, and optimization goals (speed, cost, and depth) guided model
selection. The result is transparent, auditable behavior: default to local, and
escalate to a stronger remote model when evidence is thin, stakes are high,
or tasks are complex. Because the router and interface are unified, the rest
of our application remains stable and testable.
Two end-to-end examples demonstrated portability. In healthcare, the
system answered fuzzy, recall-driven clinician questions with grounded,
cited responses, while preserving privacy when needed. In legal, the same
blueprint became a contracts-aware assistant that retrieved exact clauses,
cited their sources, and supported drill-down follow-ups. Across both, we
added conversation memory with practical guardrails (truncation and
summarization), ensuring continuity without overrunning context limits. We
now have a reusable pattern with clean seams for model choice and policy
control. This foundation is exactly what we need for the next step.
In the next chapter, we’ll build on this foundation to design multi-agent
code solutions. We’ll see how multiple specialized agents, planners, tool
users, critics, and executors can collaborate, negotiate, or even compete to
solve complex tasks that exceed a single model’s comfort zone. We’ll
introduce advanced agent frameworks, show how our existing RAG and
routing patterns plug into them, and walk through real projects where
coordination, not just generation, becomes the core capability.

Multi-Agent Solutions and
Advanced Agent
Frameworks
At this point in the book, we have seen how language models answered our
questions. We will now use agents to pursue our goals. This chapter is our
bridge from clever prompts and tidy chains to systems that can plan, choose
tools, adapt, and stop on their own, reliably and within budget. We encourage
agentic design where real work is messy: multi-step, tool-heavy, and sensitive
to context. Rather than adding more LLM calls, we introduce a structure that
makes autonomy reproducible, auditable, and cost-aware.
We will set up a clear mental model in this chapter for when agents help and
how they work, the core topologies and interaction protocols that keep teams of
agents coordinated, and a concrete orchestration runtime in Microsoft Agent
Framework (MAF). We will translate the ideas into a running blueprint, an
executive-brief system, with explicit roles, typed tools, checkpointing, human-
in-the-loop (HITL) gates, and OpenTelemetry tracing. Along the way, we will
show how collaboration, negotiation, and constructive competition raise quality
and safety without runaway spend. By the end, you will be ready to build the
full multi-agent solution and measure exactly what each design choice buys
you.
In a nutshell, here’s what you’ll learn in this chapter:
Single-agent and multi-agent systems: overview and core concepts
Deep dive into MAF and advanced orchestration frameworks
Building multi-agent solutions with MAF
Strategies for agent collaboration, negotiation, and competition

We will start our agentic journey with an overview of the core concepts, and
later dive into novel methods and coding.
What is an agent?
This chapter marks a step up the abstraction ladder. In earlier chapters, we
began from classic NLP pipelines:
Figure 11.1 – Classic NLP pipeline
Then, we progressed to modern transformer-based LLMs, then to prompt-and-
tool patterns and retrieval-augmented workflows:
Figure 11.2 - Prompt-and-tool pattern
That trajectory naturally leads to the idea of agents: systems that can pursue
goals across multiple steps, choose tools as needed, maintain state over time,
and decide when to stop.
In this book, an agent is a program whose decisions are made by a language
model, not by a fixed, hardcoded rule chain. Concretely, the LLM plans the next
step, chooses whether and which tool to call and with what arguments, observes
the result, and then revises its plan in a loop until a stop condition is met. This
aligns with Hugging Face’s framing of agents as systems where LLM outputs
control the workflow and decide tool use and sequencing. Agency can vary
depending on how much control we hand over to the model.
Let’s review the following workflow:
Figure 11.3 – Prompt-and-tool pattern with autonomous loop
Prompts give us a way to ask models for work. Chains stabilize repeatable
sequences (e.g., draft → critique → revise). Tools use grounds models in
external capabilities such as search, code execution, databases, and calculators.
The next step is autonomy: let the system decide which sub-steps to execute,
which tools to use, and how to adapt based on intermediate results. An agent is
simply an LLM-centered program with a policy for deciding what to do next,
memory for carrying context across steps, and the ability to act and reflect.
Agents excel when tasks are as follows:
Compositional and open-ended: Multi-step objectives that can’t be
solved in one pass, as in this example:
Analyze a batch of documents, extract structured facts, verify
Tool-heavy: Problems that require choosing and sequencing specialized
tools, such as vector search, SQL, web calls, code execution, and policy
checks.
Long-running or stateful: Work that spans multiple contexts or
interactions, such as monitoring a source for updates or running a research
loop until quality thresholds are met.
Ambiguous but decomposable: Objectives that benefit from dynamic
planning, such as , or
if X fails, try Y split into subtasks A, B, C,
.
then integrate
So, when does a single LLM call or simple chain suffice? Not every solution
needs an agentic approach. In many cases, a single LLM invocation or a simple
chain is the most effective and robust choice.
Prefer simpler patterns when the following applies:
The task is well-specified and short-lived, such as
Summarize this one
document in 5 bullets
Latency or cost constraints are tight and do not allow for iterative
reasoning or tool use
The domain is predictable, and a static pipeline covers the vast majority of
cases
Observability is limited, and we can’t inspect or trace multi-step behavior,
as agents without observability are hard to debug
A practical rule of thumb is that if we can write down the exact sequence of
steps and it doesn’t need to adapt based on the data it sees, then we should start
with a chain. If the step order, tool choice, or stopping conditions depend on
what happens along the way, consider an agent to assert decision-making in real
time.
Understanding the core
concepts of single-agent and
multi-agent systems
This section marks a conceptual transition point in the book. Up to now, we
have focused on how to make language models useful through prompts, tools,
retrieval, and structured orchestration. Those techniques showed us how to
extend a model’s reach. What they did not fully address is how systems decide
what to do next when the path forward is not predetermined.
The objective of this section is to introduce the mental model required to move
from scripted workflows to decision-making systems. Agents represent that
shift. Instead of encoding control flow entirely in code, we allow a language
model to participate in planning, execution, and revision across multiple steps.
This is the foundation that enables autonomy, adaptation, and sustained problem
solving.
We begin with single-agent systems because they capture the core ideas in their
simplest form. By understanding how policy, memory, tools, and feedback
loops work together inside one agent, we gain clarity on where agents add
value, where they introduce risk, and how to design them responsibly. These
concepts recur throughout the chapter and later chapters, regardless of whether
the system contains one agent or many.
Only after establishing these fundamentals do we expand outward to multi-
agent systems. Multi-agent designs do not introduce fundamentally new
building blocks. Instead, they introduce coordination challenges. They amplify
both the strengths and the failure modes of agents through specialization,
interaction, and negotiation. That is why the discussion starts with anatomy and
guardrails, then builds toward collaboration patterns, protocols, and trade-offs.
In short, this section exists to give you a durable framework. One that helps you
decide when an agent is the right abstraction, how to design it cleanly, and how
to reason about scaling from a single decision-maker to coordinated systems
without losing control.
Anatomy of a single agent
A single agent wraps four pillars: policy, memory, tools, and an observe-act
loop governed by explicit termination criteria. The observe-act loop is the
mechanism that lets the agent iteratively take actions, inspect their outcomes,
update its internal state, and decide what to do next. Termination criteria define
when this loop must stop. They encode the conditions under which the agent
considers its objective complete, its budget exhausted, or further progress
unlikely. Making these stop conditions explicit is essential. Without them,
agents risk running indefinitely, revisiting the same states, or accumulating
unnecessary cost and latency. Understanding these components clearly will save
us time, money, and headaches.
Policy: planner/controller
The policy decides what to do next. At the preliminary and basic level, it maps
the pair to the next action. In LLM systems, the policy
(goal, current state)
is often implemented with a prompt-conditioned model call plus a compact,
structured schema for the action space, such as the following:
call search(query=...)
Here is another example:
draft(answer=...) and stop.
Here are some points to keep in mind for maintaining a robust design.
We may constrain the agent’s actions with JSON schemas or function-calling
specs to prevent hallucinations around the tool names or the names of their
arguments. We can also assert guardrails, such as allowing or denying tools
based on data sensitivity and user permissions. Applying budget-aware
planning could be a useful approach as we include tokens, cost, or latency in
the prompt so the agent plans within limits.
Memory: short and long term
Agents need a defined state to avoid going in circles and to improve over time.
Let’s review several approaches to handle such states. A short-term
scratchpad can be employed for step-by-step notes, intermediate results, partial
hypotheses, and pending sub-goals. Conversation and session memory will
externalize history across the current run. It will include messages, tool outputs,
and decisions made. On the other hand, long-term memory is where we log
facts worth reusing across runs, such as a user’s style guide, project glossary, or
validated citations. Broader memory configurations may include domain
memory stores, which include vector databases for RAG, relational databases
for facts and metrics, or key-value caches for context on recent answers, and
cost usage.
A tip for managing all these is to keep the working set small and relevant. Use
methods to reduce the scope of content, such as summarization and state
compaction to prevent context bloat, and build a memory hygiene routine that
handles expiration, deduplication, and perhaps Personally Identifiable
Information (PII) minimization.
Tools
Tools turn a model from just processing text into a capability router. They
enable it to search a corpus, run code, hit an API, execute SQL, check policy,
fetch exchange rates, use a math engine, or invoke a secondary model. For best
practice, a robust tool layer includes several design properties that directly
affect reliability, safety, and cost control:
Typed arguments and explicit return schemas are used to constrain calls
and make outputs machine-checkable.
Idempotent or retry-safe operations ensure that transient failures can be
retried without duplicate side effects. We prefer reads and
UPSERT
semantics, require idempotency keys for mutating actions, and auto-retry
with exponential backoff when the operation is safe to repeat.
Quotas and rate limits act as safeguards to prevent runaway loops from
draining budgets and to enforce fairness under load.
As a good practice, side-effect containment is achieved through
sandboxing, least-privilege credentials, and a clear separation between
read-only and mutating tools.
Observation loop (act → observe →
revise)
After each action, the agent observes (tool output and environment change),
updates state/memory, and replans. This loop enables reflective patterns (e.g.,
“self-critique” before finalizing) and adaptive routing (e.g., “fallback to local
model if the API is down”). Ensure that each loop step logs what happened
(action, parameters, result, time, and cost), as we’ll need these traces for
debugging and evaluation.
Termination criteria
Autonomy needs brakes. To keep agent behavior predictable, safe, and cost-
bound, we define explicit stop conditions. These conditions determine when the
observe-act loop must halt, even if the agent could technically continue
reasoning or acting. Common termination criteria include the following:
Goal is achieved
Budget exhausted: Triggered when hitting token/cost/latency ceilings
Max depth/hops: Enforced based on the number of actions or planner
cycles
No progress: Applied to detect repeated states or oscillation and bail early
Human checkpoint: Used in high-risk domains, requires approval before
final action
Failure modes and guardrails
Let’s observe some common issues and how to mitigate them. In practice, these
failure modes tend to surface once agents operate autonomously over multiple
steps, making it essential to pair agentic flexibility with explicit guardrails. Tool
loops and thrashing occur when an agent repeatedly invokes the same actions
without making progress. Some possible practices include loop detectors,
capping the number of retries, and penalizing revisiting identical states. In such
cases, we could incorporate action diversity prompts of the “try a different tool
or plan” kind.
Goal drift is another frequent issue where the agent gradually deviates from the
original objective. To ensure that the goal is kept in focus, we can try
regrounding on the original objective at each step. We can do that by keeping a
goal reminder visible in the prompt.
Latency and cost blow-ups often emerge as a side effect of unconstrained
planning or excessive tool use. This may be directly linked to system
constraints that we must meet. For that, we could set budgets, surface them to
the policy, and build short-circuit paths.
Unverifiable outputs pose a different class of risk, particularly in production or
high-stakes settings. We can reduce risks by mandating structured outputs with
evidence and validators: syntax/consistency checks, unit tests for code, and
schema validators for data.
Multi-agent patterns
A single agent gives us adaptive sequencing and tool choice. Multiple agents
give us specialization and interaction. The design space is rich, but most real
systems boil down to three topologies and a handful of interaction protocols.
Topologies
Topologies describe the shape of coordination among agents and determine
how decisions, data, and accountability flow. We choose a topology to balance
control, adaptability, and failure blast radius while keeping latency and cost
predictable. We treat the topology as an explicit graph so we can test each edge
and node, trace outcomes, and evolve the design as requirements change. We
often begin with a simple shape that fits the constraint we care about most, then
introduce hybrid patterns as the system matures, for example, a hub
orchestrating a few peer exchanges inside one stage. We also plan for migration
paths so a pipeline can gain peer review at a critical step or a peer network can
add a coordinator/planner during peak-load periods:
Hub-and-spoke (planner + executors): A planner decomposes the
problem and delegates to specialized executor agents that take on the role
of specialists, such as a researcher, analyst, editor, and auditor. The planner
aggregates, resolves conflicts, and decides to stop or continue. The pros
are clear control, easier observability, and scalable specialization. The con,
however, is the risk of forming a bottleneck, as the planner may create a
single point of failure.
Peer-to-peer (role specialists): Here, the agents converse as equals, each
with a defined role. Work emerges from their negotiation. One common
scenario is a programmer-reviewer duo. The pros here come from the way
the agents complement each other’s roles, and so they tend to be more
resilient to failures, they tend to derive more creative solutions, and they
can achieve more validated results. The cons could be a challenge around
bounding costs and the need for stronger protocols.
The pipeline/assembly line: In this setting, the work passes through fixed
stages, such as the following:
Figure 11.4 – The pipeline/assembly line design
Each stage is an agent with clear I/O contracts. Here, the pros come from
the predictable pattern. It is easier to plan and anticipate latency and cost,
and it lends itself to forming tests for each stage in the process. The
analogous cons are that it is less adaptive and is sensitive to unexpected
inputs.
If we want control and cost predictability, we will start with a hub-and-spoke or
a pipeline topology. If we want diverse reasoning and resilience, we will
consider a peer-to-peer topology and add strong stop rules.
Interaction protocols
Interaction protocols are the rules of engagement that keep multiple agents from
talking past each other. They define the sequencing of who speaks when, the
state and evidence for what is shared, designate who has authority, and define
what must hold true, such as budgets, stop rules, and SLAs. Picking an explicit
protocol turns a free-form LLM conversation into a reproducible, auditable, and
budget-bounded workflow. We can trace decisions, replay from checkpoints,
and enforce guardrails. In practice, we may wish to choose the lightest protocol
that satisfies our constraints.
In practice, the goal is to adopt the lightest protocol that still satisfies our
constraints. The simplest place to start is structured turn-taking. In this setting,
the agents speak in rounds, often with a moderator enforcing order and even the
time or budget limits. This approach is good for peer-to-peer debates or
programmer-reviewer loops.
As coordination needs grow, turn-taking alone can become inefficient,
particularly when agents need to reference shared facts or intermediate results.
In these cases, a shared blackboard provides a natural extension. Designated
agents write to a common scratchpad that holds facts, partial results, or open
questions. Other agents read, update, or resolve items. This reduces redundant
work and supports asynchronous contributions if needed.
For production systems that require loose coupling, concurrency, and stronger
observability guarantees, interaction often shifts again toward message buses or
event-driven designs. Instead of calling each other directly, agents publish
events and subscribe to the types they care about. This enables concurrency,
natural fan-out/fan-in, and easy scaling, while the event stream doubles as an
audit trail. We keep events small but structured, and make consumers
idempotent so retries don’t create duplicate side effects. We pair the bus with a
shared blackboard like this: a state is written to the blackboard, then an event is
published pointing to the update, while keeping sensitive data out of the bus.
Task decomposition strategies
Task decomposition breaks a high-level goal into discrete, prescribed sub-
tasks, each with clear inputs/outputs and success predicates, so agents can work
in parallel, be tested in isolation, and recombine results deterministically.
A common starting point is role prompting. Here, each agent is given an
explicit mission along with well-defined inputs and expected outputs, often
enforced through schemas. This keeps responsibilities clear, reduces ambiguity
in handoffs, and makes individual steps easier to test and evaluate.
Once roles are defined, we can further refine execution through skill routing.
Instead of sending every sub-task to the same agent or model, we route work to
the most appropriate capability based on heuristics or learned policies. For
example, short code transformations may go to a small local model, complex
database joins to a SQL tool, and open-ended synthesis to a larger, more
capable model. This improves both cost efficiency and quality without changing
the overall workflow.
In more adaptive systems, roles themselves do not have to remain fixed. With
dynamic role assignment, the coordinator can initiate, retire, or reassign roles
on the fly based on intermediate results, confidence signals, or budget pressure.

that we covered:

At this point, we have all the conceptual pieces on the table. In the next section,
we will walk through a concrete, end-to-end multi-agent setup in code, showing
how planners, executors, protocols, memory, and termination criteria come
together in practice, and how the abstract trade-offs discussed previously
translate into concrete design and engineering decisions.
Building an executive brief
assistant from end to end
To make the agentic routing concepts concrete, we’ll build a simple pipeline

at runtime and orchestrates a sequence of tools and agents to transform raw text
into a concise, cited brief. The following is a step-by-step guide with code

def enc(self):
try:
return tiktoken.encoding_for_model(self.model)
except Exception:
return tiktoken.get_encoding(“cl100k_base”)
def count_tokens(self, text: str) -> int:
return len(self.enc().encode(text or “”))
def log_call(self, name: str, prompt: str, output: str, dt: flo
tin = self.count_tokens(prompt)
tout = self.count_tokens(output)
self.total_tokens_in += tin
self.total_tokens_out += tout
self.total_cost += (tin / 1000.0) * self.input_cost_p
self.timings.append((name, dt))
def snapshot(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
return {
“model”: self.model,
“tokens_in”: self.total_tokens_in,
“tokens_out”: self.total_tokens_out,
“cost_usd”: round(self.total_cost, 4),
“steps”: len(self.timings),
“durations”: self.timings,
}

Ingest and index documents
The pipeline must parse documents from a folder, break them into overlapping
chunks, embed them using SentenceTransformers, and store them in a FAISS
vector index for retrieval. The following helper functions load PDF, HTML, or
text files, slice them into chunks, and build the index:
DOC_DIR = “/content/docs”
os.makedirs(DOC_DIR, exist_ok=True)
CHUNK_SIZE = 700
CHUNK_OVERLAP = 100
model_embed = SentenceTransformer(“all-MiniLM-L6-v2”)
index = None
store: List[Dict[str, Any]] = []
def _chunks(text: str, size=CHUNK_SIZE, overlap=CHUNK_OVERLAP):
text = re.sub(r”\\s+”, “ “, text).strip()
i = 0
while i < len(text):
yield text[i:i+size]
i += size - overlap
def load_pdf(path: str) -> str:
doc = fitz.open(path)
return “\\n”.join(page.get_text(“text”) for page in doc)
def load_html(path: str) -> str:
with open(path, “r”, encoding=”utf-8”, errors=”ignore”) as f:
soup = BeautifulSoup(f.read(), “html.parser”)
return soup.get_text(“ “)
def load_txt(path: str) -> str:
with open(path, “r”, encoding=”utf-8”, errors=”ignore”) as f:
return f.read()

Retrieval is a simple top-K nearest neighbor search over the indexed
embeddings:
def retrieve(query: str, k: int = 6) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
if index is None:
return []
idx, embs = index
q = model_embed.encode([query], convert_to_numpy=True)
faiss.normalize_L2(q)
D, I = idx.search(q, k)
out = []
for rank, j in enumerate(I[0], 1):
out.append({
“id”: int(store[j][“id”]),
“source”: store[j][“source”],
“text”: store[j][“text”],
“score”: float(D[0][rank-1])
})
return out
Define quality control tools
Two helper functions ensure that each bullet in our draft is grounded in
evidence. The function tests whether a claim is sufficiently
citation_checker()
similar to any evidence chunk and whether numeric values match. The
function calculates what fraction of bullets pass the citation
coverage_score()

NUMERIC_RE = re.compile(r”[-+]?\\d[\\d,]*(?:\\.\\d+)?%?”)
def citation_checker(claim: str, evidence_chunks: List[Dict[str,Any
if not claim or not evidence_chunks:
return False
vec_claim = model_embed.encode([claim], convert_to_numpy=True)
faiss.normalize_L2(vec_claim)
vec_e = model_embed.encode(
[c[“text”] for c in evidence_chunks],
convert_to_numpy=True)
if vec_e.size == 0:
return False
faiss.normalize_L2(vec_e)
sims = (vec_claim @ vec_e.T).flatten()
if sims.max() < threshold:
return False
nums = NUMERIC_RE.findall(claim)
if nums:
best = evidence_chunks[int(np.argmax(sims))][“text”]
for n in nums:
if n.replace(“,”, “”) not in best.replace(“,”, “”):
return False
return True

draft_text: str, evidence_chunks: List[Dict[str,Any]]

return 0.0

return ok / max(1, len(bullets))

Build a multi-agent hub-and-spoke
system
While the single-agent baseline works, a multi-agent approach mirrors our
earlier design discussion and supports specialization. Here, each agent handles a
specific role:
Coordinator: Defines the plan and monitors budgets
Researcher: Retrieves evidence
Analyst: Proposes claims from the evidence
Auditor: Verifies each claim using the citation checker
Editor: Assembles a concise draft from the surviving claims
PolicyGate: Appends a risk note if needed
The blackboard shares the state among all agents. A simple class stops
Budget
execution after too many steps or seconds:
@dataclass
class Blackboard:
question: str
evidence: List[Dict[str,Any]] = field(default_factory=list)
claims: List[Dict[str,Any]] = field(default_factory=list)
draft: str = “”
final: str = “”
logs: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
def add_log(self, msg):
ts = time.strftime(“%H:%M:%S”)
self.logs.append(f”[{ts}] {msg}”)
@dataclass
class Budget:
max_steps: int = 8
max_seconds: float = 60
Each agent’s method updates the blackboard:
act()
class Coordinator:
def __init__(self, llm: LLMWrapper, budget: Budget):
self.llm = llm
self.budget = budget
def plan(self, bb: Blackboard) -> List[str]:
bb.add_log(“Coordinator: plan Research → Analyst → Auditor
return [“research”, “analyze”, “audit”, “edit”, “policy”]
class Researcher:
def __init__(self, k=10):
self.k = k
def act(self, bb: Blackboard):
found = retrieve(bb.question, k=self.k)
bb.evidence.extend(found)
bb.add_log(f”Researcher: added {len(found)} chunks”)
class Analyst:
def __init__(self, llm: LLMWrapper):
self.llm = llm
def act(self, bb: Blackboard):
evidence_json = json.dumps(
[
{k:v for k,v in e.items() if k!=”score”}
for e in bb.evidence
],
ensure_ascii=False)

class Auditor:
def act(self, bb: Blackboard):

class PolicyGate:
def __init__(self, llm: LLMWrapper):

Orchestrate the agents
The class holds the shared budget and coordinates the steps.
Orchestrator
After each agent’s action, it checks whether coverage meets a threshold; if not,
it loops back to once more. Execution stops
research/analysis/audit/edit
when the budget of steps or seconds is exhausted:
@dataclass
class Orchestrator:
llm: LLMWrapper
budget: Budget = field(default_factory=Budget)
coverage_threshold: float = 0.7
def run(self, question: str) -> Dict[str,Any]:
if index is None or not store:
return {
“final”: “⚠ No documents indexed. Upload files to
“blackboard”: {“evidence”: [], “claims”: [], “logs”
“meter”: self.llm.meter.snapshot(),
}
bb = Blackboard(question=question)
steps = 0
t0 = time.time()
coord = Coordinator(self.llm, self.budget)
researcher = Researcher(k=12)
analyst = Analyst(self.llm)
auditor = Auditor()
editor = Editor(self.llm)
policy = PolicyGate(self.llm)
for stage in coord.plan(bb):
if time.time() - t0 > self.budget.max_seconds or steps
bb.add_log(“Budget hit → early good enough release”
break
if stage == “research”:
researcher.act(bb)
elif stage == “analyze”:
analyst.act(bb)
elif stage == “audit”:
auditor.act(bb)
elif stage == “edit”:
editor.act(bb)
cov = coverage_score(bb.draft, bb.evidence)
bb.add_log(f”Coverage={cov:.2f}”)
if cov < self.coverage_threshold:
bb.add_log(“Coverage below threshold → refining
researcher.act(bb)
analyst.act(bb)
auditor.act(bb)
editor.act(bb)
elif stage == “policy”:
policy.act(bb)
steps += 1
return {
“final”: bb.final or bb.draft,
“blackboard”: {
“evidence”: bb.evidence,
“claims”: bb.claims,
“logs”: bb.logs,
},
“meter”: self.llm.meter.snapshot(),
}
To run the multi-agent system, instantiate and call :
Orchestrator run()
ORCH = Orchestrator(LLM, Budget(max_steps=8, max_seconds=60))
ma_result = ORCH.run(“Produce an executive brief with metrics, tren
print(ma_result[“final”])
print(“Meter:”, ma_result[“meter”])

def meter_to_rows(tag: str, m: Dict[str,Any]):
dur = sum(t for _,t in m.get(“durations”, []))
return {
“run”: tag,
“tokens_in”: m.get(“tokens_in”, 0),
“tokens_out”:m.get(“tokens_out”, 0),
“cost_usd”: m.get(“cost_usd”, 0.0),
“steps”: m.get(“steps”, 0),
“latency_s”: round(dur, 2),
}

That sums up our first complete agentic process. We will now learn about new

Deep dive into MAF and
advanced orchestration
frameworks
The goal of this section is to bridge the conceptual foundations of agentic
systems with a production-grade implementation that you can reason about,
extend, and operate in real-world environments. Earlier in the chapter, we
focused on what agents are, when they help, and how single- and multi-agent
designs behave at an architectural level. Here, we turn those abstractions into
concrete engineering practice.
This section moves from what agents are to how to build, orchestrate, and
operate them. Specifically, we focus on how modern agent frameworks encode
policy, memory, tools, orchestration loops, observability, and guardrails in code,
and how these design choices influence reliability, cost, and governance. We
now introduce what we feel is one of the most significant code bases for agentic
design: MAF.
This deep dive serves two purposes in the context of the book. First, it provides
a realistic reference implementation that reflects the design principles discussed
throughout the chapter. Second, it prepares the ground for the hands-on multi-
agent system we will build later, where concepts such as planners, executors,
protocols, checkpoints, and termination criteria must work together under real
constraints.
In this book’s previous edition, we capitalized on Microsoft’s AutoGen as the
agentic design code base. AutoGen was released several months before our
first edition, and since then, it has gotten a lot of support and enhancements
from Microsoft. Simultaneously, Microsoft developed another code base that’s
dedicated to designing solutions with LLMs, called Semantic Kernel. MAF
represents the convergence of these efforts. MAF is the successor framework
with official migration guides from both AutoGen and Semantic Kernel.
Over the remainder of this section, we will build a working mental model of
MAF, examine its core abstractions, understand how it supports both
autonomous agents and deterministic workflows, and evaluate how it compares
to other orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph. The emphasis is not on
API memorization, but on understanding how architectural choices in the
framework map to the agent design patterns discussed earlier in the chapter.
At a glance, MAF gives us the following:
Agents that could run on various provider backends: Azure AI, Azure
OpenAI, OpenAI, custom chat clients, and local models, such as Ollama,
and can call tools and MCP servers, which we covered in Chapter 9
Graph-based workflows with checkpointing, streaming, HITL, and time-
travel debugging, designed for multi-agent orchestration
Observability via OpenTelemetry, plus a middleware pipeline for retries,
error handling, rate limiting, and policy controls
Connectors to enterprise systems such as Microsoft Graph, Fabric,
SharePoint, Oracle, Bedrock, MongoDB, and Logic Apps, to wire agents
to real business data
Let’s review the core abstractions:
Agent: In MAF, agents work over mainstream providers, such as Azure,
OpenAI, and so on, and can also run over any chat client that implements
the appropriate interface, which is fantastic for looking to work with local
LLMs.
State: Each agent maintains conversation/session state and can participate
in workflows where state is checkpointed and replayed.
Plans: A plan is the agent’s working idea for what to do next, updated by
the plan → act → observe → revise loop, which we will look deeper into
next. Plans frequently involve tool invocations, sub-goal creation, or hand-
offs to other agents in a workflow.
Tools/functions/MCP servers: Tools can be functions that are described
by JSON schema or external services exposed via MCP. For robust tool
use, we want typed arguments and explicit return shapes. The framework
encourages this approach as it relies on provider capabilities that support
function calling.
Memory: This addresses all types of memory: short-term scratchpads,
long-term stores, and workflow-level checkpoints. In MAF, checkpointing
elevates memory from “prompt context” to a managed runtime feature.
Connectors: MAF introduces built-in integrations to business systems and
data planes such as Microsoft Graph, Fabric, SharePoint, Oracle, Bedrock,
and MongoDB. These let agents work with enterprise data.
Orchestration loop: plan → act →
observe → revise
MAF treats orchestration as more than just chaining model calls. In the typical
cycle, the agent plans (chooses an action/tool or delegates), acts (executes a
tool call or emits a message), observes (records outputs, updates state), then
revises (updates plan or terminates). The framework provides both agent
orchestration (LLM-driven autonomy) and workflow orchestration
(deterministic, graph-based routing), allowing us to mix creative reasoning with
production guardrails.
It is worth stressing how well MAF lends itself to testing and observing. In
prior chapters, we stressed testability and observability. A plan/act loop with
structured state and tool schemas is testable. We can trace actions, inputs,
outputs, time, and cost, then replay the run later to debug or improve
prompts/tools.
Observability hooks and policies
Observability in MAF is built directly into the runtime through a combination
of telemetry, tracing, and control points. Telemetry and tracing are provided
through OpenTelemetry integration, so every action, tool call, and handoff can
emit spans and metrics. This pairs with the DevUI for debugging complex runs.
At the workflow level, control is further enforced through checkpointing and
HITL gates, which are built into the graph runtime. This allows us to pause or
approve high-risk steps, then resume from a checkpoint if needed.
Advanced features
MAF has some great features that are worth highlighting before we start
developing.
Tool schemas and constraints
Function calling, with typed arguments and fixed return shapes, is our primary
defense against hallucinated tool names/parameters, which is an evident risk.
When our model supports function calling, we expose tools with schemas. This
way, the agent runtime and provider client ensure only recognized tools are
invoked, and only with valid arguments.
Here are some design tips we’ll implement later in the chapter:
Validate tool arguments server-side and reject unknown tools.
Keep tool outputs structured to feed downstream evaluators.
Enforce allow/deny lists at the middleware layer.
Multi-step planning and sub-goal
tracking
MAF supports both agent-driven planning, where an LLM decides the next
step, and workflow-driven planning, where a graph path decides the next node.
Its workflow engine supports sequential, concurrent, handoff, and magnetic
styles. These are all patterns we’ll use in the multi-agent build, and we will
review them.
Evaluators and critics
While “critique” is a pattern rather than a single MAF API, the framework
makes it easy to attach critics because we can model a critic agent in the
workflow graph to validate outputs such as facts, schema, and style. We can
route through critics only on certain conditions, such as low confidence or
expensive queries, using graph type-based routing and HITL gates to keep
latency and cost on budget. Labs and samples cover benchmarking hooks so we
can measure deltas after adding critics.
We’ll apply this pattern later by inserting an Auditor node that enforces
evidence coverage before the final draft is emitted.
Eventing and callbacks for tracing and
audit
We’ll often need to hook into steps for compliance logs, tokens/cost metering,
or dynamic budget cuts. With MAF’s OpenTelemetry traces and middleware
pipeline, we can add callbacks that stamp each tool call with correlation IDs
and user/session metadata. We can set them to short-circuit loops when budgets
are at, say, 80%. Or we can emit audit artifacts such as inputs, outputs, and
evidence IDs into our data plane.
Figure 11.6 captures the plan, act, observe loop with MAF.
Figure 11.6 – The plan, act, observe loop with MAF
Comparing two different
frameworks
Think of MAF and LangGraph as complementary approaches that can both
model agentic systems. They prioritize different ergonomics.
In LangGraph’s graph-oriented orchestration, the philosophy is that we design
an explicit state machine/DAG. Agents and tools are nodes/edges, and control
flow is deterministic unless we give a node autonomy. Its strengths are its
persistence, streaming, debugability, and deployment ergonomics, which are the
headline features in LangGraph’s docs. It is excellent when we need precise
control over topology and state. The trade-off is that it requires the graph to be
thought of up front, as exploratory autonomy patterns such as free-form debates
need more scaffolding.
Conversely, with MAF’s unified model, it explicitly supports agent
orchestration and workflow orchestration in one runtime. The former is LLM-
driven, while the latter is deterministic multi-agent graphs. This way, we can
start dynamically and gradually lock down critical paths with graphs, HITL
gates, and checkpoints. With regards to interoperability and connectors, rich
enterprise connectors and compatibility with any IChatClient interface
(including Ollama) mean we can wire local models and enterprise data planes
into the same system. Ops and governance are manifested in the form of built-in
OpenTelemetry, middleware for retries/limits/policies, and documentation that
centers operational concerns such as rate limits, caching, and graceful
degradation.

Table 11.2 – Reviewing the differences between MAF and LangGraph
As we review those differences, we can form some intuition for which approach
to go for. For greenfield projects that need fast iteration, we will start with
MAF’s agent orchestration + a thin workflow spine. As requirements stabilize,
we will introduce graph constraints (either MAF workflows or LangGraph)
around high-risk segments and add HITL gates and checkpointing.
Implementing a simple agent
using MAF and Ollama
To make the agentic protocol concepts tangible, let’s walk through a minimal
example using MAF with a local Ollama model. In just a few dozen lines of
code, we’ll show how an agent can plan, act, observe, and revise once, calling a
single read-only tool. This demonstration stays self-contained and cloud-free,
focusing on the control flow rather than performance.

Start an Ollama model via LLMPop
We begin by spinning up a local model and wrapping it in an OpenAI-style chat

llama3.2:1b
