With these metrics in place, we can express performance as product requirements rather
than as an after-the-fact tuning effort.
Designing product requirements
around performance targets
With a shared vocabulary and percentile view in place, we can return to the product
perspective. Performance requirements should be explicit parts of the product specification,
discussed from the earliest design reviews and revisited as the product evolves.
A practical workflow for product managers and engineers includes the following:
1. Start from the user journey and context:
Is the interaction conversational and live?
Is it a background batch job?
Is it a multi-step workflow with human review in between?
2. Choose primary performance metrics for that journey:
For chat and code assistance, TTFT and end-to-end latency P95 are often
primary
For back-office document processing, goodput and throughput at cost are often
primary
3. Propose initial targets and validate them with prototypes:
Build thin vertical slices that exercise the full path, including retrieval, model
calls, and logging
Observe actual latencies and adjust targets to be ambitious but realistic
4. Encode these targets into service objectives and acceptance criteria:
Include them in design docs, runbooks, and dashboards
Tie them to gradual rollout plans and capacity investments
To make this concrete, consider three examples.
Example 1 – chatbots for customer support
These systems often handle frustrated users who are waiting for help. TTFT dominates
perception. Reasonable targets might be the following:
TTFT P50 under 0.7 seconds
TTFT P95 under 1.5 seconds
End-to-end P95 under 4 seconds for standard questions
If a route involves complex retrieval or multi-agent debate, the system might display an
interim message. However, frequent trips beyond these thresholds will feel like being on
hold. To stay within bounds, teams often use smaller or distilled models to generate an
initial response, defer deeper analysis to follow-up messages, and limit answer length unless
the user explicitly requests more detail.
Example 2 – code assistants
For code completion in an integrated development environment, the experience is even
more sensitive. Suggestions that appear quickly can feel like an extension of our own
typing. Suggestions that appear slowly are ignored. Targets might be the following:
TTFT P50 under 0.3 seconds
End-to-end P95 under 1.5 seconds for inline completions
Larger refactorings or multi-file explanations can have looser bounds and may appear in
separate panels so that they do not block editing. Engineering teams might choose to cache
embeddings and context windows aggressively, route simple completions to local models,
or reserve larger remote models for explicit refactor commands.
Example 3 – document processing tools
Here, the dynamic is different. A legal review assistant that summarizes a contract can take
several seconds, as long as the user trusts that the result is accurate and well grounded in
citations. Performance targets can be written in terms of goodput:
At least 95 percent of documents under 20 pages processed within 30 seconds
At least 90 percent of documents under 50 pages processed within 60 seconds
Goodput is measured as the fraction that meets both latency and quality checks
These targets will influence architecture choices such as batching, streaming previews, and
parallelization across sections.
Across all examples, performance becomes a multi-dimensional trade-off:
Model size and architecture versus decoding speed and cost
Context length and retrieval complexity versus TTFT
Number of agents and tools versus tail latency and reliability
The role of the AI-native product manager is not to dictate the exact hardware or serving
stack but to codify these trade-offs as product requirements. The role of the AI architect is
to propose designs that honor those requirements while keeping room for evolution as
models improve.
In the next section, we move from measurement to action and review the concrete serving
and caching techniques that teams use to improve TTFT, throughput, and tail latency.
Performance enhancements in
modern AI systems
In the previous section, we treated latency, throughput, and goodput as the core
performance vocabulary for AI-native products. Metrics alone do not improve a system.
They only tell us where the experience breaks. In this section, we turn to the mechanisms
that modern systems use to achieve real gains: semantic caching, token prefill with key-
value (KV) caching inside transformers, and KV cache sharing systems such as LMCache
that operate across engines and queries.
These enhancements are not just low-level tricks. They are now central design choices that
determine whether a product meets its TTFT, P95 latency, and cost objectives. The same
pattern that we saw with RAG applies here: what began as research or infrastructure work is
becoming part of the product manager’s toolbox, alongside user journeys and pricing
models.
Semantic caching for repeated or
structured workloads
As LLM usage grows, many workloads show strong repetition. Customer support chats
revisit the same policy questions. Enterprise RAG systems receive similar questions about
the same document sets. Internal tools run the same classification or extraction prompts
across thousands of records. If every request is treated as new, we pay full retrieval and
generation costs each time, and we increase latency unnecessarily.
Semantic caching treats LLM calls as reusable functions rather than one-off events. Instead
of caching only exact string prompts, we cache structured queries and responses in a way
that is aware of meaning. This is the same motivation we saw in retrieval, where semantic
similarity often matters more than exact string matches.
We can think about three levels of caching sophistication. Exact caching uses the full
prompt string plus model configuration as the key and registers a hit only when a new
request is identical to a previous one. It is simple and safe, but it misses near duplicates.
Normalized caching introduces a preprocessing step, such as lowercasing when safe,
trimming whitespace, expanding templates, or sorting JSON keys. The normalized form
becomes the key, and a cache hit occurs when two inputs are equivalent under that
normalization. This is especially useful for API-style workloads with structured inputs.
Semantic caching goes further by embedding the input into a vector space and storing it
alongside the output. New requests are embedded and compared using similarity measures,
and if the similarity exceeds a defined threshold, the previous answer is reused. This allows
reuse across paraphrased or slightly reformulated questions.
Figure 13.3 shows a geometric illustration of a new query being processed and embedded,
and similar pre-cached queries are found based on a similarity circle/sphere. The axes
represent the embedding dimensions. Each cached query has its corresponding answer
linked to it in a separate table. The diagram is intentionally abstract, but it captures the key
idea that near-duplicate intents can reuse validated outputs.
Figure 13.3: Simplified illustration of the embedding space
Semantic caching fits naturally into RAG architectures. We already maintain embeddings
for documents. Extending the same machinery to store request embeddings and their
outputs is a small conceptual step.
The similarity threshold becomes a product lever. A conservative threshold, for example,
cosine similarity above 0.95, behaves almost like normalized caching. A more aggressive
threshold, for example, above 0.85, will increase the hit rate but risks occasional
mismatched answers. For public-facing products that answer queries in many domains, we
typically keep thresholds conservative. For narrow internal tools that operate over a fixed
schema, we can be bolder.
Where semantic caching helps most
Semantic caching brings the strongest benefits in workloads that have at least one of three
characteristics:
High repetition: Public FAQs, policy questions, and code migration utilities
Structured prompts: Classification, extraction, and scoring tasks where only fields
change
Expensive context: Long conversation history or long retrieved context in RAG
In these cases, cache hits reduce both TTFT and end-to-end latency because we avoid
retrieval, prefill, and generation. They also reduce costs, since each avoided model call
saves tokens and compute.
For example, an internal contract review assistant may receive many variations of
“summarize the risks in section 7 of this template.” Once the system has answered this for a
given template and section, semantic caching can instantly respond to paraphrased versions
of the same request, provided that the underlying document version and user access controls
still match.
There is also a strong synergy with goodput. If we cache only answers that passed
downstream checks, such as citation verification or classifier approvals, then the cache
effectively stores a subset of high-quality responses. Cache hits increase not only speed but
also the probability that the response meets our quality bar.
Design challenges: staleness,
personalization, and safety
Caching introduces new responsibilities for AI-native products:
Staleness: When underlying policies or documents change, we must invalidate
affected cache entries. This ties back to the lineage and versioning strategies we
introduced earlier in the chapter. Cache keys should reference document versions and
model versions, not just embeddings.
Personalization: Answers may depend on user identity, role, or region. We can scope
cache entries by user segment, or factor the personalized parts into a small second-
stage LLM call while caching only the general portion.
Safety and privacy: We must avoid mixing answers between tenants or leaking
sensitive identifiers through cached output. This usually means partitioning caches by
tenant and performing redaction before caching.
The broader theme is that semantic caching is a product-level decision, not just an
engineering optimization. It affects correctness, safety, and trust, so it should be governed
by the same policies that apply to RAG indexing and logging.
Token prefill and KV caching
While semantic caching avoids entire model invocations, KV caching attacks a different
source of cost: the repeated transformer operations over long sequences.
Recall from Chapter 7 that a transformer layer computes attention over queries, keys, and
values. When we generate text autoregressively, at each step we feed the model the entire
prefix plus previously generated tokens, and the model recomputes attention unless we
reuse past work.
KV caching stores the projected keys and values for previous tokens so that the model does
not recompute them on each decoding step. This is the workhorse optimization that makes
streaming generation practical at scale, especially for long contexts.
How KV caching works in practice
At a high level, the flow looks like this:
1. We run the model over an input sequence, for example, the prompt and retrieved
context. For each transformer layer, we compute keys and values for each token and
store them in a cache.
2. When we decode the next token, we only compute queries for the new token. Attention
in each layer then uses the following:
The cached keys and values for all previous tokens
The new key and value for the current token
3. We update the cache with the new key and value, and continue to the next token.
As a result, the cost of decoding one new token becomes proportional to the number of
layers and the number of cached tokens, but we avoid recomputing earlier keys and values.
This is especially powerful when long prompts or conversation histories are involved.
KV caching directly reduces TPOT and token generation time, especially for workloads
with long shared prefixes. It typically does not change TTFT because the first pass still
needs to compute keys and values for the initial prompt.
Token prefill and shared prefixes
Many production systems take the idea further through prefix or prefill optimizations. In
RAG, multiple follow-up questions can share the same retrieved context for a period of
time. In chat systems, multiple users might use the same long system prompt and tool
definitions, whereas in code assistants, a long file or project context may stay constant
across many small completions.
In these cases, serving stacks can perform a prefill step over the shared prefix once, store
the resulting caches, and then reuse them across multiple decoding streams. Some
frameworks expose this explicitly through an API that creates a “prefilled” handle that other
requests attach to. This is one of the key ideas behind high-performance LLM engines.
Prefill and KV caching are not free. They consume GPU memory, require careful eviction
policies, and can complicate scheduling. The trade-offs depend on workload patterns:
Having high concurrency with many distinct prompts favors dynamic batching and
more modest KV caching
Having fewer distinct prompts with many continuations favors larger, longer-lived
caches
In practice, teams often combine both patterns by using modest per-request KV caching
alongside higher-level reuse for stable prefixes.
Reducing TTFT with LMCache – a
dedicated cache orchestration layer
Semantic caching improves performance by skipping entire requests. KV caching improves
decoding speed once we start generating. LMCache focuses on the missing piece: reducing
TTFT and increasing throughput by sharing KV caches across engines, queries, and storage
tiers.
At a high level, LMCache turns KV caches into a first-class resource. Instead of treating
each engine as an isolated worker that computes its own prefix from scratch, LMCache
stores KV caches in a dedicated layer and lets engines reuse them across requests and even
across machines.
That shift makes cache management look more like data infrastructure, with its own storage
tiers, eviction policies, and observability.
What LMCache does
LMCache is an open source extension to modern serving engines such as vLLM and
SGLang. It stores KV caches for reusable text fragments across GPU memory, CPU
memory, and even local or remote disk. It also allows non-prefix reuse, meaning it can
reuse KV caches for repeated text spans beyond simple shared prefixes. In addition, it
supports cache offloading, moving KV data to cheaper storage while keeping it quickly
retrievable, and enables disaggregated prefill and decode workflows, where one engine
performs the heavy prefill step and then hands KV caches to others for decoding.
vLLM is named after “virtual memory” techniques that power its
PagedAttention mechanism. This is the same reason LMCache can integrate
tightly with vLLM. They share the assumption that KV cache is a
structured, pageable, externalizable resource.
SGLang is a high-performance inference engine and structured generation
framework for LLMs. It combines an optimized serving runtime with a
declarative language that allows developers to specify schema-constrained
outputs, tool interactions, and multi-step logic.
The documentation reports significant gains when LMCache is combined with vLLM. In
multi-round question-answering and RAG scenarios, developers have reported 3 to 10 times
lower TTFT along with reduced GPU cycles. The associated research paper reports up to 15
times throughput improvement across diverse workloads when KV caches are shared and
offloaded efficiently.
For the purposes of this chapter, we treat LMCache as one example of a broader class of
KV cache orchestration systems that sit alongside vector stores and retrieval pipelines as
core performance infrastructure in AI-native products.
How LMCache interacts with product
architecture
From a product and architecture perspective, LMCache introduces a new layer into the
baseline end-to-end RAG architecture:
The source database and ingestion pipeline still prepare documents and embeddings
The vector store still serves retrieval for RAG
The LLM engines now interact with a KV cache layer that can live partly in GPU
memory and partly in external storage
When a request arrives, the serving path can look like this:
1. Retrieve relevant documents and build the prompt.
2. Query LMCache for KV caches that correspond to chunks of the prompt or
conversation history.
3. If caches are found, load them into engine memory and skip recomputing those
segments.
4. Perform any remaining prefill for new parts of the prompt.
5. Decode output tokens using standard KV caching inside the engine.
In chat products, this reduces TTFT directly because long conversation histories do not
need full recomputation for every turn. In RAG systems, repeated questions over the same
documents or sections reuse their prefills, shrinking both TTFT and GPU utilization. In
multi-agent systems, repeated tool calls and plan templates benefit from reuse as well,
especially when different agents share similar scaffolding.
Where LMCache fits in our performance
toolbox
For AI-native product teams, LMCache and similar systems are part of a layered
performance strategy. We typically begin by optimizing the obvious factors: selecting
appropriate model sizes and quantization levels, and ensuring that KV caching inside the
engine and efficient batching are configured correctly. Next, we apply semantic and
structured caching to avoid full inference when the same or similar questions reappear, and
to cache high-quality responses with clear lineage. Only after these layers are in place do
we introduce KV cache orchestration, which enables sharing KV caches across requests,
across engines, and in some cases across different products that reuse common prompts or
contexts.
The last step requires more coordination, but it unlocks gains that simple scaling cannot
match, especially in environments where GPU capacity is scarce or expensive.
As with any optimization, we must align LMCache deployment with product goals and
workload characteristics. Products that rely on long prompts, deep conversational history,
and recurring contexts, such as RAG search systems, multi-turn chat applications, and
complex agent workflows, tend to benefit the most because they repeatedly process
substantial shared prefixes. In contrast, products built around very short prompts, such as
narrow classification APIs or lightweight transformations, are less likely to see significant
gains from KV cache orchestration and can often achieve better returns by focusing on
semantic caching and careful model selection instead.
In the next section, we extend this performance view into organizational and product
realities, where tool adoption, governance, and change management shape whether these
technical gains translate into business value.
Internal enterprise tools as AI-first
systems
Enterprise environments are often where AI-native design quietly proves itself first. Internal
tools sit closer to proprietary data, domain experts, and compliance teams. They also give
us more control over rollout, monitoring, and iteration than public consumer products.
When we treat these tools as AI-first rather than adding an assistant on top of legacy
dashboards, we can redesign analytics, knowledge access, and approvals in ways that were
not feasible with traditional software.
This section follows the life cycle of such internal tools. We start with analytics, where
organizations move from static dashboards to conversational analysis. We then cover
enterprise search as a RAG-powered question-answering fabric. From there, we design
approval flows that keep humans in control when AI drafts or recommends work. Finally,
we discuss how to roll these systems out across large organizations where security, legal,
and risk teams must be part of the journey. The patterns build directly on the RAG and
system design material introduced in earlier chapters of the first edition.
Migration from legacy dashboards to
conversational tools
For the last two decades, business intelligence in many enterprises has been defined by
dashboards. Analysts publish curated views. Stakeholders learn which filters and drilldowns
answer their recurring questions. New questions require either manual exports to
spreadsheets or tickets to a data team. Adoption often stalls. People fall back on emailing
colleagues instead of exploring the data themselves.
LLM-based tools may start as a thin “ask a question” panel beside existing dashboards, but
the real change comes when we treat analytics as a conversational workflow rather than a
static gallery of charts. That shift forces us to design for correctness and trust, because the
system is now generating the analysis path, not just rendering a prebuilt view.
A legacy dashboard-centric pattern has a few common limitations. Questions must be
translated into the specific filter logic and structure of each dashboard, which assumes users
already understand how the data is organized. Cross-dashboard questions require mental
joins and manual reconciliation, forcing users to switch contexts and stitch together answers
on their own. Explanations of what a chart means, including metric definitions and caveats,
are typically left to external documents or training sessions rather than being embedded
directly within the tool.
An AI-first analytics tool inverts this. We start from the question and let the system choose
which data sources, aggregations, and visualizations will best answer it. Concretely, this
means the following:
Natural language queries such as:
Show us monthly revenue for EMEA over the last 12 months and highlight
anomalies
Compare churn between our self-serve customers and our enterprise
contracts
Automatic proposal of visual forms. For example, the system may answer with a short
narrative, followed by a time-series chart, followed by a breakdown table.
Follow-up questions that refine or challenge the answer, such as
exclude promotional
or .
discounts zoom in on Q3
Behind the scenes, such tools compile natural language into structured queries, often using
LLMs to generate SQL, Spark, or API calls, then using RAG to bring in metric definitions
or business rules from internal documentation.
The result is not just “chat in front of a database.” It is a workflow where we have the
following:
Charts become evidence in a conversation, not the starting point
Metric definitions and caveats are surfaced inline when relevant
Analysts spend more time validating and less time writing boilerplate queries
Figure 13.4 illustrates how AI-first analytics have evolved the user experience:
Figure 13.4: How AI-driven analytics have evolved the user experience for mining in-house information
Safety, correctness, and trust
Of course, compiling natural language into queries introduces risks. Misinterpreted metrics
can cause incorrect decisions. AI-first analytics must therefore incorporate several
safeguards:
Schema-aware prompting with explicit metric and dimension catalogs
Strict use of read-only roles for generated queries
A visible “show query” function so that advanced users can inspect or copy the
generated SQL
Runtimes that enforce limits on row counts, time windows, and scan size
For regulated environments, we typically design tiered capabilities. Simple descriptive
questions over hardened views can flow through an automated path. Complex financial or
risk metrics may require that an analyst review the generated query before it runs.
Modernizing enterprise search
Enterprise search has long been promised to be a “Google search for within the company.”
Many implementations fell short. Keyword-based systems could not bridge synonyms,
abbreviations, or variations in phrasing. Results were entire documents, leaving employees
to scroll and search within PDFs or wikis.
RAG and LLMs give us a realistic path to fulfill that promise, provided we design indexing
and retrieval explicitly for AI consumption. Earlier in this chapter, we already discussed
chunking, metadata, and vector stores as part of product evolution. Here, we focus on how
those choices show up in an internal search experience.
In practice, the product succeeds only if it can answer quickly, cite precisely, and respect
access boundaries without forcing us back into document hunting.
Measuring and improving relevance
In an AI-first search system, relevance is shared between retrieval and generation. Retrieval
must surface appropriate passages. The LLM must respect the evidence and avoid
hallucinating unsupported statements. Practical systems often do the following:
Log which passages were retrieved and which ones the model cited
Use automated checks that ensure numeric values and named entities in the answer
appear in the retrieved text
Ask users whether answers were helpful and whether citations were correct, feeding
this into an evaluation harness similar to the ones described for multi-agent systems in
other chapters
New metrics such as “precision at evidence” and “supported answer rate” sit next to classic
search metrics. They make relevance concrete for business stakeholders who depend on
these tools for compliance, due diligence, or customer support.
Designing approval flows for AI-
generated work
Internal tools are not just about finding information. Increasingly, they generate drafts of
emails, tickets, code changes, risk reports, or policy updates. In regulated industries such as
finance, healthcare, and law, no AI output can become final without human approval. This
pushes us to design explicit approval flows that integrate AI capabilities without violating
control frameworks such as maker-checker, three lines of defense, or formal sign-off
procedures.
A maker-checker control is a two-person workflow in which one
individual prepares an action and a second individual independently reviews
and approves it before execution, ensuring segregation of duties and
reducing operational risk.
The three-lines-of-defense model separates responsibility for risk into
business operations as the first line, risk and compliance oversight as the
second line, and independent internal audit as the third line, creating layered
protection against errors and misconduct.
Workflow checkpoints and risk tiers
A simple but powerful design is to treat the AI assistant as a “first drafter” inside an existing
workflow, with new checkpoints tailored to the risks of each action. This often includes the
following:
Draft stage: The AI generates a proposal: an email, report section, classification, or
decision rationale. The output is clearly labeled as AI-generated and is attached to a
specific case or task.
Review stage: A human reviewer inspects the draft, edits it, and either approves or
rejects the suggestion. The tool may assist the reviewer by highlighting which parts
deviate from standard templates or previous similar cases.
Approval stage: For higher-risk actions, a second approver or a specialized role, for
example, compliance, signs off before the action is executed or communicated
externally.
The number and type of checkpoints depend on risk tiers. A low-risk internal summary
might require only a single human check. A public market communication or a regulatory
filing may require multiple explicit approvals and a full audit trail of edits, comments, and
model versions.
Human review layers in regulated
environments
Regulated organizations already operate with well-defined control layers. AI-first internal
tools should align with these, rather than inventing new governance from scratch. Here is an
example:
First line: Business teams use AI to draft work but remain responsible for final
decisions
Second line: Risk and compliance teams define which workflows may use AI and
under what constraints, as well as what evidence must be logged
Third line: Internal audit periodically reviews samples of AI-assisted decisions and
validates that policies were followed
The technical guardrail architecture described elsewhere in this book, including input
filters, output checks, and policy enforcement services, supports these flows by doing the
following:
Tagging each AI output with a policy identifier and model version
Logging prompts, retrieved evidence, and decisions in an “evidence shelf” that
auditors can inspect
Blocking actions when safety checks fail or when required approvals are missing
When we design internal tools as AI-first systems, we should consider approval experience
with the same care as we consider chat user experience. Approvers need clear affordances:
which parts were generated by AI, which rules or thresholds were applied, and what
alternatives exist if they disagree.
Once approval flows are clear, the remaining risk is rollout, because enterprise trust is
earned gradually through pilots, training, and stakeholder alignment.
Rollout planning across large
organizations
Even the best-designed internal AI tools can fail if rollout is mishandled. Large
organizations contain heterogeneous teams, legacy systems, and multiple control functions
that must be convinced that the new tools are safe and valuable. AI-first products demand a
rollout strategy that addresses stakeholder alignment, change management, and common
blockers such as security reviews.
Stakeholder alignment and sponsorship
Successful deployments usually begin with a small number of high-value use cases and
strong local sponsors. Typical stakeholders include business owners with a clearly defined
pain point, data and engineering teams who can integrate the tool into existing systems,
security and privacy teams who validate data flows, and legal and compliance teams who
review risk, particularly for external-facing outputs.
Early in the project, teams should agree on what metrics define success for the internal tool,
such as time saved, error reduction, backlog clearance, or satisfaction scores. They should
also clarify which data sources and actions are in scope for the first version and what
limitations will be explicitly communicated, including forbidden use cases or experimental
status.
Aligning expectations early reduces the chance that an otherwise successful pilot will be
blocked later by concerns that were not addressed.
Change management and user adoption
Internal AI tools change how people work. Analysts who were proud SQL experts may
worry that a conversational interface will diminish their role. Support agents may fear that
automation will reduce staffing. Managers may see new metrics and oversight. Ignoring
these dynamics leads to quiet resistance and low adoption, even if the tool is technically
sound.
Practical change management for AI-first tools often includes the following:
Treating early users as partners in design and giving them visible credit when their
suggestions shape the product
Providing clear guidance on when and how to rely on AI-generated output, including
examples of both strong and weak performance
Investing in training sessions that feel like skill upgrades rather than compliance
mandates
Many organizations formalize “AI champions” in each department who can answer
questions, gather feedback, and escalate issues.
Common blockers and how to address them
Several blockers appear repeatedly in large enterprises. Security and data residency reviews
are often the first hurdle, driven by concerns that prompts or documents might leave the
organization or be used for model training. These concerns are typically addressed by
selecting deployment options with strict data controls, such as dedicated instances, regional
hosting, and explicit no-training guarantees.
Vendor risk management is another common obstacle, since third-party LLM providers and
vector databases must pass formal due diligence. In response, teams prepare detailed
architecture diagrams, data flow maps, and incident response plans that demonstrate how
risks are identified and mitigated. Model risk and explainability concerns also arise,
especially in regulated domains where teams must show that AI does not undermine
existing risk models or introduce unfair outcomes. Practical mitigations include restricting
AI to advisory roles, grounding responses through RAG with visible citations, and building
evaluation suites that measure bias, error rates, and consistency over time.
By anticipating these blockers and addressing them in design documents and pilot plans,
AI-native product teams can turn reviews from “hard stops” into collaborative improvement
cycles.
With internal tools in place, we can now contrast them with customer-facing products,
where expectations, risk tolerance, and feedback loops differ significantly.
Customer-facing products built
around LLMs
Customer-facing products are where AI-native design is most visible. Chat interfaces,
copilots in editors, and AI-enhanced search have shifted expectations in less than two years.
Users now assume that complex actions can be expressed in natural language, that answers
will arrive quickly, and that systems will remember context across turns. At the same time,
public products operate under stricter expectations for safety, consistency, and transparent
behavior than many internal tools.
This section looks at three aspects of AI-native customer products. First, the new user
experience patterns that emerged from streaming and conversational interfaces. Second,
how safety, traceability, and grounding become visible features rather than hidden concerns.
Third, how product tiering and pricing reflect model selection, context limits, and latency
guarantees.
The goal is not to catalog every UI trick. It is to show how product, engineering, and safety
decisions surface together in the user experience. Those same cross-cutting decisions also
reshape ownership, because AI behavior spans models, data, user experience, and
governance rather than a single feature team.
New user experience patterns that
emerged from AI
The dominant user experience for LLM products is no longer the traditional web form. It is
a conversational interface that streams partial answers, can call tools behind the scenes, and
can keep context over time. Research on conversational interfaces describes this shift as a
move from static-based interactions to dialogue-based patterns that adapt to user intent.
We will next highlight three core patterns. Each pattern improves usability, but each also
introduces new obligations around latency budgets, safety controls, and transparency.
Streaming text as a first-class feature
Before LLMs, most web applications treated responses as atomic. A user clicked a button,
the backend worked, and a full response appeared all at once. LLMs changed this because
generation is incremental. The system can stream tokens as soon as they are produced.
Streaming is no longer just a backend optimization. It is a user experience expectation.
Microsoft and others explicitly recommend streaming for chat applications, noting that it
improves TTFT and makes the interface feel responsive even when full answers take
several seconds.
In practice, streaming supports several product goals:
It shortens perceived latency. Users see progress quickly, which aligns with the
subsecond TTFT targets discussed earlier in the chapter.
It keeps the interaction conversational. Users can interrupt, stop generation, or ask a
follow-up question while text is still flowing.
It allows the system to show intermediate reasoning or tool usage in advanced setups,
for example, agent frameworks that stream thoughts and actions as they occur.
For developers and product managers, streaming is now a default choice for long-form
answers. Turning it off should be a conscious decision, for example, when responses must
be fully validated before any part is shown.
Conversational UI as the primary surface
A conversational UI looks simple, yet research and field reports show that it changes how
people explore information and services.
Several consistent patterns have emerged:
The prompt area becomes a multi-purpose input: Question, instruction, feedback, and
navigation request.
Responses mix natural language with structured elements such as code blocks, tables,
buttons, and inline charts. Practitioners describe these as “mini interfaces inside the
chat” that allow deeper interaction without leaving the conversation.
Users often start with vague or incomplete questions, then refine them in follow-up
turns instead of trying to craft a perfect query up front.
For customer-facing products, this leads to hybrid designs. The chat pane sits alongside
traditional UI elements such as filters or forms. The assistant can configure those controls,
explain them, or generate suggestions that populate them.
Examples include the following:
A travel site where the assistant proposes an itinerary while also adjusting date and
destination controls.
A developer portal where an AI copilot suggests API calls and simultaneously fills in a
code editor.
An e-commerce assistant that both answers questions and creates saved lists or carts in
the background.
The key product decision is to treat chat not as an add-on but as a primary surface that can
orchestrate existing features. That orchestration increases power, and it also increases the
need for a clear state, predictable behavior, and explicit boundaries around what the
assistant can do.
Context management and memory
Customer-facing products must manage context more carefully than internal tools.
Conversations may span multiple topics, sessions, and devices. Some information should
persist, such as preferred locations or saved projects. Other context, especially sensitive
content, should remain session-bound or be easy to clear.
From a product design perspective, context management has several dimensions:
Short-term conversational context: The last few turns in a session, used for pronoun
resolution and follow-up questions. This is usually stored in the chat history and sent
as part of the prompt.
Longer-term project context: A document the user is editing, a dataset being
analyzed, or a support case. This is often represented as a structured state outside the
LLM, for example, IDs and metadata that the system rehydrates into prompts when
needed.
Persistent preferences and memories: For example, preferred time zone, writing
style, or typical data sources. These can be stored in a profile store and included
selectively, with clear controls to edit or delete them.
The user experience should make this visible. Studies on conversational AI in sensitive
domains, such as health assistants, show that trust improves when users understand what
information is remembered and how it will be used.
Practical designs include the following:
A “conversation settings” panel that shows which memories are active and allows
deletion
Explicit boundaries such as “this mode will not use previous chats” for privacy-
sensitive tasks
Clear labels when the system draws on past interactions, for example, “using your
saved project X”
Safety, traceability, and user trust
Customer-facing products live in an environment where mistakes are public, screenshots
circulate, and regulators are increasingly attentive. As a result, safety mechanisms that felt
“internal” in earlier chapters, such as grounding, citations, and guardrails, become visible
parts of the product.
Work on trust in LLM-based conversational systems stresses that transparency, source
attribution, and control over data use are key to user confidence. We focus on three design
levers that translate safety architecture into user-visible behaviors that shape trust more than
any single model benchmark.
Grounding and citations as user experience
elements
RAG, which we covered in earlier chapters, anchors answers in external sources rather than
the model’s parametric memory.
Industry articles and documentation consistently highlight three benefits of RAG in
customer scenarios:
Grounded answers can be traced to specific passages and updated by changing the
underlying content.
Citations act like footnotes in a research paper. Users can click through to verify
claims, which increases trust.
Sensitive content can be excluded from the index, which simplifies compliance and
data minimization in regulated domains.
For customer products, this means that we design citation behavior as carefully as we
design the narrative. Common choices include the following:
Inline numeric markers that expand to show snippets and document titles
A “sources” panel that lists documents with confidence scores
Toggling between “answer” and “evidence” views
The important point is that citations are not just a compliance checkbox. They are a central
part of user experience and trust.
Hallucination mitigation as product behavior
Hallucination remains one of the main obstacles to deploying LLMs in real-world products.
Recent surveys and evaluations emphasize that unchecked hallucinations undermine
reliability even when average quality is high.
Modern customer products increasingly treat hallucination mitigation as a layered behavior
rather than a single model improvement. Typical layers include the following:
Grounding through RAG: Retrieval reduces hallucinations by providing direct
evidence for the model to quote.
Validation and detection: Separate checks compare generated statements with
retrieved passages, or use specialized detectors to flag unverifiable claims. Cloud
providers and open source tools now ship prebuilt detectors for RAG applications.
Fallback behavior: When confidence is low, the product may answer conservatively,
ask clarifying questions, or switch to a “search results only” mode instead of
generating a confident paragraph.
For example, the product might display a clear “low confidence” banner prompting users to
double-check the answer, or switch to a different response style when it cannot ground a
claim, such as presenting a list of relevant links with a short, generic explanation instead of
a confident narrative. In addition, errors should be logged and surfaced in a structured way
that enables customer support teams to reproduce the interaction and investigate
problematic answers efficiently.
Research on trust and user experience in LLM agents notes that users respond better when
systems are explicit about uncertainty and provide levers to inspect or override decisions.
Transparent prompts and data use
Customer-facing products must also explain how user data feeds into prompts, history, and
long-term learning. Reports on global attitudes toward AI show that willingness to use AI
depends strongly on perceived control, clarity of purpose, and confidence that personal data
will not be misused.
Practical patterns include the following:
Clear mode switches, such as “use this chat to improve the product” versus “do not use
this conversation for training”
Short, contextual disclosures in the UI that describe where data is stored and how long
it is retained, instead of burying everything in a long privacy policy
A “show instructions” feature that reveals the system prompt or key rules that govern
the assistant’s behavior, at least in a simplified form
Combined with grounding and hallucination mitigation, these practices help customers
understand not only what the model says but how it arrived there and how their data
participates in the process. Once trust and transparency are designed into the surface, the
remaining question is sustainability, which is where tiering and pricing decisions become
inseparable from model and latency choices.
Product tiering and pricing for AI
services
Customer-facing AI products live at the intersection of user expectations and economic
constraints. Different users need different levels of capability and performance. At the same
time, providers pay real costs per token, per context window, and per latency target. This
leads naturally to tiered products.
Cloud providers already expose cost differences by model size, quality, and context window
length. For example, pricing pages distinguish between higher-end models and lighter
models, and often charge more for longer context windows because they consume more
compute per request.
AI-native product teams translate these technical levers into plan design.
Model selection and feature sets
One dimension of tiering is model selection:
Entry tiers may rely on smaller or “mini” models that provide reasonable quality at a
lower cost
Professional tiers may use larger, more capable models for complex tasks such as long-
form drafting, code generation, or data analysis
Enterprise tiers may offer model choices, including domain-tuned or privately hosted
models for regulatory reasons
Model choice often aligns closely with feature differentiation across tiers. For example, free
plans may restrict access to advanced tools such as file analysis, web browsing, or plugin
integration, since these capabilities increase both cost and operational risk. Paid plans, by
contrast, can justify higher rate limits, access to more capable models, and priority
treatment in shared queues, reflecting the additional compute and support guarantees
required to sustain those experiences.
From a product perspective, this is a balancing act between inclusiveness and sustainability.
Free or low-cost access seeds usage and experimentation. Higher tiers support heavy
workflows and justify the additional infrastructure, evaluation, and safety investment.
Context windows, latency, and quotas
Another dimension comes from context windows and latency guarantees. A longer context
window allows users to work with larger documents, longer histories, or richer multimodal
inputs. However, provider documentation makes it clear that long contexts cost more
because both prefill and attention scale with sequence length.
Product tiers often reflect this through the following:
Different maximum document sizes or number of files per session
Limits on conversation length before requiring a reset, especially on lower tiers
Latency and availability commitments, where enterprise plans receive stronger
performance and support guarantees
Quotas and rate limits also play an important role in tier design. Products may impose daily
or monthly token limits for individual users, per-minute rate limits for API-style usage, and
separate usage pools for experimental or resource-intensive features. The performance
metrics introduced earlier in this chapter become design tools here: we can decide, for
instance, that a “Pro” tier targets P95 TTFT under one second for most chat flows, while a
free tier may tolerate higher tail latency during peaks.
Aligning pricing with value
Finally, AI products must align pricing with perceived value, not just technical cost.
Research and industry experience suggest that users are more willing to pay for outcomes
and capabilities than for raw tokens or API calls. This leads to several sustainable patterns.
Teams often bundle AI features into workflows that directly save time or improve quality,
such as drafting contracts, summarizing meetings, or reconciling financial records.
Integrated assistants inside existing products are frequently offered on a per-seat basis,
where the value is framed around productivity gains rather than metered usage. Pure usage-
based or token-based pricing is typically reserved for developer and platform offerings,
where customers are already accustomed to consumption-based models and can map cost
directly to application traffic.
Throughout, transparency remains important. This includes clear explanations of what is
included in each tier, what models and limits apply, and how data is handled reduce
surprises and build trust, particularly in enterprise sales cycles. Clear limits and clear value
definitions also reduce support burden, because customers can predict when the assistant
will be fast, grounded, and capable, and when it will be constrained.
The role of the product manager in
AI-native development
As products become AI-native, the product manager moves closer to the center of the
system. The product manager is no longer only prioritizing feature backlogs and optimizing
funnels; they now connect model capabilities to concrete business outcomes, align technical
constraints such as latency and data readiness with user expectations, and steer cross-
functional governance around safety and compliance.
Studies of AI transformations show that organizations capture significantly more value
when AI is treated as a managed product capability that spans strategy, operating model,
data, and adoption, not just as a technical pilot. At the same time, research on AI product
roles finds that AI product managers still share the core responsibilities of traditional
product managers, but add deeper work on data, model risk, and human AI collaboration.
In this section, we will view AI-native product management through four lenses. Let’s dive
in!
Identifying opportunities with
measurable value
The first responsibility of the AI-native product manager is to distinguish real opportunities
from hype. Research on AI product management emphasizes that AI product managers
perform all the usual discovery tasks, but also ask a harder question: “Is this a problem AI
can truly solve better, or are we adding AI because it is fashionable?”
We can frame AI opportunities using three dimensions:
Outcome quality: Does AI allow us to generate higher-quality outcomes than existing
tools? For example, a code assistant might reduce defects and increase test coverage by
catching issues early and suggesting stronger patterns. A claims summarizer could
generate more consistent and structured medical summaries than manual drafting,
improving clarity and auditability. Similarly, a customer support assistant might
increase first contact resolution rates by surfacing relevant knowledge and drafting
more accurate responses in real time.
Effort and cost: Does AI reduce the effort to achieve a given outcome? For instance,
McKinsey reports that generative AI can materially shorten time to market for software
products when used to draft specifications, interfaces, and test cases, which reduces
cycle time for product managers and engineers.
Risk profile: Does AI meaningfully lower operational or strategic risk? This can
happen when AI helps detect anomalies earlier, screen for policy violations, or
improve documentation quality in regulated workflows.
Guides on identifying and scaling AI use cases recommend starting from existing journeys
and pain points, then asking where AI can remove friction or amplify expertise rather than
designing from models outward.
A practical pattern for product managers is to articulate a clear value hypothesis for each
potential AI feature. For example, a team might state that adding an LLM-powered assistant
to the analytics tool will reduce the time analysts spend writing SQL by 30 percent while
maintaining or improving query correctness. Another hypothesis might propose that
introducing AI summarization for call center transcripts will allow supervisors to review 50
percent more cases per day without reducing satisfaction scores. Each hypothesis should
clearly define the outcome being improved, whether time, quality, or coverage, identify the
user segment affected, and specify both a baseline metric and a realistic expected
improvement range.
Empirical reports on AI adoption show that organizations that focus on smaller, measurable
wins rather than ambitious but vague AI projects tend to succeed more often and build
confidence for larger initiatives.
Scoping for capabilities, data
readiness, and latency expectations
Industry guides on AI product strategy stress that product managers need a working grasp
of model classes, typical failure modes, and alignment constraints in order to scope realistic
features and avoid overpromising. Once an opportunity looks promising, the product
manager must determine whether it is technically and operationally feasible. That requires a
grounded understanding of three elements: model capabilities and limitations, data
availability and readiness, as well as latency and reliability expectations for the target
journey. Let’s understand each of these elements more deeply.
Capabilities
The product manager does not choose the exact architecture, but must align model
capabilities with the intended use case. For example, if a feature requires precise
calculations or legally sensitive language, it will likely demand a high-quality model
combined with grounding mechanisms and human approval steps. In contrast, if the goal is
to generate rough suggestions or support brainstorming, a lighter model with lower cost and
latency may be sufficient.
Scoping documents can include a capability envelope for each feature:
Supported task families, such as summarization, question-answering, or code
completion
Explicit non-goals, such as “will not provide tax advice” or “will not make final credit
decisions”
Required integration types, such as RAG over internal documents, tool calling, or
multi-agent orchestration
Data readiness
AI guides from OpenAI and others emphasize that high-impact use cases depend on clean,
accessible data and robust pipelines more than on model novelty. For each feature, the
product manager should work with data and engineering leads to answer questions such as
the following:
What data sources are required? Are they already collected in a structured form?
Are there ownership, privacy, or regulatory constraints on using that data in prompts or
training?
How often does the data change, and how fresh must it be?
Can we construct ground-truth or high-quality labels for evaluation?
AI product guides frequently note that data issues are the main blocker for shipping AI
features at scale, more so than model performance.
Latency and reliability
In an earlier section, we introduced TTFT, token generation time, and end-to-end latency.
For AI-native products, product manager scoping must include explicit latency targets.
Otherwise, we risk designing journeys that feel impressive in demos but frustrating in
production.
Here are some examples:
A customer chat assistant might target TTFT under 0.8 seconds and P95 end-to-end
latency under 4 seconds, with streaming enabled
A batch document summarization job might tolerate higher latency per document, but
needs predictable throughput and cost for thousands of files
Provider documentation and user experience guidance for copilots consistently emphasize
matching interaction patterns to latency budgets. For example, Microsoft’s user experience
guidance suggests different surfaces for immersive copilots versus embedded assistants and
highlights streaming and progressive disclosure when responses take longer.
The product manager should collaborate with engineering to translate these budgets into
concrete requirements, then feed them into design discussions on model choice, caching,
and infrastructure.
Once feasibility is clear, the next challenge is sustained execution across functions, which is
where cross-functional ownership becomes the core operating system.
Cross-functional ownership
AI-native products cut across traditional boundaries. A product manager who treats AI work
as a local project within a single engineering team will quickly run into friction.
McKinsey’s work on AI transformations describes successful programs as those that align
strategy, operating model, data, and risk management across business and technology
stakeholders. Responsible AI playbooks from Microsoft and academic institutions likewise
stress that AI systems need clear roles across legal, security, compliance, and operations.
For an AI-native feature, a product manager typically coordinates at least the following
partners:
Engineering and ML: Responsible for model selection, serving architecture,
observability, and incident response
Data and analytics: Own data pipelines, labeling strategies, evaluation harnesses, and
reporting
Design and research: Shape prompts, flows, affordances, safety messaging, and user
education
Security and privacy: Define boundaries around data use, storage, access control, and
vendor risk
Compliance and legal: Translate regulations and internal policies into product rules,
disallowed use cases, approvals, and documentation
Operations and support: Handle escalations, user feedback loops, and training for
frontline staff who interact with AI outputs
The product manager’s role is not to replace these functions but to hold a coherent view of
the AI system as a product. That means the following:
Maintaining a “policy of record” for the feature: supported use cases, disallowed
intents, and risk tolerances
Keeping a shared map of dependencies and ownership, for instance, which group
approves changes to prompts, guardrails, or data sources
Coordinating decision-making when trade-offs span teams, for example, choosing
between a faster but less interpretable model and a slower but more transparent one
Table 13.2 exemplifies how a product manager may monitor ownership among the various
functions in the product development life cycle.
Responsible AI standards, including the Microsoft Responsible AI Standard, suggest that
product leaders document how principles such as fairness, reliability, privacy, and
transparency are implemented at the system level. AI-native product managers can treat that
guidance as a checklist mapped to concrete product behaviors and governance processes.
