Metrics and experiments for AI-
enhanced journeys
Finally, AI-native product managers must prove that AI improves real journeys. Adoption
alone is not enough. Surveys show that while a large majority of organizations report using
AI in at least one function, a much smaller fraction see material impact on earnings or core
KPIs.
We can group AI metrics into four layers:
Usage and adoption: This includes the number of active users engaging with the AI
feature, the frequency and depth of AI usage within existing workflows, and the share
of tasks completed through AI-assisted paths compared with non-AI alternatives.
Task-level outcomes: This layer includes success rates for AI-assisted sessions versus
non-assisted sessions, time required to complete tasks, and operational indicators such
as error rates, escalation rates, or rework rates. Microsoft’s AI leadership has described
tracking a “successful sessions rate” for Copilot, defined as the share of sessions where
users achieve their goals, derived from feedback and sentiment analysis. This is a
concrete example of a task-level outcome metric that goes beyond raw usage.
Business outcomes: These metrics should capture tangible outcomes such as revenue
growth, conversion improvements, or upsell performance directly linked to AI-enabled
features. They may also include cost savings from automation or reduced manual
effort, as well as portfolio optimization gains when AI supports better assortment,
pricing, or configuration decisions.
Risk and safety outcomes: This includes the frequency and severity of safety
incidents, such as policy violations or harmful outputs, rates of hallucination detected
by validation layers or reported by users, and any compliance exceptions or regulatory
findings associated with the AI system.
Case studies of AI adoption in customer journeys highlight the importance of continuous
experimentation, such as ongoing A/B tests for AI-driven recommendations, copy, and
flows. Product managers should treat AI behaviors as hypothesis-driven experiments, not as
fixed features.
A typical experiment design for an AI enhancement can include the following:
A clear primary metric, such as reduction in average handle time or increase in self-
serve resolution
Guardrail metrics, such as satisfaction scores, error rates, or safety incident counts
A control group without the AI intervention or with a simpler baseline
Sufficient duration and sample size to observe stable effects
Generative AI appears particularly powerful when integrated into existing workflows rather
than as a separate destination, but the impact depends on how well those workflows are
measured and tuned.
In the next section, we extend that idea further by showing how the build process itself
adapts when AI becomes part of day-to-day engineering work.
How the build process itself adapts
to AI
The previous sections focused on how products evolve in structure and performance when
LLMs enter the picture. In parallel, the build process itself is changing. The software
development life cycle is no longer only a sequence of human-driven steps that occasionally
call a model. Planning, design, implementation, testing, and maintenance are increasingly
co-produced by humans and LLMs working together across the toolchain.
In this section, we look at five places where the build process is already adapting. We keep
the emphasis on practical patterns for teams that ship AI-native products rather than on
speculative future practices.
AI-driven code generation and
refactoring
Code assistants are the most visible way in which AI has entered the build process. Tools
such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Amazon CodeWhisperer, and similar offerings from
JetBrains and cloud providers provide in-editor suggestions ranging from small line
completions to entire functions and scaffolds.
Research across several studies reports significant speedups for certain tasks. A controlled
experiment run by GitHub and Microsoft showed that developers implementing an HTTP
server in JavaScript with access to GitHub Copilot completed the task around 55 percent
faster than the control group without AI assistance. Other field and survey studies report
that AI coding assistants are used across tasks such as implementing new features, writing
tests, triaging bugs, and refactoring. At the same time, systematic reviews highlight that the
gains are uneven and depend on task type, developer expertise, and integration into the
workflow.
From a product engineering perspective, the important shift is not any single tool. The shift
is that meaningful parts of the code base are now the output of a model. That changes how
we plan, review, and evolve software.
Common patterns for AI-driven code generation include the following:
Boilerplate and glue code: HTTP handlers, data transfer objects, ORM entity
definitions, and framework wiring are often straightforward to generate from function
signatures, OpenAPI contracts, or short natural language prompts.
Scaffolding and project setup: Given a target framework and a description of the
product slice we want to build, LLMs can scaffold folders, sample modules,
configuration files, and CI stubs. This is especially useful when exploring new stacks
or spinning up internal tools.
Example-driven implementation: When we have one or two clear examples of a
pattern, we can ask the model to replicate it for additional endpoints, event handlers, or
data transformations. In that sense, we turn existing code into a prompt that defines
local style and conventions.
Refactoring and migration: Recent work on refactoring with LLMs combines
structural program representations such as control flow graphs and abstract syntax
trees with natural language prompts, in order to propose refactorings or migrate code
across APIs. This blends static analysis with generative models: the tool identifies a
refactoring opportunity and the model proposes concrete code edits.
For AI-native products, these uses shorten iteration cycles on features that touch LLM
interactions themselves. We can adjust prompt formats, instrumentation hooks, or guardrail
wiring and let the assistant apply similar changes across tens of call sites.
As code generation becomes routine, teams adopt patterns to keep control:
Prompt-as-contract for code: Prompts for code generation are treated as structured
contracts. For instance, a team may standardize on prompts that explicitly specify
logging, error handling, and telemetry requirements. This reduces variation between
model calls and makes generated code easier to review.
Explicit boundaries for AI edits: Some teams reserve certain layers as human-owned,
such as core domain logic or safety-critical routines, and restrict AI assistants to
peripheral layers such as adapters and presentation code. This mirrors how we draw
architectural boundaries for third-party libraries.
Refactoring through small, safe steps: Research highlights that AI-generated
refactorings can be brittle when they touch many files at once. A practical pattern is to
ask the model to generate proposals in natural language or as pseudo-diffs, then apply
them incrementally with tests after each step.
Pairing human expertise and model suggestions: Studies on real projects suggest
that productivity gains are highest when experienced developers use AI assistants to
offload mechanical work while still driving design decisions. That framing is
important culturally. The assistant is not a replacement for senior judgment; it is a
power tool that amplifies it.
Specification drafting with LLMs
Specification work was historically a text-heavy activity that depended on templates,
stakeholder interviews, and manual editing. LLMs fit this space naturally since they can
consume natural language descriptions, examples, and existing documents, then produce
structured drafts such as Software Requirements Specifications (SRSs), Product
Requirement Documents (PRDs), and user stories.
Empirical work on using LLMs for SRS drafting shows that modern models can produce
coherent, well-structured drafts that follow standard templates when given a reasonable
description of the system. A 2024 study on using LLMs in SRS documents found that
models reduce the time required to create initial drafts and help surface ambiguities,
although human validation remains essential.
In practice, we see several patterns emerge:
From free-form notes to structured SRS: A product manager or architect collects
unstructured notes from stakeholder interviews and domain documents. They then ask
an LLM to synthesize a first SRS draft that separates functional requirements, non-
functional requirements, assumptions, and open questions.
Design option exploration: Given a target capability, such as “document-centric RAG
search for internal policies,” we can ask the model to propose several architecture
sketches, trade-offs, and risk lists. This does not replace architecture review, but it
expands the option space early and surfaces assumptions that need validation.
Requirements query and consistency checks: Systematic reviews of LLMs for
requirements engineering describe tools that classify requirements, detect
contradictions, and generate UML-style representations from text. For AI-native
products, this can also include checks that requirements explicitly mention latency
targets, safety constraints, and observability needs introduced in earlier sections of the
chapter.
Specification-to-artifact pipelines: Some teams connect requirement repositories to
LLM-powered tools that can generate related artifacts: user stories for agile boards,
test case outlines, or high-level sequence diagrams. Research prototypes show that
LLMs can transform textual requirements into structured task flows or models,
although procedural correctness still requires human review.
The key shift is that specification writing becomes a high-leverage “prompting” activity. We
spend more time clarifying intent, constraints, and examples, and less time on repetitive
formatting.
Test creation and automation with
LLMs
Testing is another area where LLMs are already changing the build process. There is now a
growing body of work on using LLMs to generate unit tests, integration tests, and scenario-
based tests.
A 2023 study on automated unit test generation for JavaScript evaluated a tool called
TestPilot built on gpt-3.5-turbo. With only function signatures, implementations, and usage
examples as input, the generated tests achieved median statement coverage above 70
percent and branch coverage above 50 percent, substantially higher than a traditional
feedback-directed testing baseline. More recent empirical studies across multiple languages
and open source LLMs confirm that models can generate high-coverage unit tests when
guided by appropriate prompts and light static analysis.
Industry blogs and case studies report similar patterns in real systems. For example, IBM’s
ASTER project shows that LLM prompting combined with program analysis and mocking
can generate “natural” tests for Java and Python that cover complex interactions with
external dependencies. An AWS case study on automotive software testing demonstrates a
workflow where requirements exported from a management system are fed to an LLM-
based service that generates candidate test cases, which are then reviewed and imported into
existing test tools.
In the context of AI-native products, we can distinguish several uses:
Unit tests for pure functions and adapters: For deterministic components such as
parsers, format converters, or feature calculators, LLMs can propose unit tests that
cover edge cases and boundary conditions. We can treat these as suggestions and refine
them in code review.
Integration tests around LLM interactions: For features that call LLMs, tests are
often scenario-based. The model can help produce input payloads and expected shapes
of responses, as well as negative scenarios such as malformed prompts or missing
context. Actual text equality is usually brittle, so we focus on structural assertions and
downstream behavior.
Test mechanisms from specifications: When paired with the specification workflows
in the prior subsection, tests become another derivative of requirements. Given a well-
structured SRS, models can propose test cases that ensure each requirement has at least
one associated test.
Test maintenance during refactoring: When we change APIs or refactor modules,
test updates can be repetitive. LLMs can assist in transforming existing tests to new
APIs, updating mocks, or aligning test data formats. This is especially useful when
deprecating legacy REST endpoints in favor of event-driven or streaming interfaces.
Despite these capabilities, studies consistently emphasize that generated tests can contain
incorrect assertions, redundant coverage, or false assumptions about external systems. That
means we must treat them as draft material to be validated by human reviewers and by
running tests against real systems. The practical takeaway is to treat test generation as
acceleration for coverage and scaffolding, while keeping expected behavior anchored in
domain rules and trusted baselines.
Impact on development velocity,
staffing, and cost
Once AI tools touch code, specifications, and tests, they inevitably affect team structure and
economics. Controlled experiments with GitHub Copilot report speedups of around 55
percent for specific coding tasks. Field studies in enterprise settings find more modest yet
substantial productivity gains, on the order of 20 to 30 percent for certain categories of
work, along with higher perceived satisfaction among developers who adopt AI tools.
At the same time, surveys of hundreds of programmers show that effects are not uniform.
Developers report the largest perceived benefits when using AI tools for boilerplate and
routine tasks, and smaller or even negative effects when working on complex or unfamiliar
code bases. Systematic reviews of LLMs for software engineering highlight concerns about
over-reliance, erosion of skills, and increased cognitive load when suggestions conflict with
a developer’s understanding.
For leaders responsible for AI-native products, several patterns emerge:
Velocity composition, not a single “x percent faster”: Rather than asking “how
much faster is our team,” it is useful to break work into components such as design,
coding, testing, and review. AI tools may double the speed of certain coding tasks
while having a smaller impact on architecture or incident response. We can then target
investments where the gap between current and desired throughput is largest.
Staffing mix and role evolution: As AI handles more mechanical coding and test
scaffolding, teams can shift the mix of skills. For example, we may place a larger
emphasis on product-minded engineers who can translate ambiguous domain problems
into well-specified tasks for both humans and models. There is early evidence that AI
tools reduce the time spent on repetitive coding and free capacity for higher-level
work, though rigorous longitudinal data is still emerging.
Cost models for AI-enhanced development: The direct costs of AI tooling now
include per-seat licenses for coding assistants and per-token or per-call costs for LLM
APIs used in CI, documentation generation, or test creation. These costs are offset by
reduced engineering time on specific tasks and potentially shorter cycle time to deliver
features. Several industry guides propose ROI frameworks that compare license and
API costs against metrics such as time to merge, defect rates, and developer
satisfaction.
Specialized expertise in AI tooling: Many organizations introduce AI enablement
roles or guilds that focus on prompt patterns, internal tooling, and measurement. These
specialists help the rest of the team use assistants effectively, maintain internal prompt
libraries, and monitor usage against legal and compliance requirements, for example,
around source code origin.
AI-native products amplify these dynamics because the product code base itself often
contains prompts, evaluation harnesses, and guardrails. That makes development tooling
choices a product risk decision, because they directly influence how reliably the team can
evolve prompts, policies, and evaluation over time. Investing in effective AI-assisted
development directly impacts both the build process and the user-facing experience.
Quality considerations in AI-assisted
development
Speed gains come with new risks. When code, specifications, and tests are partially
generated by a model, quality assurance must adapt. Several systematic surveys and
position papers on LLMs for software engineering note that generated artifacts can be
syntactically correct yet semantically wrong, and that non-determinism in model outputs
complicates reproducibility and debugging.
In AI-native products, these concerns are especially acute because the boundary between
application logic and AI interaction is thin. A mistake in a prompt template or a missing
guardrail can show up directly in the user experience. Key considerations include the
following:
Correctness and hidden defects:
AI-generated code tends to look fluent and well formatted, which can give reviewers
a false sense of security. Studies on code generation with LLMs show that while
many suggestions compile and pass basic tests, subtle bugs and security issues still
appear at non-trivial rates, especially in edge cases or when domain knowledge is
required. This reinforces the need for robust test suites and domain expert review.
Specification drift and ambiguity:
When LLMs help draft and evolve specifications, there is a risk that changes implied
by generated text are not fully understood by stakeholders. Requirements engineering
research highlights that LLM-generated specs may introduce or mask ambiguities,
and that systematic validation techniques are needed. Practical mitigations include
traceability matrices that link each generated requirement back to the original
stakeholder input and to associated tests.
Test quality and expected outcome reliability:
Test generation studies report high coverage but also note that some generated tests
encode incorrect expected behavior or overfit to the current implementation. If we
treat generated tests as ground truth, we may lock in bugs. A healthier pattern is to
combine generated tests with clear expected outcomes derived from domain rules,
external specifications, or golden datasets.
Non-determinism and change management:
Because LLM outputs can vary across runs, seemingly small prompt or context
changes can alter generated code or documentation. This complicates code review
and incident analysis. Teams mitigate this by doing the following:
Pinning model versions for build pipelines
Capturing prompts and significant model outputs in version control
Using deterministic evaluation harnesses where the model under test is treated as
a black box while inputs and expected properties remain stable
Ethics, security, and compliance:
Finally, adopting AI assistants in development raises questions that connect back to
the guardrail chapter. For example, we need policies on using AI tools with
proprietary or regulated code, on attribution and license compliance for generated
snippets, and on avoiding leakage of secrets in prompts. Surveys of practitioners
stress the importance of clear organizational guidelines and training as conditions for
safe adoption.
From a process standpoint, the main principle is that AI assistance increases the need for
disciplined engineering rather than replacing it. Clear specifications, versioned prompts,
comprehensive tests, and observability become even more important when a generative
model participates in the build. With the build process updated, we can now expand our
discussion to an evolving domain in the LLM-driven products.
Running LLMs on smaller and edge
devices
So far in this chapter, we have treated LLMs as server-side infrastructure. In practice, a
growing share of AI-native experiences run on devices that sit much closer to the user:
phones, laptops, browsers, cars, and embedded controllers. On-device and edge LLMs are
attractive because they promise lower latency, stronger privacy, and reduced bandwidth use.
The constraint is obvious. Edge devices have limited memory, energy, and compute
compared to data center GPUs. This tension drives a wave of work on Small Language
Models (SLMs), extreme quantization, and edge-aware runtimes. Those advances matter
because they shift product decisions from a binary cloud versus local choice into a spectrum
of placements and capability tiers.
In this section, we will explore four questions:
Why run LLMs on devices and at the edge?
How do compression and small models make that feasible?
What runtimes and platforms exist today?
What hybrid patterns and product trade-offs follow?
Why on-device and edge LLMs?
Several drivers keep pushing capabilities closer to the user. These drivers are not
independent, because latency, privacy, and availability often reinforce one another in mobile
and regulated settings:
Latency and responsiveness: Running at least part of the model locally cuts out
network round-trips and congestion. Surveys on mobile edge intelligence for LLMs
highlight latency reduction as a primary motivation for on-device and edge
deployments, especially in conversational and interactive applications. This matters for
the TTFT budgets we discussed earlier. A small local model can often produce a first
token in tens of milliseconds for tasks such as autocomplete or basic suggestions.
Privacy and data locality: Keeping prompts and context on-device reduces the need
to send sensitive information to remote servers. Apple’s Apple Intelligence architecture
is a prominent example. It runs many generative features locally on A17 Pro and M
series chips and uses Private Cloud Compute only when larger models are required.
Analysis of Apple’s strategy notes that it leverages rich personal data, such as photos
and messages, precisely because that data is processed locally whenever possible.
Bandwidth and availability: Edge deployments save bandwidth by avoiding repeated
large requests to the cloud and by caching models near the user. This is important in
constrained networks, such as mobile and industrial settings, and for applications that
must remain functional offline. A recent survey on edge LLMs emphasizes that mobile
edge computing can bridge the gap between cloud-based and purely on-device AI by
placing models at base stations or local gateways.
Regulatory and product control: In some jurisdictions, keeping data within a specific
device or network boundary simplifies compliance. Competitions such as the NeurIPS
Edge-Device LLM Competition showcase the growing interest in measuring what is
possible under strict on-device constraints.
Compressing models for edge
deployment
To fit within device budgets, we need models that are both smaller and more efficient per
parameter. Three families of techniques dominate practice today: quantization, architecture-
level design of small models, and distillation or fine-tuning for narrow tasks. In practice,
teams combine all three because compression alone rarely delivers the quality, memory, and
power profile needed for a production edge experience.
Quantization and low-bit inference
Quantization reduces the number of bits used to represent weights and sometimes
activations. Practical systems often use 8-bit or 4-bit integer formats. A recent Microsoft
research blog on low-bit quantization for edge LLMs describes how reducing bit width
improves memory footprint and energy use while still maintaining competitive accuracy if
done carefully.
Surveys of edge deployment techniques summarize quantization, pruning, and compression
as the primary means to run large models on constrained devices. The key idea is that we
trade some representational precision for much lower memory and compute cost.
A particularly interesting direction is extreme quantization. BitNet b1 and b1.58 are 1-bit
and 1.58-bit LLM architectures in which each weight takes a value in a small discrete set,
for example, {-1, 0, 1}. The JMLR article on BitNet b1 and b1.58 shows that these models
can match or outperform strong 8-bit and FP16 baselines at a much lower energy cost, by
using custom BitLinear layers and efficient integer additions. Microsoft’s bitnet.cpp project
demonstrates that such 1.58-bit models can run efficiently on CPUs and GPUs, and targets
NPU support in the near future.
For product teams, the implication is that bit width is becoming a first-class design variable.
We can choose between 16, 8, 4, or approximately 1.58 bits, depending on the available
hardware and accuracy tolerance.
SLMs and edge-oriented architectures
In parallel, there is a strong line of work on SLMs, which are designed to be efficient from
the start. Microsoft’s Phi family is a good example. Phi-3 and later Phi models are trained
with carefully curated data and architectural choices that allow them to outperform larger
models of similar or even greater size on many language, coding, and math benchmarks.
Microsoft positions Phi models explicitly as candidates for edge and on-device scenarios.
Official documentation notes that Phi models “offer cost effective, high performance AI
solutions at the edge.” Independent evaluations of Phi-3-mini report that it can deliver
performance comparable to GPT 3.5 class models while running on devices with as little as
4 GB of memory, especially when combined with 4-bit quantization.
Similar trends appear with other families, such as Gemma and optimized Llama variants,
which report multi-thousand TPS throughput on mobile GPUs under INT4 quantization.
Distillation and specialization
Even with small and quantized models, we rarely aim for general-purpose capability on
edge devices. Instead, we distill or fine-tune models for narrower roles, such as offline
translation, smart replies, or on-device ranking.
Surveys on edge LLMs emphasize task-specific distillation as a key ingredient. A large
teacher model trains a smaller student that focuses on specific intents, domains, or
languages, enabling better trade-offs between accuracy and resource use.
In practice, this can look as follows:
A small on-device classifier that decides which queries can be handled locally and
which should be escalated to the cloud
A local summarizer tuned on short notification and message content
A speech assistant model trained for a specific language pair and wake word behavior
Runtimes and platforms for local LLMs
Model design is only part of the story. To make edge deployment practical, we also need
runtimes that understand device constraints, exploit hardware accelerators, and expose clean
APIs. This is where the ecosystem has accelerated, turning research prototypes into portable
runtimes and platform services that product teams can adopt with minimal friction.
General-purpose local inference runtimes
The llama.cpp project is one of the best-known examples. Its stated goal is to enable LLM
inference with minimal setup and strong performance on a wide range of hardware, both
locally and in the cloud. llama.cpp supports CPU and GPU backends and quantized weight
formats, and can even distribute inference across multiple machines.
On the BitNet side, bitnet.cpp provides an official inference framework for 1-bit LLMs,
exposing optimized kernels for CPUs and GPUs and aiming to support NPUs. Together,
these projects illustrate a trend toward portable, low-level runtimes that can take advantage
of whatever resources are available.
Platform-specific ecosystems
Major platform vendors increasingly treat on-device LLMs as part of their core OS
offerings:
Apple Intelligence integrates local generative models with A17 Pro and M series
chips and uses Private Cloud Compute only when larger models are needed. Features
such as Writing Tools, image editing, and notification summarization rely on device-
based processing whenever possible. Apple’s roadmap includes opening local models
to third-party developers through an SDK that exposes summarization, rewriting, and
image tools, while keeping heavier cloud models separate.
Browsers and on-device APIs: Microsoft’s Edge browser exposes an on-device
model, Phi-4-mini, through experimental web APIs that allow developers to add text
generation, summarization, and editing to web apps using local compute. This mirrors
similar moves by Google with Gemini Nano in Chrome and on Android, targeting low-
latency AI features without server round-trips.
Mobile edge and gateway platforms: Mobile edge intelligence architectures envision
LLMs running not only on phones but also on base stations and local edge servers that
serve many devices with better latency and privacy than distant clouds.
For teams building AI-native products, this means edge capabilities are increasingly
accessible as platform services rather than as custom deployments. Figure 13.5 captures the
components we discussed for on-device LLM applications.
Figure 13.5: On-device product layers
As you can see, the bottom layer represents the hardware used for running the models, the
middle layer represents the runtime low-level code, and the top layer represents the
applications.
Hybrid edge-cloud patterns
Running all AI locally is rarely optimal. Instead, successful systems combine on-device
models with edge servers and cloud services. Surveys on mobile edge intelligence for
LLMs describe this as a continuum: on-device for privacy and very low latency, mobile
edge for stronger compute near the user, and cloud for the largest models and training
workloads.
We can structure hybrid patterns along three dimensions:
Routing by task complexity:
Simple tasks and low-risk transformations, such as autocomplete, local search,
or formatting, run on-device
Medium-complexity tasks, such as multi-turn summarization or multi-document
comparisons, may run on an edge server or powerful gateway
Heavy or high-risk tasks, such as multimodal reasoning over large archives or
tasks requiring specialized compliance checks, go to the cloud
Routing by privacy sensitivity:
Queries that include personal messages, health data, or highly sensitive business
content can be constrained to on-device or private edge environments
Less sensitive or already-public content can leverage cloud LLMs
Apple Intelligence provides a concrete illustration: it performs many
tasks locally and escalates to dedicated Apple silicon servers only
when necessary, using encrypted Private Cloud Compute.
Routing by resource availability:
When network connectivity is weak, systems fall back to local models
When the device is charging and on Wi-Fi, background tasks may sync with
cloud services, refresh embeddings, or precompute results
From a product standpoint, these patterns need clear user experience signals. Users should
understand when a query is handled locally and when it leaves the device, at least at a high
level. Without that transparency, users cannot calibrate trust, especially when routing
decisions affect both quality and data locality.
Design trade-offs and implications for
AI-native products
Edge and on-device LLMs do not replace cloud models. They add new degrees of freedom
in how we design user journeys, infrastructure, and governance.
Key trade-offs include the following:
Quality versus responsiveness: Small, on-device models will usually lag frontier
cloud models on complex reasoning benchmarks. At the same time, they can meet
much tighter TTFT targets and provide offline behavior. For some tasks, such as basic
drafting and on-device classification, this trade can be attractive. Benchmarks and field
reports on Phi-3-mini and similar SLMs show strong performance when prompts are
designed for their capabilities.
Hardware reach versus feature richness: Features that require NPU-class hardware
will only be available on recent devices. For example, Apple Intelligence is limited to
devices with A17 Pro or M series chips. That means product managers must decide
which capabilities are core to the product and which are “premium on supported
hardware.”
Operational simplicity versus flexibility: Relying on platform APIs for on-device AI
simplifies deployment but gives less control over model versions and configuration.
Running our own quantized models through runtimes such as llama.cpp provides more
control and experimentation room, but increases maintenance, packaging, and security
responsibilities.
Safety and update cadence: When logic runs on-device, updates must propagate
through app or OS releases. We gain privacy and reduced dependency on network
connectivity, but we must plan for how to patch safety issues, update prompts, and
rotate models. Hybrid patterns can mitigate this by keeping sensitive behavior checks
in a central policy service while letting local models handle low-risk tasks.
For AI-native product teams, the main message is that “edge” is now a design axis
alongside “model size,” “RAG depth,” and “multi-agent architecture.” We decide where
intelligence lives, how much of it runs locally, and how we cooperate with platform
ecosystems to deliver responsive, private, and reliable experiences.
Figure 13.6: Performance traits
Figure 13.6 illustrates how the hybrid approach of edge-cloud architecture balances the
characteristics of both individual designs. No single choice dominates all dimensions as
hybrid designs often balance the trade-offs best for AI-native products.
The next step is to translate those placement choices into a repeatable reference architecture
that can be implemented, governed, and observed in production.
Practical architecture patterns
By this point in the chapter, we have seen that AI-native products depend on more than a
single model invocation. We make choices about cloud versus local inference, routing
between models of different sizes, where to place guardrails, and how to observe and
control the system in production.
This section turns those ideas into concrete patterns. We look at when cloud inference
makes the most sense, when local inference is preferable, and how hybrid designs route
between the two. Then, we finish with a blueprint-style walk-through of an end-to-end AI-
native product.
Throughout, we connect back to the metrics from earlier sections: TTFT, token generation
time, goodput, and safety and cost envelopes. Those metrics become the common language
that lets product, engineering, and risk teams evaluate trade-offs across cloud, edge, and on-
device deployments.
When to use cloud inference
Cloud inference remains the backbone of many AI-native products because it provides
access to large models, elastic capacity, and managed infrastructure. One of its primary
strengths is access to frontier and specialized models. Cloud platforms host very large
models that would be difficult or impractical to run on typical enterprise hardware or user
devices, including multi-hundred-billion-parameter systems and specialized variants for
code, vision, or multimodal reasoning. This broad model portfolio is consistently cited as a
key advantage in practitioner guidance.
Cloud infrastructure also offers elastic scalability, allowing capacity to expand or contract
as traffic fluctuates. Autoscaling across GPUs and regions helps absorb peak demand
without long-term overprovisioning. In addition, managed services offload operational
burdens such as patching, model hosting, scaling, and safety updates, enabling product
teams to focus on prompts, data integration, and user experience rather than cluster
management. Finally, cloud APIs provide consistent behavior across mobile, web, and
backend clients, which is often simpler than embedding and maintaining separate on-device
models for each platform.
Cloud inference is a good default in the following cases:
We need the highest-quality reasoning, coding, or multimodal understanding
We must support large context windows, such as 128k or more tokens, for complex
RAG or multi-document tasks
We want to centralize safety, logging, and governance around a small number of model
endpoints
We can tolerate network latency in the expected journeys
For example, reference architectures for enterprise chat with Azure OpenAI and similar
services place a secure entry point, retrieval tier, and agent service in front of large cloud
models. Performance guides, such as Amazon Bedrock’s latency optimization posts, focus
on how to keep TTFT and tail latencies acceptable even while calling large models, by
using strategies such as streaming, right-sizing model selection, and caching prompts and
completions.
Cloud inference is also the natural place for batch workloads. For example, overnight
summarization of thousands of documents or large-scale evaluation jobs across many
prompts are easier to run in cloud environments that can schedule GPU time efficiently.
When to use local inference
Local inference was the focus of the previous section. Here, we revisit it briefly from the
perspective of architecture decision-making. When we say “local,” we include both on-
device models and models deployed very close to the user, such as in a branch office or
factory.
Comparative analyses of on-device and cloud AI consistently highlight a few core benefits
of local processing. One of the most visible advantages is lower latency and tighter TTFT.
On-device AI can avoid round-trips to remote servers and provide instant responses for
tasks such as autocomplete, AR filters, or voice assistants. Another key benefit is privacy
and data locality. Local processing avoids sending raw data to external servers, which
strengthens privacy guarantees and simplifies compliance. Apple’s Private Cloud Compute
design, for instance, keeps many Apple Intelligence features entirely on-device and only
sends encrypted data to dedicated servers when a larger model is required.
Local deployment also supports offline and degraded connectivity scenarios. Local models
keep core features available even when the network is weak or unavailable. This matters for
travel, field work, and industrial environments, and industry articles on on-device AI
consistently stress offline functionality as a key reason to invest in local models.
Finally, there is the economic dimension. Once a local model is deployed to a device, there
is a marginal cost per inference, essentially just for power and wear. This can be attractive
compared to per-token cloud pricing, especially for frequent micro interactions such as
typing suggestions.
Local inference is often the right choice in the following cases:
The task is latency sensitive and lightweight, for example, local ranking, predictive
text, quick summarizations of local content, or intent classification
The data is highly sensitive, such as personal photos, messages, or health information,
and policies strongly favor on-device processing
Connectivity is unreliable or expensive
The platform vendor already provides strong on-device models that we can call
through an SDK, such as Apple Intelligence or small models integrated into browsers
Architecturally, local inference often appears as a library or system API within the
application process. Instead of sending a prompt to a remote endpoint, we call into a local
runtime such as llama.cpp or a platform AI framework, which then uses CPU, GPU, or
NPU resources on the device.
When to combine both
Most AI-native products land in the middle. They use small or specialized models locally
and rely on cloud models when tasks are complex or high-stakes or require heavy compute.
Research on hybrid edge-cloud LLM systems and model routing shows that this
combination can deliver cost savings and latency improvements while maintaining high
accuracy.
We can think about hybrid designs along three axes.
Routing by complexity and confidence
Hybrid LLM research describes patterns where a small local model handles easy parts of
the workload and escalates more difficult inputs to a cloud model. Here is an example:
A small device model classifies requests into categories or estimates difficulty
If confidence is high and the task is simple, the system returns a local answer
If confidence is low or the task appears complex, the request is sent to a larger cloud
model
The Hybrid Edge-Cloud Resource Allocation (HERA) framework shows that such
routing can offload around 45 percent of subtasks to a small model while maintaining
accuracy comparable to a cloud-only baseline. Other model routing approaches use data-
augmented features and performance histories to decide which model to call, improving
cost and latency trade-offs in enterprise deployments.
Routing by privacy and policy
Hybrid designs also help express privacy and regulatory constraints. Sensitive queries can
be restricted to on-device or private edge processing, while non-sensitive queries can
benefit from powerful cloud models.
Apple’s Private Cloud Compute is a clear example. Apple runs many Apple Intelligence
features locally and routes more demanding tasks to dedicated servers that use strong
privacy protections and hardware isolation. Google’s Private AI Compute initiative follows
a similar pattern, providing a space where cloud processing can augment on-device models
while keeping data opaque to operators.
In enterprise settings, policies might state that certain data classes never leave a particular
region or network boundary. A hybrid architecture lets us enforce that through routing rules
and gateway policies, while still calling external models for less sensitive traffic.
Routing by resource and experience
Finally, hybrid patterns respond to varying device and network conditions:
When the device is powerful and the network is weak, more work is done locally
When the device is constrained and the network is strong, the product leans on cloud
models
When the model quota or cost budget is tight, more queries are handled by cheaper
local or edge models, with routing logic preserving quality where it matters most
Tools and services are emerging to make this routing easier. For example, Requesty’s
routing platform and similar products advertise “smart routing” across on-device, edge, and
cloud models in order to optimize cost and performance.
Figure 13.7: Policies updated over time with real performance and safety data
Example blueprint for an AI-native
product
To make these patterns concrete, we will close with a blueprint for an AI-native product that
combines cloud, local inference, RAG, and safety controls. We describe it as a multi-tenant
reference architecture for an enterprise chat assistant, although the same structure appears in
document analysis tools and AI-enhanced SaaS products.
We can think of the system in five layers.
At the top sit the client experiences. These include a web application, a mobile app, and
integrations into tools such as IDEs or office suites. Each client presents a conversational
UI, sometimes combined with traditional controls such as filters and forms, as described in
earlier sections. Clients send user messages and context metadata to the AI gateway over
HTTPS. That metadata may include tenant identifiers, feature flags, and explicit latency or
cost budgets associated with the request.
The AI gateway and policy layer acts as the central entry point for AI traffic. Multiple
vendors describe this pattern as an AI or LLM gateway, a middleware layer that abstracts
underlying models, enforces policies, and provides unified observability. Within the
gateway, we typically find authentication and authorization with tenant-scoped access, rate
limits, and feature flags. We also see input validation and redaction, including checks for
prompt injection, PII filtering, and structural validation of payloads. A routing component
determines whether to use cloud, edge, or local models and selects the specific model based
on policy and performance data. Finally, the gateway performs request shaping,
constructing canonical system prompts, inserting tenant- or role-specific instructions, and
attaching retrieved context. By hiding provider-specific details from clients, the gateway
allows the organization to evolve its model portfolio without requiring changes in client
code.
Behind the gateway sits the retrieval and tools layer. Its responsibilities include RAG
retrieval, where vector search runs over tenant-specific and shared knowledge bases,
followed by ranking and context assembly using the practices discussed in earlier chapters.
This layer also includes business tools and agents that fetch data from internal systems,
perform calculations, or execute workflows. These capabilities can be exposed as callable
tools to the LLM or coordinated through a lightweight agent framework. In addition,
optional safety tools may run separate checks on candidate answers, such as hallucination
detectors, policy classifiers, or citation validators. In some designs, a dedicated agent
service manages this layer, coordinating tool calls and composing a response before
handing it back to the gateway for final model interaction.
Below this layer sits the model pool and routing logic. Architects often distinguish
between cloud models for frontier reasoning, code generation, and multimodal tasks; edge
or regional models running in closer proximity to users for lower latency and improved data
locality; and on-device models embedded directly within desktop or mobile clients. Routing
rules determine where each request is sent. A low-risk autocomplete request on a capable
device may use an on-device SLM. A tenant operating under strict regional regulations may
be routed to a regional or private deployment. A large multi-document RAG request may be
directed to a cloud frontier model with a long context window. Research on hybrid LLM
routing and AI gateways offers guidance on optimizing these decisions using historical
performance data and enriched routing features.
Finally, observability and governance tie the entire architecture together. Every request
passing through the gateway emits traces and metrics, often using OpenTelemetry-based
tooling tailored for LLM observability. These traces capture TTFT, total latency, token
counts, cache hits, model selections, and tool invocations. Safety and compliance logs
record which guardrails were triggered, which content was blocked or redacted, and which
policy versions were active at the time. Feedback and evaluation signals, including user
ratings, offline test results, and business metrics, flow back into routing policies, prompt
templates, and model selection decisions. In this way, observability and governance close
the loop described earlier around goodput, performance, and continuous improvement.
Summary
AI-native products are not simply old products with an LLM bolted on top. Throughout this
chapter, we treated LLMs and AI systems more broadly, as first-class parts of the product.
We began by reframing products around capabilities rather than static features. Instead of
asking where to bolt on a chat interface, we asked where a model can remove friction,
amplify expertise, or unlock new workflows. That shift led naturally to conversational
analytics, AI-first search, and assistants embedded inside existing tools. From there, we
made performance concrete. Metrics such as TTFT, token generation time, tail latency, and
goodput changed the conversation from “fast enough” to measurable experience. These
metrics shape model choice, caching strategy, routing logic, and infrastructure design.
We then looked at how systems and organizations evolve around those decisions.
Techniques such as batching, KV cache reuse, and orchestration layers such as LMCache
turned the LLM into engineered infrastructure rather than a black box. Customer-facing
products raised the bar further, making streaming, grounding, hallucination mitigation, and
transparent data use visible parts of the user experience. At the same time, the build process
itself changed. Code generation, specification drafting, and test automation increased
velocity but introduced new failure modes that demand disciplined engineering and clear
policy.
Finally, we extended the discussion to edge and hybrid deployments, where small models,
quantization, and NPUs bring AI closer to the device. Across all of this, one pattern repeats:
AI-native products require a shared mental model that connects user journeys, performance
metrics, safety controls, routing decisions, and governance. Designing with the model in
mind, from the first product sketch to the last telemetry trace, is the core shift this chapter
sought to emphasize.
Questions

does each metric matter for designing AI-native user journeys?

change user perception and interaction patterns compared with non-streamed
responses?
3. In AI-first analytics, what shifts when an organization moves from dashboard-centric
chart galleries to question-first workflows, and what technical mechanisms enable that
shift?
4. What safeguards are required when natural language is compiled into structured
queries, and how do tiered capabilities reduce risk in regulated environments?
5. How does modern enterprise search evolve from keyword-based document retrieval
into RAG-based question answering with evidence, and what new relevance metrics
make quality measurable?
6. Why do AI-generated drafts in regulated workflows require explicit approval flows,
and how do maker-checker and three-lines-of-defense models map into concrete
product checkpoints and audit trails?
7. For customer-facing LLM products, how do grounding, citations, hallucination
mitigation, and transparent data-use controls become visible product behaviors rather
than back-end concerns?
8. Why do AI-native products naturally converge on tiered pricing, and how do model
choice, context limits, quotas, and latency guarantees translate into plan design and
perceived value?
9. How is the software development lifecycle changing as LLMs co-produce code,
specifications, and tests, and what new quality and change-management risks emerge
from non-determinism and generated artifacts?
10. What are the primary trade-offs between cloud, edge, and on-device inference, and
how do hybrid routing policies based on complexity, privacy, and resource conditions
shape a practical end-to-end reference architecture with governance and observability?

Appendix A
Mathematical formulation
of the feasibility test
This appendix provides the full mathematical derivation that underlies the
feasibility test introduced in Chapter 5. The main chapter presents only
the intuition so that the case-study narrative remains focused. Here, we
include the formal equations and probability relationships for readers who
want the complete details.
Independence and conditional
probability
We know that for two random variables, and , if they are statistically
independent, then we get the following:
Alternatively, we get the following:
This happens for every , value that yields a non-zero probability.
Conversely, we could use Bayes’s rules:
Applying the formulation to
binary text features
Now, let’s think about any two random variables that aren’t necessarily
statistically independent. We would like to evaluate whether there is a
statistical relationship between the two.
Let one random variable be any of our numerical features, and the other
random variable be the output class taking on values 0 or 1. Let’s assume
the feature engineering method is binary, so the feature also takes on values
of 0 or 1.
Looking at the last equation, the expression on the left-hand side presents a
very powerful measure of the ability of the relationship between and :
It is powerful because if the feature is completely nonindicative of the class
value, then in statistical terms, we say the two are statistically independent,
and thus this measure would be equal to 1.
Conversely, the bigger the difference between this measure and 1, the
stronger the relationship is between this feature and this class. When
performing a feasibility study of our design, we want to see that there are
features in the data that have a statistical relationship with the output class.
For that reason, we calculate the value of this expression for every pair of
every feature and every class.
We present the most indicative terms for class “0,” which is the class of
tweets that don’t indicate a company or product information, and we also
present the terms that are most indicative of class “1,” meaning, when a
tweet is discussing information about a company or a product.
This proves to us that there are indeed text terms that are indicative of the
class value. This is a definite and clear success of the feasibility study. We
are good to go, and we are expecting productive outcomes when
implementing a classification model.
As a side note, keep in mind that, as with most evaluations, what we’ve just
mentioned is just one sufficient condition for the potential of the text to
predict the class. If it had failed, it would not necessarily indicate that there
is no feasibility. Just like when the linear correlation between and is
near 0, this doesn’t mean that can’t infer . It just means that cannot
infer via a linear model. The linearity is an assumption that’s made to
make things simple if it prevails.
